So, if your concern is SEO/rankings, changing title/meta tags alone is not shown here to matter. For crawler recognition of jQuery changes, this evidence doesn’t answer that directly.

If the page is served as HTML, a meta tag placed at the top will be treated as part of the head and search engines will process it normally. So yes, a robots meta like noindex should work for crawlers in that form.

I can’t say from this alone whether changing title/meta later via jQuery will be honored the same way by all crawlers. The supported guidance here is only that meta tags in the HTML document itself are processed normally; it doesn’t cover crawler behavior for JavaScript-driven changes after load.

Yes, duplicate page titles/meta tags can be a problem, and having multiple pages with the same titles can lead to issues. In your case, because the site is in 3 languages and has duplicate pages, that setup can contribute to repeated store names or titles appearing in Google results.

The closest guidance available is to look into “multiple languages SEO” for the right approach. That would help you avoid duplicate titles/meta data across language versions and reduce related indexing issues.

Google may be ignoring the text in your title tag and instead using the page’s H1 content for the search result title. In the example, Google couldn’t create a title from the Danish in the title tag, so it displayed the H1 text instead, which made it look duplicated or wrong.

The closest guidance supported here is to provide a clearer title, possibly in English for google.com, and use proper multilingual versions of the site if needed.

Google can treat the lowercase and CamelCase versions as separate URLs, which can lead to duplicate title/meta warnings. The guidance supported here is to specify the canonical URL, for example with:

<link rel="canonical" href="/deutschland/Bayern/Camping-Allweglehen-19062">

That tells Google which version to index as the preferred one. The evidence does not show other fixes, but it does indicate that using consistent lowercase URLs would also help prevent crawlers from seeing the same page twice.

Google may not have been able to use the text in your title tag, so it substituted the H1 text instead. That can make the title look duplicated or wrong in search results.

The closest guidance supported here is to make sure your title is clear and usable for Google, possibly in English for google.com, and consider having proper multilingual versions of the site if you serve multiple languages.

Use the alt attribute on the tag. That’s what it’s for, and it can help search engines understand the text content of the image. If you want the actual sentence indexed, add descriptive alt text that matches the image content, for example: If the page is only images, alt text is the closest supported way to provide the text for indexing.

The supported guidance here is to put the text on the page normally, then place the image versions of that same text over it. That way search engines can read the real text while visitors still see the scanned artwork.

The answer also points to a CSS technique for overlaying the image on top of foreground text. It does not say that alt/title text, comments, or hidden JavaScript text are enough for indexing.

Yes, there can be a trade-off. In the basic form described, content loaded only by Ajax on scroll may not be seen or indexed by Google, so it may not appear in search results or Google’s cache. That can affect ranking if the content matters for SEO.

The guidance here is to be careful about what you lazy-load. Use lazy loading for content that is secondary to the user. If the content is important for indexing, make it statically available, make it crawlable with an Ajax-crawling approach, or include it in a sitemap. Also, lazy loading does not necessarily make the page faster overall; the Ajax can still run in the background and may even slow things down.

You can make it public by adding it to your web page, like the example you cited. A more elegant option is to upload it to a public PGP key server and then place a link to that key on your site.

If you want easier maintenance, use the same link in your emails and files so you can update the key in one place.

If your concern is bots, you can add a CAPTCHA to block indexing or use JavaScript to copy the key text between the BEGIN and END blocks.

Making more pages public can help get traffic, because people are more likely to link to them, especially player profiles and possibly some forum threads. That can bring visitors from blogs, other websites, social profiles, or signatures.

It may not help much with search ranking if the links are nofollowed, but it can still attract traffic. Game statistics are less likely to help.

A good approach is to make player profiles easy to share or embed in other pages, in a format people will want to link to.

Search engines can index your site even if it has no visitors yet, so they can still help get a new site discovered. But you’ll likely face competition, so your pages may appear lower at first.

To help people find it, publish good quality content and get connected with other good sites linking to yours. Also, don’t rely on search engines alone—use other media to tell people about the new website.

If you just need a temporary staging setup, the closest guidance here is to use a real domain name and restrict access to it by IP address in your web server settings (for example, Apache). If the temporary `~username` URL already works with your CMS, it may be fine for development, though it’s not ideal. This doesn’t specifically cover creating a staging server on a home machine, but it does support using a private, restricted test site instead of a public temporary URL.

Yes, the supported approach here is to put the section in an iframe and block that iframe URL in robots.txt. That would keep search engines from indexing that separate content, while the rest of the page can still be indexed.

The evidence does not mention a way to mark just one inline section of the same page as “do not index,” so it only supports this iframe-based workaround.

A small number of relevant keywords in the footer is unlikely to cause a penalty, but it’s not a strong SEO practice. Google treats unnatural lists of keywords as keyword stuffing. It’s better to place those keywords in normal, user-focused text on the page, such as instructions or other useful content. So adding footer keywords probably won’t help much for SEO, and if overdone it can look unnatural.

Putting post tags in a footer inside the article is semantically correct and should not cause harm for SEO. The supported guidance says there’s no evidence that Google reduces ranking weight just because links are in a footer, and even if it did, the effect would likely be small. So, using a footer for related tags is fine, but it’s not something that by itself will improve SEO.

“links:www.mysite.com” is not a valid Google search operator, so Google treats “links” like a normal search term. The proper operator is “link:www.mysite.com”.

That said, this only helps you search for pages that link to a site; it is not a reliable way to measure all inbound links. The answer provided doesn’t mention sitelinks or domain-name differences beyond that. If you want to check backlinks, “link:” is the closest supported option here.

Google’s sitelinks are automated, so there isn’t a way to directly choose when they appear for one query variant versus another. The only control mentioned is that you can demote a page from a sitelink for up to 90 days if you don’t want it shown.

So, for “G2 Builder” vs. “G2 Builders,” the supported answer is that Google decides separately for each search and doesn’t offer a manual fix to force sitelinks on both.

The issue may be that the site isn’t easy for standard parsers to read, not robots.txt. A crawler was able to visit the site, but sitemap generators and other parsers may stop after the first page if the HTML is not well formed.

The suggested fix is to validate the site with a W3C validator and correct the markup. The reported problems included no DOCTYPE, an unknown root element, and other HTML errors. Making the site W3C-compliant should help sitemap tools crawl it properly.

No, if a sitemap has already been submitted or discovered, you generally do not need to resubmit it every time it changes. Google will periodically reload it to check for updates. You can also list the Sitemap URL in robots.txt so search engines can find it automatically. If you want faster discovery after changes, you can notify search engines using the sitemap protocol’s “ping” URL.

Yes, this approach should work. Google can merge multiple sitemaps and generally ignores duplicate entries, so submitting an extra sitemap containing just the homepage should not cause a problem.

The only downside is maintenance: it’s better to fix the sitemap generator so the homepage is included automatically, since that’s simpler and less error-prone long term.

No. If you want a bot to follow every link, robots.txt is not needed for that, and sitemap.xml is not required either. The provided guidance only shows robots.txt being used to control which user agents may access a site, and it includes a sitemap line as an extra pointer.

If your goal is simply “let the bot crawl everything,” the closest supported setup is to avoid blocking it in robots.txt. A sitemap can still help discovery, but it isn’t necessary for following links.

No, you do not need a robots.txt if you want bots to crawl everything. If it’s missing, that is generally interpreted as allowing all content to be crawled. A blank robots.txt is still recommended by the answer quoted, mainly to avoid unnecessary 404 errors in your stats.

This does not say anything about sitemap.xml.

An XML sitemap isn’t strictly required, but it can help Google discover and crawl pages if your site is meant to be indexed. The issue described is not about the sitemap format itself; it means Googlebot can’t reach your robots.txt, so the problem is likely on the hosting/server side. If your social network should appear in search results, make sure robots.txt and sitemap.xml are publicly accessible, or ask your hoster why requests are being dropped.

An XML sitemap is for web crawlers, not something you insert into an HTML page. It should be a separate XML file on your server. You can also use a plain text sitemap with one absolute URL per line, though it has no metadata.

To help crawlers find it, reference the sitemap in your robots.txt. You can also submit it manually through Google’s Webmaster Tools.

Whether a social network needs one isn’t directly covered here, but if you want crawlers to discover your public URLs, this is the supported way to provide it.

An XML sitemap is meant to point to all pages you want search engines to discover, not just entry pages. For a social network, that would generally include the pages you want indexed, though the evidence does not say whether every user/profile/post page is required.

If you want a proper sitemap that updates automatically, use Google’s sitemap guidance as a starting point. You can also create one with an online tool. If the sitemap is large, the evidence suggests using the sitemap format’s priority tag and keeping in mind sitemap/page size limits.

If you use a sitemap index file, Google says you only need to submit one HTTP request for the sitemap index itself, not each sitemap listed in it. If your index includes correct lastmod values, Googlebot should be able to tell which sitemap changed and avoid reloading the others.

So to encourage indexing of all records, submit or ping the sitemap-index.xml, and make sure the updated sitemap and lastmod dates are correct. If you want to verify behavior, check your access logs to see which sitemap files Google actually fetches.

You can’t make Google index every sitemap URL. A sitemap only helps Google discover pages; Google still decides whether to index them.

If only some URLs are indexed, the supported explanation here is that the others may not be considered worth indexing because of thin content, duplicate content, poor content, or similar issues. Google may also already find pages through normal crawling, and still choose not to index them.

So the closest guidance is: make sure the pages are unique, useful, and crawlable, and use the sitemap as a discovery aid rather than a guarantee of indexing.

If you’re trying to acquire a legacy domain, the closest thing to a historical record is a service like whois.sc, which can show past registration information if you pay for historical access. From that history, you’d want to look for prior owner information and when transfers happened, since that’s the kind of change-over record the question describes. The evidence doesn’t give a broader checklist beyond that.

Look for signs of prior use and possible penalties. The main caution is that if the domain was used in a way that violated search engine terms, it may be hard to get it indexed or ranking well later. In practice, it’s often difficult to know much about how an expired domain was previously used, so history can be hard to verify.

If the domain has known traffic, that’s more useful. A common approach is to use a 301 redirect to your main domain so you can capture traffic without hosting content on the potentially penalized domain.

Look for signs of past spam or algorithmic issues in the domain’s history, especially paid link networks or other sketchy links, since Panda/Penguin were algorithmic and not manual actions. All current manual actions would still show in Webmaster Tools even if they started under a previous owner. Also check whether any old settings could affect the domain after the move, especially URL parameter handling and geotargeting. If you find problematic links, removing them or disavowing them is the supported approach. Changes may still take time to recrawl, reindex, and reflect in rankings.

To submit a sitemap to Google, the best-supported guidance here is to sign up for Google Webmaster Tools / Google Search Console and add your sitemap there. You can also list it in your robots.txt file, for example:

Sitemap: http://www.mysite.com/sitemap.xml

The text also mentions a Google ping utility, but says it assumes a webmaster tools account and that ping utilities seem to have fallen out of favor.

You don’t need a separate sitemap for the blog. One sitemap can include pages from different parts of your site, and search engines generally only care about the final pages, not what software generated them.

So if your current Magento sitemap already includes the blog article URLs, Google can pick them up from that. A separate sitemap would mainly be for your own organization, not for SEO.

If you do create another sitemap, the supported guidance here doesn’t explain the submission steps.

If you want Google Search Console to report on your sitemap and show errors/index status, you need to submit it there. A sitemap just uploaded to your server root is not enough by itself.

You can also point search engines to it in robots.txt, for example:

Sitemap: http://example.com/sitemap.xml

That may help Google find it, but it won’t appear in Search Console reports unless you submit it there.

Yes, it can happen in the sense that competitors may be able to cause a penalty if they point a redirected penalized site at your domain. The evidence says you could “redirect your domain to a competitor and get them penalized.”

It also says a penalty follows a redirection, so redirecting a penalized site to a new domain won’t fix the problem. The closest guidance supported here is to remove unnatural/paid links and, if needed, submit a reconsideration request.

Yes, it’s possible for someone to try to hurt your rankings by pointing suspicious, low-quality backlinks at your site with exact-match anchor text. The evidence says Google may detect those unnatural linking patterns and issue a warning, such as in Webmaster Tools.

That said, the evidence doesn’t prove a competitor can always successfully penalize you. It only supports that harmful link-building can trigger scrutiny and possibly a ranking problem.

Closest guidance supported here: monitor your backlink profile for spammy links, especially sudden bursts of optimized anchors, and investigate if you get an unnatural linking warning.

The evidence only says that spammy backlinks can hurt your site’s performance, and that Google may take action if things reach a serious threshold. It also says Google may not notify you unless there’s a serious algorithmic or manual action.

It does not directly confirm that competitors can get your website penalized. The closest supported guidance is that harmful spammy links can exist in your profile and affect performance, so keeping your link profile clean is recommended.

The supported way to check or challenge a Websense categorization is to use their Site Lookup / URL Category tools if you have access, or email suggest@websense.com to ask for a review or category change.

The material here does not show a direct way to find out why a site was blocked by Sophos, only that Websense blocks can be due to misclassification and that Websense’s categorization inquiry/review contact is suggest@websense.com.

If you’re trying to diagnose the block, the closest guidance supported here is to ask the blocking vendor for the exact category and review the site’s classification through their lookup tools or support contact.

If Websense is blocking your site, it may be categorized as “Potentially Damaging Content.” The suggested way to find out and address it is to ask the affected organization’s Help Desk or IT administrator to check or override the category. You can also request that Websense reevaluate the categorization by emailing suggest@websense.com.

The material provided does not mention Sophos-specific steps, so I can’t say how to check Sophos from this evidence alone.

If you think Sophos blocked the URL as a false positive, submit a reassessment request to Sophos and complete all fields in the form. If you’re not a Sophos customer, try to find out which Sophos product raised the alert, because that helps them investigate faster. If you can’t identify it, enter your best guess in the required “Product” field.

The provided information does not explain Websense specifically, but the same practical first step is to identify which product is flagging the site before requesting a review.

Google’s +1 button was described as affecting search results, not necessarily as a direct global ranking factor. The support material says +1s can help people find better results, and Google may show +1 counts in search results even when they’re not from your friends. So the closest supported answer is: yes, it can influence what users see in search and may improve click-through, but this does not clearly prove a direct SEO ranking boost.

Anti-hotlinking is done by checking the HTTP referrer and blocking or redirecting image requests that don’t come from your allowed domains.

For example, with Apache rewrite rules:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER} !^$
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER} !^https?://www\.domain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER} !^https?://subdomain\.domain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule .*\.(jpg|jpeg|gif|png|bmp)$ http://google.com/thief.png [R,NC,L]

If you want to allow direct viewing too, use:

RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER} ^$ [OR]
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER} !^https?://www\.domain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER} !^https?://subdomain\.domain\.com$ [NC]

This redirects matching image requests to another image, like a warning image.

Anti-hotlinking here is done with an Apache .htaccess rewrite rule that checks the HTTP_REFERER header. If the referrer is not your own domain and not empty, the rule blocks image requests with a forbidden response.

The example needs one fix: escape the dot in the domain name, so use article-stack\.com instead of article-stack.com.

Example:
RewriteEngine on
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER} !^http://(.+\.)?article-stack\.com/ [NC]
RewriteCond %{HTTP_REFERER} !^$
RewriteRule .*.(png|gif|jpg)$ - [N,F,L]

This is the closest working approach shown.

The supported approach is to use an aws:Referer bucket policy in Amazon S3. That is the only concrete anti-hotlinking method mentioned in the evidence.

The thread also describes an alternative technique where an HTML file is served for hotlinked image requests and includes a backlink, but the accepted answer recommends the bucket policy instead. I can’t say more about the exact policy rules from the provided text.

For database-driven sites, Google bots generally crawl the page URLs your site exposes, not the database itself. So the important thing is that each distinct page you want indexed has its own URL and returns crawlable HTML content.

From the evidence here:
- Google’s bot downloads pages from the site from time to time.
- It does not understand dynamic content loaded only by Ajax, so content should be generated into the HTML response.
- This supports using unique URLs like `http://example.com/thread?id=101` rather than only one root page with changing widgets.

The evidence does not fully explain Google’s internal indexing or AdSense behavior beyond that, but the closest guidance is: make sure each database-backed page has a unique URL and includes the important content in the HTML returned to users and bots.

Google bots work like other search-engine spiders: they crawl pages they can reach, and the “good ones obey robots.txt.” For a database-driven site, that means the bot still requests URLs; if those URLs are generated dynamically from database content, the bot can crawl those pages too.

The evidence doesn’t explain any special Google handling for database-backed sites, but it does support these points: allow major search bots if you want search traffic, use robots.txt, and verify bots by domain/IP because agent names can be faked.

If your database-driven pages have crawlable URLs and are not blocked, Googlebot can index them.

Google bots generally crawl whatever pages your site makes available, including database-driven pages, as long as those pages can be reached by URLs and aren’t blocked. The guidance here is not to block known robots with robots.txt if you still want search engines to crawl your site.

Instead, let the bots crawl and separate bot hits from real user hits in your database. The suggested method is to check the client’s user agent and only log hits that match your criteria, rather than blocking them from accessing the site. This way you can keep search engine crawling working while avoiding bot traffic in your click counts.

Google does not prefer HTML sites over WordPress sites just because of the platform. The evidence only supports that Google may penalize sites with too many ads or pop-ups above the fold, especially on mobile, if they interfere with content. A content-rich WordPress site can rank well, and an HTML site can rank poorly if its layout or content is weak. So the main SEO factor here is page quality and user experience, not whether the site is HTML or WordPress.

There’s no evidence here that Google prefers WordPress or other CMS sites over hand-coded HTML sites. The only supported guidance is that the question was asked about local business SEO, but the thread has no answer on record.

So, based on this evidence alone, you can’t conclude that WordPress is favored for SEO. The closest safe guidance is that site platform choice isn’t shown to be a ranking advantage here; focus would still need to be on the site’s content and local relevance.

The evidence doesn’t show that Google prefers HTML sites over WordPress sites. It only says some people believe WordPress may help with SEO, possibly because it can configure meta information correctly, while other sources say it doesn’t matter. So, based on this, there’s no support for a general preference for HTML versus WordPress. The closest guidance is that SEO likely depends more on correct configuration than on the platform itself.

If your current URLs already include the main keywords, there’s little benefit in changing them. In the example, the existing URL already contains “cosplay” and descriptive text, so moving to a new structure is unlikely to improve rankings and could even hurt them despite 301 redirects.

The closest guidance here is: keywords in URLs can help, but only modestly, and changing a working structure on a site getting heavy search traffic is generally not worth it unless the current URLs are clearly poor or unusable.

The easiest supported approach here is to keep the old URLs working and use 301 redirects to the new URLs, then drop the file extensions. That preserves existing link authority and gives you cleaner, more future-proof URLs. If you want to keep the same appearance of URLs, the evidence suggests using server rules like .htaccess to map requests without exposing the .php extension, but the clearest recommendation given is 301 redirects plus extensionless URLs. Rankings may stay the same, improve, or drop; the evidence says that depends more on search engine algorithm changes than on redirects themselves.

The easiest approach is to use a PHP microframework with “pretty URL” routing, such as Slim, Flight, Limonade, or Glue. These work by using Apache rewrite rules in .htaccess to send all requests to index.php, where you define routes like /products/tables/green/little-wood123/.

If you don’t want a framework, you can write your own front controller and use rewrite rules, but for a small project the framework route is usually the simplest.

Google crawlers can see PHP-generated dynamic content as long as PHP is processed on the server and the crawler receives the resulting HTML. They do not need to see the PHP itself, only the output. If your script generates many pages from database content, that is fine for Google. If the page title keeps changing frequently, that can hurt SEO because important elements like the title and h1 are unstable.

Googlebot fetches sitemap files itself, and the fetch frequency seems tied to PageRank and how often the site changes. Submitting a sitemap should help; if Googlebot finds new URLs in it, it should crawl them right away. If it doesn’t find URLs in the sitemap, it will crawl them as quickly as it otherwise would.

This doesn’t directly explain PHP dynamic content, but the closest guidance is that Google can crawl URLs the same way it crawls other pages, and regularly updated sites tend to be crawled more often.

For database-generated content, the best supported approach here is to create real, linkable URL pages for useful searches and let them be discovered through internal links, not by trying to prebuild every possible query.

What this supports:
- Expose search results as crawlable pages like /?q=search
- Link to a small set of these pages from the home page, such as “recent searches,” “trending searches,” “popular tags/categories,” or “related searches”
- Add more links from result pages so crawlers can move deeper into the site

The key idea is to generate a handful of useful, navigational pages automatically from your query data, rather than making a huge manual list. Google is unlikely to want to index arbitrary search results pages, so focus on pages that function as hubs and are useful to users.

Create separate, indexable URLs for each result page, and make them accessible with GET rather than POST. For example:

example.com/search.php?coatcolor=brown
example.com/search.php?coatcolor=black&spots=white

The idea is that search engines can crawl and index these pages directly. This is better than dumping everything on one page and redirecting, because users can bookmark, share, and revisit specific results, and browser history works properly.

So the closest guidance is: give common searches their own URLs, and structure the site so those URLs return the relevant database results statelessly.

If each URL points to enough distinct content, it should be fine. Google can understand keyword-rich paths and query strings similarly, so switching to query strings does not really avoid risk.

For database-generated pages, the safer approach is to make them look like categorized pages with clean, descriptive URLs, not long strings of many keywords. Keep only a few relevant terms in the URL if needed; you do not need to stuff all keywords there.

Also, keywords in the URL are not necessary for search visibility if you can include them in the page content and metadata.

For a database-driven ASP.NET site, make each page output unique SEO tags from the database: especially the `<title>`, `<h1>`, and `<meta description>`. Google prefers pages with different content and users do too.

For URLs, use human-readable ones instead of numeric IDs. For example, use `/cats` rather than `?id=54637`. A common approach is to store a unique alias/slug field in the database for each page and use that in the URL.

So the basic idea is: dynamic pages are fine, but each page should render unique, descriptive content and readable URLs.

For ASP.NET, the closest guidance here is about deployment, not SEO. You need a hosting company that supports .NET and MS SQL, create the database on the host, use the provided connection string in your app, and upload the site.

For SEO on a database-driven site, the key implication is that the site must be deployed and accessible so search engines can reach the pages. This thread does not cover SEO techniques like URL structure, metadata, or crawlability. It only supports setting up the web app and database correctly, which is the first step before SEO work.

In general, yes: .com is often seen as more trustworthy, at least partly because it’s more widely used and .net can feel like a fallback when .com wasn’t available.

If you control both, the best practical choice is usually to use .com as the public/external domain and keep .net redirecting to it. A 301 redirect is the key step.

If you already have a lot invested in .net and it’s working well, the change is mostly about branding and consistency, not functionality.

The practical difference is mostly convention:

.com is the most recognized and is generally best if you can get a memorable one. It’s associated with commercial/company sites.

.net was intended for web/network presence, and was commonly used by ISPs. Today it’s often just an alternative when .com is taken.

.org is intended for organizations, typically nonprofits.

In practice, many people choose .net or .org when a good .com isn’t available. A clear, memorable .net or .org is usually better than a hard-to-remember .com. Also, users often type .com by habit, so .com has the strongest recognition advantage.

`.com`, `.org`, and `.net` are all generic top-level domains, so they can rank worldwide. The main difference in SEO is not the extension itself, but the site’s reputation and relevance.

Owning `.com` can be advantageous mainly because it’s the most familiar and often the default choice for a global audience. If someone else owns the same name on another generic extension, Google will favor the domain with more reputation, not necessarily the `.com` by itself.

Country-specific domains can help when targeting users in that country, and Google can rank them better there than a generic domain.

The drop is explained by low-quality, duplicated content. Pages that are just keyword-replaced versions of existing content are exactly the kind Google may remove from its index. The trend may continue, and the site could even be removed more broadly. There isn’t a workaround suggested here other than improving the content quality and reducing duplication.

A sudden drop in reported indexed pages can happen even when pages are still in Google’s search index. In the example given, the site had been hit by Panda, and the reported indexed page count fell sharply about a month after the traffic drop. Improving crawlability helped over time, and the reported count later returned to normal.

The main changes that were made:
- redirected poor-quality pages to newer, more relevant pages
- fixed broken links
- removed links to poor-quality pages from higher-quality pages

So the closest guidance is to check for quality and crawlability issues rather than assuming the pages were fully removed from the index.

A sudden drop in indexed pages can mean Google is having trouble accessing your site, such as server downtime/overload, DNS problems, robots.txt blocking, redirects, or security/configuration issues. In your case, Google reported DNS lookup errors, which points to access problems.

A practical next step is to crawl your site yourself with a tool like Xenu’s Link Sleuth to find broken links or inaccessible pages. Then remove or redirect broken links, for example with .htaccess or the equivalent in your CMS.

The drop is explained as Google deindexing low-quality, duplicate-ish pages rather than a server, DNS, or page error. The guidance given is that the content was created by replacing keywords in existing content, which is exactly the kind of content Google tends to remove from its index. The trend may continue, and the site could be hit harder if the pattern persists.

A drop in the reported indexed-page count can happen after a Panda hit: the pages may still be in the search index even though Webmaster Tools shows fewer of them. In the example, the count fell from over 1000 to almost zero, then later recovered after crawlability improvements.

The improvements described were:
- redirecting poor-quality pages to newer, more relevant pages
- fixing broken links
- removing links to poor-quality pages from higher-quality pages

That doesn’t prove the same cause for your site, but it’s the closest supported explanation.

If the pages are still showing up in Google search, this points more to a Google Webmaster Tools/Sitemap reporting problem than to an actual deindexing issue. The suggested checks are:

- Look for a Sitemap error in the Issues column
- Test the Sitemap in Webmaster Tools
- Open the Sitemap directly in a browser
- Make sure the URLs in the Sitemap exactly match the live/indexed pages
- Check Health > Index Status

If none of those show a problem, it may just be a temporary reporting glitch in Google Webmaster Tools and can correct itself within about 24 hours.

Yes. The limit shown is 20 properties per account. Once that limit is reached, additional properties cannot be created. Existing properties can still be updated and reused.

The evidence refers to the API and says it may reflect general account usage limits, so this is the closest guidance supported.

No direct answer here about Google rankings or bounce rate is provided. The only supported point is that Google Analytics metrics and Alexa rankings are separate and do not affect each other. So, based on this evidence, a site’s bounce rate is not shown to influence rankings in the way asked.

The evidence only says you can use event tracking so a specific click won’t count in Google Analytics bounce rate. It does not say that bounce rate affects Google rankings.

So, based on this, I can’t confirm any ranking impact. The closest supported guidance is that bounce rate is a Google Analytics metric you can adjust with event tracking, but no SEO/ranking relationship is mentioned.

According to the cited answer, no: Google does not use Google Analytics information, including bounce rate, as a ranking factor. So a high bounce rate by itself would not negatively impact rankings based on that source.

A meta description is still useful because it lets you suggest the summary text shown in search results instead of leaving Google to choose article text from the page. It does not control the extra info before the result, like a date; that kind of display is rich snippet data.

The evidence says that to influence that kind of SERP content, you should use Schema markup, such as BlogPosting schema for an article page. So meta description helps with the snippet text, while schema helps provide richer search result details.

Meta descriptions are still useful because Google does not always build the SERP snippet from on-page text. If the search terms don’t appear on the page, or Google thinks the meta description is a better summary, it may use that instead. Google also uses descriptions from the META tag as one of several sources and often prefers them when available because they can give users a clearer idea of the page’s content and reduce click-and-backtracking.

So even if Google can show article text sometimes, a meta description helps control the snippet in cases where the page text isn’t the best match or doesn’t contain the searched terms.

Meta descriptions are still useful because they can help persuade people to click on your result. Even though Google does not use the meta description tag as a direct ranking factor, a good description can improve click-through, and that can indirectly help if users keep choosing your site.

If you do not provide one, Google may show article text from the page instead. But that text may not be the best summary or marketing message for your page.

So the meta description is mainly for:
- better search-result snippets
- more appealing, controlled messaging
- potentially more clicks

It is not mainly for direct ranking.

If the page or PDF is truly gone, returning 410 Gone is a good option. The supported guidance here is to use 410 and, ideally, show a page with similar products or documents the user may still want to view. That can still help recover some users into sales.

The evidence does not support nofollowing the links just because Google can’t index the documents.

If the partner’s site is gone and the page now returns 404, the link won’t be followed by search engines anymore. Based on this, you don’t need to disavow or take other action. You can simply do nothing and wait for the backlink to disappear from your backlink profile.

Yes—based on the answer, you can 301-redirect deleted HTML files to a WordPress page or “pretty URL” page.

It suggests using separate redirect lines for each deleted file, for example:
Redirect 301 ^/about.html http://www.mscaspian.com/fa/about
Redirect 301 ^/contact.html http://www.mscaspian.com/fa/contact

It also says that if WordPress uses index.php and pretty permalinks are enabled, redirecting to the extensionless URL is valid. It does not specifically show a general wildcard rule for all deleted files, only individual redirects.

If the deleted page is not being replaced with new content, the guidance here is to send a 410 Gone HTTP status rather than a 301 redirect. The page should explain to users why it’s gone and offer helpful options like your home page, site map, search page, and links to similar content if available.

This evidence does not support redirecting deleted content to a file or a different web page with 301.

A 301 redirect is generally a bad idea when the destination is not relevant to the deleted page. It can create a poor user experience, and there’s also concern about Google treating lots of non-relevant redirects poorly.

If the pages are being removed for copyright reasons and there isn’t a similar replacement page, a 410 Gone is often the safer choice. If you do redirect, it should ideally be to closely related content, not just the homepage.

If you own the site, you can remove pages from Google’s index through Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console. To prevent most major search engines from indexing parts of the site, use a robots.txt file and add Disallow rules.

Examples:
Disallow: /private_file.html

Disallow: /directory/

This covers blocking pages or directories from being crawled/indexed.

Use a robots meta tag on the pages you want controlled. The suggested approach is to let the index page be indexed with:

<meta name="Robots" content="INDEX, FOLLOW" />

and put this on the other pages:

<meta name="Robots" content="NOINDEX, NOFOLLOW" />

This would keep Google from indexing the rest of the site while allowing the main page to be indexed. The evidence does not mention a broader sitewide method for all search engines, only this page-by-page meta tag approach.

Repeated blocks like headers, footers, sidebars, author blurbs, newsletter widgets, and featured items are generally not treated as duplicate content if they aren’t the main content of the page. Sites normally have these repeated sections without issue.

If you want to reduce any risk, use semantic HTML5 tags like aside and footer, and you can also add schema.org metadata to help search engines understand what those repeated elements are.

No, not if those URLs all show identical or very nearly identical content and each has a canonical link pointing to www.mysite.net.

But this can still be a crawl-efficiency issue because bots may crawl www.mysite.net, www.mysite.net/, and www.mysite.net/index.html separately. For that kind of fixed URL variation, a 301 redirect to the canonical form is usually better than relying only on canonical tags.

Use a 301 redirect from the old URL structure to the new one. That tells Google the old URLs have permanently moved, and Google should eventually replace the old results in its index. A robots.txt disallow on the old URLs is not the supported fix here and may prevent crawling the redirects. It won’t happen quickly, but the index should update over time.

Using a plural vs. singular in the domain or URL is not very important for SEO. The guidance here is to choose the URL structure that is more logical and reads better for users, rather than trying to target both forms in the URL.

Google already understands that “house” and “houses” are related, so it may return results for one when someone searches the other. Keywords in the URL count very little toward SEO, and using both forms just for keyword targeting is not recommended.

Yes, it can matter if the plural or alternate spelling is part of the same confusion issue. The guidance here is that a brand should be easily identifiable, and multiple spellings can create confusion and weaken recognition. If you want to reach different markets, it’s better to choose a name that works in both rather than relying on pluralization or spelling variants. If you can only get one version, it can still work, but a single, consistent spelling is the safer choice.

The only clear advantage of plural vs. singular is if people are more likely to search for the plural term; you’d need to check search volume to know.

Otherwise, there’s no inherent branding advantage to one form over the other. If possible, the safest approach is to buy both versions and 301 redirect one to the other, so you avoid losing traffic to a competitor or squatter. If budget is tight, choose the version that matches how people are most likely to search.

404 pages are not covered directly by the evidence. What it does say is that shortened outbound URLs generally aren’t harmful to SEO; they may only lose a little link juice because they act like 301 redirects. Based on that, the closest guidance is that not every error or redirect page necessarily hurts ranking, but the provided material does not say whether 404 pages affect rankings. If you want, I can help interpret common SEO behavior for 404 pages, but that would go beyond this evidence.

No. Proper 404s are normal and do not affect how your site’s other valid pages rank in search results. Search engines expect pages to disappear sometimes, and they even prefer a real 404 or 410 over a “soft 404.”

What matters is that your important pages return 200 and the removed pages return proper 404/410 responses. If the old URLs are still linked or indexed, you can clean up internal links or redirect users to the closest relevant page, but the 404s themselves won’t hurt ranking.

If the requested page doesn’t exist, returning a 404 status is the correct behavior and won’t hurt your site’s SEO. It may cause that URL to drop from search results, but that’s expected. Showing search results or other helpful content on the 404 page can improve usability and give visitors another path into your site. So, based on this, 404 pages themselves do not hurt website ranking.

No, not based on this. The accepted answer says Google only retrieves the HTTP header for 404s, not the page content, so hiding or showing images on the 404 page won’t affect SEO. It also says no PageRank is assigned to the 404 page or links on it. If you redirect to a 404 page, that just adds an extra step and has no SEO benefit.

Hiding images on a 404 page is not shown here to affect SEO directly. The supported guidance is that 404 errors generally don’t impact Google rankings, and 404 pages can be fine as long as they return a real 404 status. What can become a problem is if your site keeps linking to many missing pages, which may be seen as poor maintenance and a bad user experience. So the closest answer is: hiding images itself isn’t addressed as an SEO issue, but make sure the page sends an actual 404 and avoid creating lots of links to non-existing pages.

If you mean using `find-new/posts&recent=1` as the homepage, the provided material doesn’t address SEO for that URL structure directly. It only says you can check a page’s Google PageRank with `prchecker.info`, and mentions free SEO evaluation tools at `seolab.com/webapp/`.

So the closest guidance supported here is: if you want to assess SEO impact, check the URL’s PageRank and use general SEO readiness tools. It does not say whether that homepage choice is good or bad for SEO.

A homepage that shows the latest posts can still be good for SEO, especially if you also optimize it for your primary keyword. The guidance here is to mix both: keep a well-optimized homepage and include fresh/latest content. Fresh content may encourage search engines to crawl the page more often. So using something like `find-new/posts&recent=1` as the homepage is not inherently bad for SEO, as long as the page is also optimized for the keywords you care about.

URLs with ?page=something are not shown here as being bad for SEO. The issue described is 404 errors for URLs Google is finding, likely from other sites linking to old or invalid pages. The suggested fix is to return a 410 Gone status for pages that are permanently removed, so Google knows they are gone for good. If your ?page= URLs are valid, they are not covered by this answer; if they are invalid and causing 404s, handling them with 410 is the closest guidance given.

No clear SEO benefit is implied by adding an extension. The guidance says changing the URL to include “.html” does not improve rankings, and can add unnecessary processing overhead. By the same logic, using `?page=something` is not inherently bad for SEO either. The main takeaway is that the URL format itself is less important than avoiding unnecessary complexity and making sure the site is handled cleanly by the server.

Not by itself, based on this. The answer says the order of URL parts like `/page/mytitle/123/` vs `/page/123/mytitle/` is not different enough to matter for search engines. It also suggests you may be overthinking the structure.

The bigger concern mentioned is keeping an ID in the URL when it doesn’t serve a purpose, because changing CMS later could change IDs and lead to new URLs, broken links, and re-indexing.

So `?page=something` is not shown here as inherently bad for SEO; the evidence only supports that URL structure differences usually don’t matter much, and stable, meaningful URLs are preferable.

You need to use the DNS nameservers provided by Network Solutions, not the FTP server name. In GoDaddy, go to Domains, select the domain, then choose to set nameservers and enter the Network Solutions DNS servers, such as dns1.networksolutions.com and dns2.networksolutions.com. Enter at least two nameservers if possible. After that, upload your site files to the new host and wait for DNS propagation before the domain points to the new hosting.

It’s generally better to change the domain’s nameservers to GoDaddy’s, rather than manually editing the A record. The guidance says to point the domain to your web host’s nameservers unless you have a static IP, because the IP can still change if the host moves or restructures servers. Manually creating an A record is described as something you’d very rarely want to do instead of using the proper nameservers.

The closer a page is to the root domain, the better. In the example given, a shorter URL like www.example.com/products/page_name/123 is preferred because it is simpler and closer to the domain root, while still giving useful path information.

The evidence does not say that the exact number of parameters alone is the key issue; rather, it suggests that being too deep in the URL path can reduce prominence. So reducing the URL to fewer elements may help, but the main supported guidance is to keep it short and simple, not necessarily to target an exact number of parameters.

If `category` and `subCategory` change the content of `itemList.php`, you generally don’t need to set anything in Google’s URL Parameters tool. The default “let Google decide” is usually the right choice.

That tool is site-wide, so if you tell Google that `category` changes content, it will treat that as true for the whole site. That usually isn’t a problem because Googlebot only applies it to URLs where it actually finds those parameters.

Use the URL Parameters tool mainly for tracking or other parameters that do not change page content, so Google can ignore them.

SEO-friendly URLs can help, but they shouldn’t come at the expense of clarity. The guidance here is that URLs should make sense to humans at a glance when possible, and should generally be close to the page title rather than stuffed with keywords.

Putting only expected search terms into the slug may look spammy and can resemble keyword stuffing if the terms aren’t actually relevant to the content. A practical recommendation is to keep URLs concise, ideally 10 words or fewer.

SEO-friendly URLs are important. The provided answer says keywords in the URL are one of the more important SEO ranking factors, alongside page titles and domain name. They also help users, since people still type URLs by hand, and well-structured URLs can still work if part of the URL is missing. So, if your goal is better rankings and usability, it’s worth doing.

If your target search term is “John Smith,” the evidence supports that `http://example.com/johnsmith` is more SEO friendly than `http://example.com/john`, because it matches the full query more closely. So, SEO-friendly URLs can matter when they include the exact or more refined search term you want to rank for.

That said, the evidence only addresses this specific example; it doesn’t fully establish how important SEO-friendly URLs are overall compared with other ranking factors.

Human-friendly URLs are preferred when possible: they should make sense at a glance and align with the page title/content. That can also help SEO as a by-product. Using only expected search terms in the URL can look like keyword stuffing and may seem spammy if the words don’t match the content.

So the tradeoff, based on this evidence, is:
- Friendly URLs: easier for humans, clearer, less spammy-looking.
- Keyword-heavy URLs: may target search terms, but overdoing it can hurt appearance and may not help if irrelevant.

A practical recommendation supported here is to keep URLs short, ideally 10 words or fewer, and make them meaningful to humans as well as search engines.

Friendly URLs can help with SEO because keywords in the URL are an important ranking factor, along with page titles and domain name. They can also be better for users when typing URLs by hand, and if the URL is structured well, the page may still load even if the keyword part is missing.

The evidence doesn’t give specific downsides of friendly URLs or specific benefits of query parameters. It only implies that query-parameter-style URLs may be less useful for SEO and less user-friendly when typed manually.

For SEO, the supported guidance here is to keep the query string in the redirected URL when it serves a purpose, because the search engine will evaluate the destination page’s content and the customer needs to reach the right page.

So, using friendly URLs vs query parameters isn’t fully answered here. What this does support is:
- If a parameter is part of the destination page identity or tracking you want preserved, include it.
- If the parameter is only for tracking and not needed on the final page, this source does not give a contrary SEO reason to remove it.

It does not cover broader pros/cons like readability, analytics, or caching.

Using fewer path segments is generally preferred. The accepted answer says pages closer to the root domain tend to get more prominence, and shorter, simpler URLs are better for both users and Google. So a URL like www.example.com/products/page_name/123 is preferred over a deeper one like www.example.com/products/123/1234/category_name/page_name.

That said, it does not say long URLs are “catastrophically bad,” only that shorter is better and the issue is debatable. It also doesn’t specifically address query-string URL parameters, just URL path depth/length.

The best-supported approach here is to keep URLs as simple as possible and use the fewest parameters you can. A query-string format like `http://www.example.com/category/filter?page=1&sort=price-asc&limit=20` is preferable to a path with colons.

Colons are reserved characters in URLs and should be encoded if used, so they’re not a good choice for this kind of structure.

Also, avoid submitting lots of duplicate URLs in sitemaps for different sort/filter/page combinations.

Yes. Based on this, the best practice is to keep the sitemap listing the item pages and not add pagination to the sitemap structure. The pagination on category pages is unnecessary for sitemap purposes, because the sitemap already tells Google where to find all item pages.

So for your structure, you would keep the sitemap as:
root
category1
item1, item2, ... item99
category2
item101, item102, ... item199

and not make the sitemap follow the category pagination.

For SEO, the supported guidance here is not to nofollow internal links. A link that points to just `#` arguably doesn’t really go anywhere, but there’s still no reason to use `nofollow` on it.

This doesn’t directly answer labels and tags, but the closest guidance is: don’t add `nofollow` just because they are internal site elements. If labels/tags are normal internal pages you want search engines to discover, you generally would not nofollow them.

For SEO, it’s generally not good to nofollow your own internal links to your own site. If you don’t want tag or label pages indexed, you can noindex those pages or the page that contains the cloud/list. The issue is usually the large block of links/text, not the links themselves. If it’s a huge tag cloud in a sidebar on many pages, the best supported advice here is to reduce its size.

There are many alternatives to AdSense, but the best one depends on your niche. A practical approach is to look at competitor sites and see which ad networks or advertisers they use. You can also search Google for advertisers in your topic area; if they advertise there, they may be willing to advertise on your site too, especially if your content is focused on a specific niche.

If your site is about products, affiliate programs are another option. Amazon is suggested as a good place to start.

For a small site with around 400 daily visitors, the evidence doesn’t identify a single “best” network, but it does support researching niche-matched ad networks and affiliate deals.

The available information doesn’t give a reliable answer about the best ad service or revenue model for a one-time-use high-traffic website.

It only suggests that AdSense revenue is tied to clicks or ad views, and it questions whether traffic changes the value of a click. It does not confirm whether a high-traffic site should use AdSense, CPM, CPC, or another model.

Closest guidance supported here: if your site will get many views, a model based on ad views may be relevant; if earnings depend on clicks, traffic alone won’t guarantee higher revenue unless users click ads.

The closest guidance is that a self-hosted, simple ad-serving system with advertiser payments and campaign tracking is likely to be complex and heavy-handed to build or run yourself.

The suggested easiest options are services like AdSense or AdBrite. AdBrite was noted as allowing you to place your own ads, which may help if you want more control over relevance.

If your main concern is one-time, high traffic and hosting it yourself, the evidence does not provide a specific self-hosted model that fits well; it mainly warns that payment-provider approval may be a major issue and that custom tools tend to be too complex.

For a one-time-use site, AdSense is probably not a good fit. The cited experience suggests that even with modest traffic it wasn’t worth the setup, and that on a very high-traffic site the revenue can still be disappointing if the ads aren’t well matched to the audience. It also says hand-selected, audience-targeted ads performed far better than AdSense in that case.

Closest guidance supported here: if you want ad revenue, a targeted/hand-selected ad deal would likely be better than generic AdSense. If you only need a short-term monetization option, AdSense may not justify the effort unless you expect unusually strong traffic and ad relevance.

A good option from the thread is MailChimp. The recommendation says it’s a hosted service with better deliverability and tools for making HTML newsletters look good, and it offers a free tier for small lists: up to 2,000 subscribers and 12,000 emails per month.

If you specifically want something on your PHP/MySQL server, the thread mentions PHPList and Newsberry as the ones being considered, but it doesn’t give a direct recommendation for them.

Mailchimp is a strong recommendation here: it’s described as much easier to use than the competition and free for the first 2000 users. If you need a free/open-source option for shared hosting, the only specific example mentioned is phpList, which was said to be “good,” but the thread doesn’t confirm its installation on GoDaddy.

The provided evidence does not answer whether adding Disqus to WordPress affects SEO. It only shows a resolved thread about “Disqus analogs” and mentions IntenseDebate as one alternative comments platform.

So the closest guidance supported by the evidence is that Disqus has at least one known alternative: IntenseDebate. There is no information here about SEO impact from using Disqus on WordPress.

Adding Disqus to WordPress does not help on-page SEO by default. The comments are typically loaded with JavaScript, so search engines like Google can’t see the user-generated comments in the page HTML. That means you don’t get SEO benefit from the comment text itself.

There is a documented Disqus workaround to include comments directly in the parent page, but it’s described as not pretty and requires PHP and MySQL.

So: default Disqus = no SEO benefit from comments; potential workaround exists if you need comments to be crawlable.

Yes, adding Disqus can affect SEO if it creates many internal broken URLs. The evidence describes a WordPress site where Disqus generated tens of thousands of bad internal URLs, which was followed by a large traffic drop and much lower crawl rate. It says a large number of broken links can signal low quality and may trigger Panda-related ranking drops.

It also supports that fixing the problem with 301 redirects and removing Disqus is the right step. However, it says there’s no way to speed up Google’s error count reduction, and setting crawl rate to “Fast” is only a suggestion and won’t make Google crawl faster.

Major and minor search engines generally respect robots.txt. So if your goal is to keep search engines from crawling your site, robots.txt is commonly honored by them.

However, robots.txt is not a security measure. It won’t stop badly written or malicious bots, and it won’t hide content from anyone who already knows the URL. If you need stronger control, use access restrictions on the site itself.

If you want, I can help with an example robots.txt rule for blocking specific pages or the whole site.

robots.txt alone can’t reliably hide a site. It only asks crawlers not to index, so search engines may still show the URL with no snippet.

The stronger options supported here are server-side:
- Password-protect the site.
- Restrict access by IP in .htaccess if your customers have known IPs.
- Return HTTP 403 to crawlers, optionally combined with access control.
- You can also block crawler user agents in .htaccess, but that is less reliable than server-level access control.

If you must keep the site publicly reachable, robots.txt is not enough to ensure it is totally hidden.

PHP can’t directly “rewrite to” .htaccess; .htaccess is handled by Apache, not by PHP. The issue described is that the rewrite rules aren’t working on a VPS. The suggested fixes are to enable Apache’s rewrite module and allow .htaccess overrides:

- Activate mod_rewrite, for example: a2enmod rewrite
- In your Apache config/httpd.conf, change AllowOverride none to AllowOverride all for the relevant directory

After that, your RewriteEngine/RewriteRule directives in .htaccess should work.

Put this in your .htaccess file:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteRule ^script/(\w+)\.png$ script/image.php?name=$1 [L]

This rewrites requests like /script/esqew.png to /script/image.php?name=esqew.

It assumes the name is at least one alphanumeric or underscore character, and it only matches .png URLs.

The thread only shows the old and new rewrite patterns, but it doesn’t include a working answer for redirecting the old URLs to the new `1/` sub-directory.

The closest guidance it supports is to add rewrite rules that match the old URLs and send them to the new paths. For example, you’d need rules that capture the old `([^/]+)\.htm` form and redirect to `1/…\.htm`, but the exact `.htaccess` syntax isn’t provided in the thread.

If you want, I can help you draft the Apache rewrite rules for that redirect.

If the redirect is a 301, Bing should follow it without you changing anything. The main issue described here is that Bing can take weeks or even months to index pages, and it can be slower than Google. Also, Bing may be more selective, so make sure the pages have unique, good content and that your robots.txt and sitemap are correct.

Bing Webmaster Tools does not have a setting to choose a preferred www or non-www version. It treats example.com as the main domain regardless of the subdomain.

The practical workaround is to:
- submit a sitemap.xml
- set your preferred version with a server-side 301 redirect

For Apache, the example shown redirects non-www to www in .htaccess.

To view all indexed content, you need to register all four URL variations:

http://domain-name.com/
http://www.domain-name.com/
https://domain-name.com/
https://www.domain-name.com/

That includes both protocol and www/non-www combinations. If your site moved from https no-www to https www, make sure the https://www version is added as well, and also the other variants so you can see where Bing/Google is indexing your content.

If you want Google not to index the subdomain at all, put a robots.txt file in the root of the subdomain with:

User-agent: *
Disallow: /

That tells crawlers not to index any URLs on child.example.com. It won’t guarantee removal if pages are already indexed, but the main search engines usually follow it.

If your issue is only that Google shows the subdomain name in the search result title, this evidence doesn’t cover changing that specifically; it only supports preventing the subdomain from being indexed.

To prevent Google from showing the sitemap link or similar URL in search results, block indexing of the sitemap with an X-Robots-Tag noindex header, for example via .htaccess:

<IfModule mod_rewrite.c>
    <Files sitemap.xml>
       Header set X-Robots-Tag "noindex"
    </Files>
</IfModule>

This guidance covers the sitemap being indexed. It does not specifically address subdomain names appearing as the title in search results.

Google’s guidance supports serving different content to mobile and desktop users at the same URL, as long as you detect Google’s crawlers correctly and serve the right version to each: desktop content to normal Googlebot, mobile content to mobile Googlebot. That is not treated as cloaking if done properly.

So this arrangement should not hurt rankings just because the content differs. The key risk is incorrect detection or serving the wrong content to the wrong crawler.

Google does use separate crawlers for desktop and mobile. This answer does not say whether desktop and mobile results are fully separate in all cases, but it does indicate Google crawls each version separately when it expects different content.

The likely issue is that you’re looking at the wrong Analytics view. Make sure the tracking ID/view is the same for both sites and that you aren’t using separate IDs like -01 for mobile and -02 for desktop.

If your desktop site is being tracked with a different view/property, its visits won’t appear in the mobile view. The fix is to verify the tracking code on both versions and confirm they report into the same Analytics property/view, or review the correct desktop view.

Yes, if your mobile version is meant for mobile users and is served appropriately, Google can crawl it and it should be fine. The key is that Google uses different crawlers/user agents for desktop and mobile: desktop Googlebot should get the desktop content, and mobile Googlebot should get the mobile content. The evidence does not say you should index a separate mobile duplicate of the desktop site on a different URL; it supports serving different content at the same URL based on device detection. If your mobile pages are separate URLs, the closest guidance supported here is to make sure Google can recognize and crawl them correctly.

If your mobile site is just a reduced-layout version of the main site and contains essentially the same content, the guidance here suggests helping Google index the mobile site rather than blocking it. A mobile sitemap is specifically mentioned as a good idea, and there’s a reference to helping Google index a mobile site. It doesn’t directly say whether you should index it separately on Google, but it does support making the mobile version discoverable for indexing.

A mobile XML sitemap won’t directly affect rankings, whether it matches the desktop sitemap or not. The main concern is making sure Google puts the right content in the right index when the same URLs serve device-specific HTML. The guidance supported here is to use the Vary HTTP header when serving different content on the same URLs. So, based on this, indexing a duplicate mobile sitemap isn’t what matters; correct device handling is.

If your business is mainly targeting the UK, stick with the .co.uk. The .com is most useful if you want to target international customers.

If you do want to switch to the .com, set up a 301 redirect from the .co.uk to the .com so users and search engines are sent to the new site, and rankings/PageRank are largely passed over with only a small loss. You should also tell Google directly that the domain is changing.

Expect some ranking fluctuations and temporary 404s during the transition.

If you want to keep your current .co.uk ranking while expanding to .com, the safest approach is to keep the existing pages intact and add the new domain as a separate version rather than just redirecting everything.

The evidence suggests creating localized versions of your pages and using the correct lang attribute plus hreflang tags so search engines can serve the right version to the right audience. That should help preserve your existing SEO efforts while allowing the new domain to rank in the new market.

If you’re moving the whole site from .co.uk to .com, the evidence doesn’t directly cover that exact migration, but it does support using separate language/region versions to avoid disrupting current rankings.

Changing only the server/IP address and not the domain name is generally less likely to affect SEO than changing the domain itself, but the provided thread does not include an answer on record. It does clarify that the change described is a server move, not a domain-name change. Based on that, the closest guidance is: a domain change is more likely to affect rankings than a simple server/IP change, but any migration should still be handled carefully to avoid SEO issues.

Changing the domain can affect your PageRank/rankings, but the evidence here only says PageRank is influenced by things like backlinks, page age, and page quality, and that Google rankings can drop if you break what was working. It also says PageRank is a minor factor these days.

So, if you change domain, the closest guidance supported is: preserve the key elements and structure of pages, and avoid breaking the things that made them rank. That is more likely to protect rankings than the domain change itself.

A domain change, including changing registrars or ownership info, does not seem to have a major long-term impact on ranking by itself. The answer suggests that registration data and nameservers can be factors, but in practice registrar changes have very little long-term effect on SEO or pagerank. If anything changes, it’s more likely due to other signals tied to the domain, like nameserver history or the loss of links that previously supported the domain.

The provided thread does not give a recorded answer. It only clarifies that the change is moving the website to another server while keeping the same domain name, so only the IP address changes. Based on that, the closest guidance is that this is not a domain-name change. If you need a definitive SEO impact assessment, it would depend on how the move is handled, but that is not covered in the thread.

Yes. The guidance here says changing to a keyword-stuffed domain is a bad idea, can look spammy, and may lose a little link equity/“juice” through 301 redirects. It recommends keeping companyname.com and focusing on on-page optimization, off-page optimization, and regularly adding relevant content, such as through a blog.

- For page-level instructions: a META robots tag in <head> with values like NOINDEX, NOFOLLOW

A robots.txt file is used to give robots/search engines instructions about your site. If you don’t need any special behavior, you can leave it out, create an empty one, or use:

User-agent: *
Disallow:

It won’t be harmful if missing. Even so, it can still be useful to point search engines to your XML sitemap, and having one can avoid 404 entries in your web logs.

A robots.txt file is used to tell web crawlers what parts of a site should not be crawled. From the evidence, it can be used to disallow crawling of a folder, but it’s awkward to allow just one file inside that folder because there is no “Allow” field. The suggested workaround is to move the files you want blocked into a separate directory and leave the one file you want crawled outside that directory.

The provided information doesn’t say that setting a geographic target will hurt your ranking. It only covers that rankings are driven by normal SEO signals like title tags, headings, keyword usage, and anchor text, and that the domain name itself probably won’t help much.

So, based on this, there’s no evidence that a geographic target negatively affects search ranking; the closest supported guidance is to focus on standard SEO factors for the terms you want to rank for.

It does not show that geographic targeting will negatively affect search ranking, but it also doesn’t show a traffic boost from targeting the USA. The closest supported guidance is that changing the target may have limited impact overall, and the effect can vary by site and audience.

Using shortened URLs on your page is treated like a 301 redirect, so it generally shouldn’t hurt your SEO efforts. If you use shortened outbound links, you may lose a little link juice, but the impact is small. The main tradeoff is between user experience and that small loss of link equity. Based on this, the closest guidance is: if the short URLs improve UX, they’re acceptable; if you want to avoid passing any link equity, use rel="nofollow" on those links.

If the old URLs have equivalent new URLs, redirect to those instead of the home page; that’s best for SEO and users.

If you only want to catch dead URLs, use a custom 404 page that checks whether the requested URL matches a known list of old WordPress URLs and then 301-redirects. That limits lookups to missing pages only.

If you must handle thousands of redirects in Apache, putting them in the server config/vhost is more efficient than .htaccess.

So the closest supported guidance is: map old-to-new URLs when possible; otherwise use a 404-based lookup or server config redirects, not a blanket homepage redirect.

If you control the shortener, use a 301 redirect instead of a 302. If you host the short URLs yourself, send a rel=noindex in the HTTP header for the shortened pages. Also add a canonical URL tag on the real page, and use rel=nofollow anywhere you publish the short URL if it uses a 302 redirect or you’re not sure what redirect it uses.

Use a noindex directive when the content expires, so Google removes the page from search results. For example:

X-Robots-Tag: noindex

or

<meta name="robots" content="noindex">

If you want to tell Google the page will expire at a specific time, use:

X-Robots-Tag: unavailable_after: 7 Jul 2007 16:30:00 GMT

or

<META NAME="GOOGLEBOT" CONTENT="unavailable_after: 25-Aug-2007 15:00:00 EST">

This is the closest supported way to indicate expiring content.

Use Google’s `unavailable_after` directive. It tells Google to remove a page at a specific future time.

Example:

`<meta name="googlebot" content="unavailable_after: 25-Aug-2007 15:00:00 EST" />`

Or for non-HTML files via HTTP header:

`X-Robots-Tag: unavailable_after: 23 Jul 2007 15:00:00 PST`

This is the closest supported way to have pages indexed now and automatically dropped later, instead of waiting for Google to recrawl a `410 Gone`.
