This should also make the domain shown to users more consistent.

Yes, two different domains or subdomains can point to the same website content, and search engines generally treat a subdomain as a separate site from the main domain. So duplicated meta descriptions on a.example.com would affect that subdomain, not example.com.

For titles and meta descriptions in SERP, search engines may still choose to show different snippets for each domain/page. If both domains have the same or very similar content, having different titles and descriptions can help differentiate them, but the evidence only confirms that duplicates across separate websites are not a ranking problem for the main domain.

Google decides whether to show sitelinks, so there’s no guaranteed way to force them. The best you can do is encourage them, but in this case it may not work. Google may be interpreting your brand name as two separate words even though it’s written as one.

You can’t directly “build” SiteLinks, but you can improve your chances by having substantial traffic, keeping the site growing with great content, and using clear semantic HTML for navigation. Mark your main menu with a nav/navigation element or id so Google can distinguish it from other link lists. Avoid using JavaScript for links and menus. If SiteLinks appear, you may be able to manage which ones show through Google Webmaster Tools. There’s no public algorithm or guaranteed way to get them, and they’re rare.

No. Hosting on Amazon EC2 is not adequate protection from DDoS. Once you expose an instance on a port, EC2 does not provide explicit DDoS protection. The cloud also doesn’t automatically prevent outages; a hosted service on EC2 has been taken down by DDoS before.

What it does support is that AWS has resources and guidance on mitigating DDoS, and some techniques are general while others are AWS-specific. If you want protection, you still need to design for it rather than assume the host will block it automatically.

The supported approach here is to use a spider trap: create a hidden page, disallow it in robots.txt, and place a link to it that humans won’t see but crawlers may follow. If an IP reaches that page, block that IP from accessing anything and show a human-readable message with an unlock CAPTCHA. 

This doesn’t fully cover rate-based blacklisting or a GoogleBot whitelist, but it does support the general idea of trapping and blocking rude crawlers.

Yes—based on the example, you can point multiple custom domains to different subdomains by adding host-based rewrite rules at the root of the main hosting account. For example, one domain can redirect to blog1.mainsite.com and another to blog2.mainsite.com using separate RewriteCond/RewriteRule entries in .htaccess.

This covers aliasing custom domains to subdomains, but it does not specifically confirm Blogger support. It only shows the general method for mapping domains to subdomains.

Based on that, Blogger did not obviously support mapping multiple custom domains to the same blog through a simple CNAME alone. Blogger is not the registrar. If the domain was purchased through Blogger, it was actually registered via a partner registrar like eNom or GoDaddy. You’d manage DNS or transfer ownership through that registrar, not through Blogger itself.

Take screenshots and other proof first. Then send the site owners a cease-and-desist letter. Also send a DMCA takedown notice to their web host, which you can find via whois. You can also submit DMCA notices to search engines under their procedures so copied content can be removed from results. If that doesn’t work, the next step mentioned is to involve lawyers. Setting up Google Alerts for unique search terms may help you track further copying.

It also supports sending a DMCA takedown notice and a cease-and-desist letter to both the host and the site owner, ideally with counsel if possible.

You can try a DMCA complaint if they copied your content, even partially, but the answer you have is strongest on the broader anti-scraping options: report them to Google via its content removal request, and if the site uses AdSense, file an AdSense violation report. It also suggests helping Google identify scraper sites.

If the copied text is only 1–2 paragraphs, the evidence does not give a hard threshold for DMCA, but it notes that fair use can allow partial quoting only when the new work adds value and is related. A spam site that is mostly scraped content and pills would not fit that description well.

Yes. Reducing file size will reduce bandwidth and page load time, especially for first-time visitors who won’t have anything cached yet. For most sites, first-time visitors are a large share of traffic, so this can matter a lot.

Also, enabling gzip compression can drastically reduce bandwidth.

The provided answer doesn’t specifically address reducing the number of separate JS or CSS files, but it does support the broader idea that smaller assets load faster and use less bandwidth.

To reduce the number of JS/CSS files downloaded, combine files on each page so there is only one file, and make them cacheable so repeat visits don’t redownload them. You can also minify the files and gzip/compress them to reduce their size. If some JavaScript isn’t needed right away, move it to the bottom so the page becomes usable sooner.

The browser request can be versioned in the URL, but the file on disk is still `myscript.js`, so the Apache `FilesMatch` should match the actual filename, not the rewritten URL. Use a pattern like `\.(js|css)$` for the files on the filesystem. Then `Header set Cache-Control "max-age=15552000"` can apply to those JS/CSS files. Also, your example request looks like `common.js`; if you’re using versioned names, it should be something like `common--20140904.js`.

Usually, when a domain expires, the registrar puts it on hold for a period of time, often around 90 days. During that time, the original owner may still be able to renew or recover it, sometimes for a higher fee. After that hold period, the domain is typically released and can be registered by someone else. In some cases, the registrar may keep it and resell it through its own auction or marketplace.

The evidence only shows that for .au domains, the public WHOIS and whois.audns.net.au do not reveal the expiration date information. It does not say what happens when a domain actually reaches its expiration date.

Closest guidance: you may need to check with the domain registrar or registry for the specific domain, since expiration details are not exposed in the public WHOIS.

When a domain reaches its expiration date, it usually does not become available to others right away. It typically enters a grace period first, during which the original registrant can renew it at the normal renewal cost and no one else can take it. If it is not renewed, it then moves into a redemption period, where it still cannot be registered by others but renewal usually costs more. If renewal still does not happen, it eventually enters pending delete and then becomes available again. The exact timing and whether a transfer can continue while expired depends on the registrar, but expiration alone is not an immediate loss of the domain.

Google doesn’t take W3C validation errors into account for SEO ranking. Many large, well-ranking sites have validation errors.

Fixing W3C issues is still good practice for web semantics and can help ensure bots can read your content properly. The only SEO-related risk mentioned is when invalid HTML actually interferes with crawling or content parsing, such as an unclosed title or h1 tag.

Valid HTML/CSS/RSS probably is not a direct ranking factor. But keeping code valid is still recommended because invalid markup can break a crawler the same way it can break a browser, which could affect whether your content is properly crawled and indexed.

So, W3C compliance is not guaranteed to improve rankings by itself, but it can help search engines access and understand your page more reliably.

On StackExchange, the title links to itself mainly because the slug in the URL is useful and readable, not because the page needs a separate destination. The title in the URL helps users understand what the page is about, improves sharing, can act as anchor text when pasted raw, and may help click-through from search results. It also appears in the browser title bar, bookmarks, and can be picked up by other sites. The unique ID is what actually identifies the post; the title part is there for readability and related SEO benefits.

Because it provides a self-link for usability and consistency. It gives users another easy way to get the permalink, and the title is large and easy to click. Keeping the title as a link even on the page itself also helps the interface stay consistent, so navigation elements don’t disappear or change unexpectedly.

If the heading is just part of an article list item, don’t add H2 just for SEO. Use heading tags only when they are actually headings. Wrapping the title in a link is fine, and it’s neither especially positive nor negative for SEO. The main guidance supported here is: do the markup correctly for usability and structure, not to try to game search engines.

Google doesn’t always index every page on a site. In this case, the category/navigation pages may be seen as duplicate content of pages already on the site, so Google may choose not to index or show them. The supported guidance here is to make those pages more distinct and useful so they’re not treated as duplicates. If you want navigation pages to appear, they need unique content and clear value beyond what’s already available elsewhere on the site.

You can’t directly tell Google what to display in search snippets, but you can influence it.

Use a unique, accurate meta description on each page:
<meta name="description" content="...">

If you don’t want Google to use the ODP description, add:
<meta name="robots" content="NOODP">

If you want to prevent any snippet:
<meta name="robots" content="nosnippet">

Also make sure your main content is clear and relevant, because if there’s no good meta description, Google may show page text it thinks best matches the query.

There isn’t enough here to say how to get Google specifically to display navigation.

What the provided answer does support is that, in general, a Home menu item is usually expected to have only a single function, and sub-items are uncommon. It also suggests that if you have a real case, you should narrow the question to that specific situation.

So the closest guidance is: don’t assume Google will show navigation under “Home”; if you need a menu, use a clearer, more specific navigation item rather than relying on Home to expand.

To make your page load faster, the guidance here is to:

- Load HTML and CSS before JavaScript so the page can render sooner.
- Put script tags as close to the closing body tag as possible.
- Use a CDN for common libraries like jQuery.
- Load JavaScript from an external file so it can be cached on later visits.
- Turn on gzip/zip compression on your web server.

It also points to Yahoo’s performance suggestions as a useful resource.

Use the page speed guidance from Google or Yahoo to identify bottlenecks, then apply the common fixes listed there: leverage browser caching, enable compression, minify CSS/HTML/JavaScript, optimize images, combine assets where appropriate, defer or load JavaScript asynchronously, avoid redirects, put CSS in the document head, and remove unused CSS. If you use PHP, there are also Google tips specifically for making PHP faster. A page speed addon/tool can give you clear, page-specific recommendations.

It measures only the time Googlebot spends downloading the HTML of your page, not the full page load with images, scripts, ads, or widgets.

So the “optimum” would simply be as low as possible for HTML download time. The evidence does not give a specific target number or threshold.

If usernames are unique, you can rewrite the URL so `profile/kevinlee` maps to an internal PHP page like `profile.php?username=kevinlee`.

Example `.htaccess` rules:

Options +FollowSymLinks
RewriteEngine on
RewriteRule profile/(.*)/ profile.php?username=$1
RewriteRule profile/(.*) profile.php?username=$1

This means a request for `website.com/profile/kevinlee` is handled by `profile.php?username=kevinlee`. You’d then look up that username in your database.

If you want the old subdirectory/subdomain URLs removed faster and you do not need to preserve links to them, a 301 is not the best choice. The supported options here are:

- 301 redirect: preserves link value, but can keep both the old and new URLs in the index for a while.
- 404 not found: removes pages more slowly.
- 410 gone: signals the page is permanently gone and is typically a stronger removal signal.
- robots.txt blocking: can also block access.

If preserving existing links matters, use 301 temporarily. If not, 410 or 404 is closer to what this evidence supports for clearing the old URLs.

The evidence covers moving a WordPress site from a subdomain to a new domain while preserving PageRank. The key guidance is to set a 301 redirect from the old site to the new site, using:

Redirect 301 / http://www.newdomain.com/

It also says to update WordPress URLs in wp-config.php, copy the database/files, search-and-replace the old URL to the new one, and then remove the temporary robots.txt block after confirming the move works.

It does not specifically address moving a subdomain into a subdirectory on the same domain, but the closest supported advice is to use proper 301 redirects from the old subdomain URLs to the new subdirectory URLs and update all internal WordPress references accordingly.

Google is seeing your site as redirecting to a login page, not as a normal public page.
