Hotlinking means another website embeds or links directly to files on your server, like images or videos, so their visitors load your content from your bandwidth and server.

It’s usually discouraged because it can:
- consume your bandwidth and server resources
- slow your site down
- cost you money, especially on shared or free hosting
- create extra load if the linked content becomes popular

That’s why many hosts forbid it. Using a service like Photobucket or YouTube to host media can help because their systems are built to handle that traffic.

Hotlinking is when another site uses your original images directly instead of hosting copies of them. Based on the information here, it’s not beneficial for you; in fact, it can be the opposite. Other sites may use your images and appear higher in image rankings if their content is more recent than yours. So people generally shouldn’t do it because it can let them benefit from your images while potentially reducing your own visibility. There are also simple ways to prevent image hotlinking.

Make it as simple as possible so more people will actually use it. A plain image link is the safest SEO-friendly option: The advice here is that search engines may give some weight to the alt text, and that a regular text link is also a good alternative. The more complicated code with hidden text, H1, and extra formatting looks spammy and is more likely to be avoided or flagged. Best practice from this guidance: keep the badge code simple, descriptive, and easy to paste. Avoid keyword stuffing and text hiding.

If the usernames are unique, you can rewrite the URL so `profile/kevinlee` maps to a script like `profile.php?username=kevinlee`.

A simple approach is to move the profile logic to `profile.php`, then use this in `.htaccess`:

Options +FollowSymLinks
RewriteEngine on
RewriteRule profile/(.*)/ profile.php?username=$1
RewriteRule profile/(.*) profile.php?username=$1

That makes the browser show the SEO-friendly URL while your server reads the username from the rewritten parameter.

SEO-friendly links should support a good website, not replace one. The guidance here says SEO can help indirectly by encouraging quality content, good navigation, and usability. So for links, focus on making them clear, descriptive, and easy to navigate for users. Good SEO is a side-effect of a good website, so make the site useful first, then the links will be more SEO-friendly as part of that.

You generally can’t make text render pixel-perfect the same in every browser. Fonts are rendered differently by browser, platform, version, resolution, and screen technology.

Using images for letters could force identical appearance, but it creates other problems: SEO, accessibility, responsive design, and site speed. Also, images can still vary visually across screens.

The closest practical guidance is to choose a font that looks good across devices and accept small rendering differences. If exact visual consistency is essential, images are an option, but they come with significant tradeoffs.

You generally can’t make a font render identically across browsers. Font handling varies by browser, operating system, monitor, and graphics setup, so the same font may appear smaller, bolder, or otherwise different. There isn’t a reliable library or API that will fully standardize this across all browsers. The practical approach is to design with these differences in mind and expect that the site won’t be pixel-perfect for everyone.

You can mask one domain behind another so users see domain1.com while content comes from domain2.com, but this can hurt SEO because it creates duplicate content issues. If you do it, use canonical URLs to tell search engines which domain is the main one. That helps search engines treat links to the secondary domain as pointing to the primary domain.

You don’t need domain/url masking. You can buy the domain from any registrar and point it to your web host’s DNS servers. If your host allows it, you can add the new domain to the same hosting account as an alias or separate site.

Domain masking/cloaking is different: it hides the real URL in the browser, usually by proxying or using an iframe. That’s generally a kludgy workaround, not the recommended setup.

Not necessarily. The guidance here is that if a folder URL shows a listing in your browser, then robots can find the subfolders too. To stop directory listings, add an .htaccess file in that directory with:

Options -Indexes

That prevents the contents of the directory from being listed. This doesn’t say a homepage in a sub-folder is bad, only that you should control directory listings if you don’t want subfolders exposed.

Yes, it’s generally better not to have the homepage only in a sub-folder. The accepted guidance says pages closest to the root are usually seen as most important by search engines, so using the full domain as the homepage is preferred. It also notes that if you later move the site, links pointing to /folder would need 301 redirects to preserve link value.

From a user-experience perspective, opening the site in a folder was described as “kind of shady” and less aligned with current expectations.

So the closest supported advice is: keep the homepage at the root if possible, and use subfolders for sections beneath it.

The order or grouping of pages in a sitemap doesn’t have any known SEO effect. For public-facing site maps, there’s no indication that alphabetizing, grouping by filters, or creating silo directories helps Google search.

What this does support is using an XML sitemap to list your end pages for crawling. If you want a public navigation page, organize it in whatever way is best for users, not for Google SEO.

Set up a Google Places listing for your business. That’s the closest guidance here for getting Google to understand and show location-related information in search results, including maps and location-specific details.

This does not directly explain how to organize navigation pages on your site for Google Search, but it suggests that if location is part of the goal, adding a Places listing gives Google better business/location data to work with.

For Google, the evidence suggests navigation pages should be organized with strong internal linking and clear anchor text, since Google puts more emphasis on anchor text of incoming links than on-page factors like headings. It also says keywords in the URL are more important to Google.

So for site navigation pages, use descriptive link text and keyword-relevant URLs, and make sure the pages are well linked from within the site.

If the image date is coming from EXIF metadata, you can change the date fields with an EXIF editor, or remove the metadata entirely. Also check whether Google has cached the image in Image Search; if it has, you can request removal to help clear the old date association.

That answer is about a SERP image tied to a date, not a “coming soon” placeholder on a website. For your use case, the closest supported guidance is to avoid leaving old image metadata that could surface in search, and verify how the image appears in Google’s cache/search results.

Use a progressive JPEG for the “coming soon” image. It lets the browser show a blurred/low-detail version first, then refine it as more data loads until the full image appears. The downside is that some browsers may not display anything until the whole file is downloaded if they don’t support progressive JPEGs.

A simple “coming soon” page is fine, and it won’t help much for SEO by itself. The best-supported approach is to make the page a little more useful: explain what the site will be about, why visitors should return, and add things like a short about section, contact details, or an email signup to notify people when it’s ready.

Avoid unnecessary redirects or unrelated content. The key is to keep the page relevant to the future site, rather than a bare notice or placeholder image alone.

No. If you don’t want any special behavior, you can leave out robots.txt entirely, and that won’t be harmful. An empty robots.txt file also works. One useful reason to include it anyway is to point search engines to your XML sitemap. If you don’t have one, you may see 404 entries in your web logs.

No. The provided answer only says that if you use robots.txt, it should be placed in the root directory only, at http://www.example.com/robots.txt. It also notes that there is no general rule preventing bots from crawling directories listed there, and some bots may crawl robots.txt directories too. It does not say robots.txt is strictly required.

No. If you don’t have a robots.txt, it’s generally interpreted as allowing all content to be crawled. The guidance here also recommends using a blank robots.txt to avoid unnecessary 404 errors in your stats, but it is not required.

The thread does not give a recorded answer, so it doesn’t explain the exact reason. It only shows that one author had rich snippets implemented with microdata, the testing tool found no errors, but Google still ignored them after about three weeks. The only guidance in the thread is the mention that Google may ignore microdata in hidden fields. So the closest supported answer is that differences in how the markup is exposed to users—especially if parts are hidden or manipulated by jQuery—could affect whether Google uses it.

Shorter URIs can be better only if they stay user-friendly and descriptive. The guidance here says an SEO-friendly URL should be short and easy to remember, avoid strange characters or query strings, and describe the content rather than use random IDs. 

But shortening a URL just to make it shorter is not inherently beneficial; it can obfuscate the target and, if done without a 301 redirect, can harm PageRank flow. So the best approach is usually a concise slug from the page title, not a generic URL shortener.

Not necessarily. The evidence says the original URL is better than a shortened/redirected one for SEO-related reasons: it passes less link juice through the redirect, can be slower for users and bots, may be more descriptive with keywords, and is more trustworthy and durable. So shorter URLs are not automatically better; the original, descriptive URL is preferred.

The evidence doesn’t address shorter URIs directly. It only supports that if you’re changing domains, the SEO concern is mainly where to set up a 301 redirect so search engines and visitors are moved from the old domain to the new one.

So, based on this, the closest guidance is: use the domain you want to promote as the main one, and 301 redirect the old domain to it if you want to preserve search visibility and avoid confusion.

Google will crawl URLs it becomes aware of, but the evidence here only confirms that if the URL is linked from somewhere Google already knows about, it will certainly grab it. It also suggests Google may not actively crawl a subdomain as a separate entity if it’s only serving resources.

It does not clearly answer whether a completely unlinked static HTML URL will be crawled. The closest supported guidance is: without pointing links, Google may not discover it. If you want it crawled, make sure it’s linked from a known page.

Yes, Google can see a URL if it discovers it somehow, but if there are no links to it anywhere and no other discovery source, it generally won’t find and crawl it. The supported guidance here is that crawlers usually discover pages by following links, or from special XML files; plain-text mentions of the URL can also be found by Google. So a standalone static HTML file with no pointing link is not likely to be crawled unless Google gets the URL another way.

A free option mentioned is the W3C Link Checker, but it is slow and better suited to checking a single page. For a fairly large site, the closest recommendation given is Xenu, a desktop link-checking crawler for Windows. Screaming Frog also checks broken links, but it is not free. If you need something online and free, the evidence doesn’t give a strong recommendation beyond W3C Link Checker.

A1WebsiteAnalyzer is suggested as an easy-to-use tool, and it can be automated with Windows scheduled tasks. Another similar option mentioned is InSpyder, which is said to be the same price and do the same thing.

This doesn’t specifically name a Linux tool. The closest guidance here is that the tools discussed are Windows-based. If you need Linux specifically, this evidence doesn’t provide a confirmed Linux answer.

You can use either one. Google’s guidance says to separate your site name from the rest of the title with a delimiter such as a hyphen, colon, or pipe. So both “|” and “-” are acceptable.

If you want the closest guidance supported here, use whichever fits your branding and readability best, since Google may rewrite the title anyway.

The evidence doesn’t say whether you should use “|” or “-” in a meta title. It only says that Dublin Core meta tags may be useful for people cataloging a site, while Google is more likely to rely on microformats/schema markup for structured data like breadcrumbs, products, pricing, or articles.

So the closest guidance supported here is: this question isn’t answered by the evidence, and the choice of title separator isn’t addressed.

Use the pipe (“|”).

The guidance here says the colon can be confusing if the page title itself contains colons, and if you place the page title first, the colon no longer fits well. The recommended format is:

Top 10 list of stuff | Example.com

If you’re choosing only between “|” and “-”, the evidence directly supports the pipe.

A good approach is not to rely on special characters in the page text. Instead, create a separate, indexable URL for each tag, such as /tagged/mytag, and make pages for items under that tag use URLs like /tagged/mytag/myitem with a canonical URL.

Then, when searching, use the tag URL in the query, for example: inurl:/tagged/mytag

This lets search results match both the user’s search terms and the tag. If you’re using Google Custom Search, this is the simplest supported method described here.

For product-page URLs, the safest characters are letters a-z/A-Z, numbers 0-9, underscore, and hyphen. Other special characters can cause problems, may be URL-encoded, look messy, and can even lead to download issues or 404s in some browsers. If you need to test a character, the only guidance here is to try it in a public page and watch for failures, but the best practice supported is to avoid special characters in URLs and use simple, readable slugs instead.

Local SEO, based on this, is about creating pages that clearly identify each business location/customer with local details like address, phone number, and vendor markup, ideally organized on a single site using subdirectories or subdomains.

It differs from website SEO in that simply making separate websites with changed domain, logo, and title text is not enough; search engines can still detect duplicate or very similar content. For local SEO, the content needs to be genuinely distinct and location-specific, not just cosmetically different.

Local SEO is aimed at helping a business rank for searches in a specific country or language market. The evidence says geotargeting each site in Google and Bing can be a good idea, especially when you have separate domains for different languages/brands.

Website SEO for a single multilingual site is different: if one domain serves content in more than one language, hreflang is recommended. But if you use separate domains, like an English site and a German site, the evidence says hreflang is generally not needed.

So, local SEO here is more about targeting the right region/language, while website SEO for a single site would use hreflang to connect language versions.

Local SEO, based on this, consists of claiming and optimizing local business listings such as Google Places, Bing, and local directories like BOTW. It also includes finding where top local competitors are getting local citations and promoting your business in those places. Depending on the industry, Yelp can also be useful.

This differs from website SEO in that the focus here is on local visibility through listings and citations rather than only on on-site optimization. The provided answer does not explain all aspects of website SEO, so the closest supported guidance is that local SEO is about local directory presence and competitor citation sources.

To rank better for local search, the guidance here says to get listed in Google Places and use the right keywords and relevant categories in that listing. It also recommends putting the city/state in page titles, and showing your address and phone number on every page, plus having About Us, Contact Us, hours, and directions. For local businesses, it helps to list towns/zip codes served, get good reviews on Google and Yelp, create a Facebook page, and earn links from local directories and other local businesses. Make sure every listing has consistent business name, address, phone, and website.

Impressions in Google Webmaster Tools may be much lower than the local search volume even if you see your site ranking highly. The evidence says this can happen because results are personalized by a “filter bubble,” so your site may rank #1 for some users but not for others. It also notes that Webmaster Tools data is not real time and can lag.

So ranking #1 for you does not mean it is #1 for everyone, and impressions won’t necessarily match total search volume.

Google appears to determine those important links by analyzing the breadcrumb navigation on your pages. If you add standard navigational breadcrumbs that show where the page sits in the site hierarchy, Googlebot can pick up that structure and use it in search results. The result is a hierarchy-style snippet with clickable sections.

The provided evidence doesn’t explain how Google determines important links for search results. It only says that Google Custom Search Engine results can be shown on your own site by hosting them in an iframe.

So, based on this evidence, the closest guidance is that you can display Google CSE results on a page you host, but it does not cover how Google selects or ranks important links for search snippets or search results.

Google can infer click behavior from the links it serves, since search results are wrapped with Google parameters when clicked. For making links seem important in results, the answer only supports this much: users are more likely to click results whose title and description match what they’re searching for. So using relevant keywords in your page’s title and description tags can make Google show a more appealing title/snippet, which may increase clicks. It doesn’t say Google ranks “important links” purely from click data, only that clickability and keyword matching can affect what users see and choose.

Create or claim a Google Places page for each location and point it to the matching city-specific landing page. Make sure the NAP information matches exactly across the Places page, your site, and city directories. Getting reviews from customers in each area can also help local rankings.

For the location pages, avoid making them near-identical. Add area-specific specials, photos of the store and staff, a Google Map, and directions. That helps reduce duplicate-content concerns while giving each page enough unique value to support “City Name Service X” searches.

If you have physical offices in only two towns, those are the easiest locations to rank for in local results. For the other counties, it’s harder but still possible if you tell Google the areas you serve and build more citations, social mentions, backlinks, and overall authority.

Having multiple actual offices helps more than just listing service areas. If you don’t have offices in every county, you generally can’t expect the same local visibility there as in the towns where you do have addresses.

Best supported approach: set up your Google/Places listing to reflect your service areas, and focus local SEO efforts on the counties you serve.

It’s hard to rank in Google local results for cities where you don’t have a physical location. The guidance here supports these options: create unique landing pages for each location, include the full address and phone number for each location, use relevant internal links, get inbound links from locally and topically relevant sites, and collect positive reviews for each relevant location page. It also suggests that moving your business location closer to the area you want to rank in can help. For service-area businesses, Google’s local results are strongly address-based, so ranking in a neighboring city is generally difficult without a real location there.

Google local/maps results are ranked by search terms, proximity, relevance, and prominence. A listing can appear in Google web search but not in Maps if those ranking factors don’t favor it. Proximity may depend on your current location, the map area already shown, or location terms in the search. Google Places, Maps, and local listings are not described here as separate listings with a conversion step; the guidance only says ranking affects visibility. If the client wants better Maps/local visibility, the closest supported advice is to review relevance, prominence, and proximity signals in the listing and search terms.

Map listings are ranked mainly by relevance, prominence, and proximity. To improve your position, make sure your listing matches the search terms well, has complete and accurate profile details, and that your location is as relevant to the search as possible. Proximity can depend on where the searcher is, what map view they’re starting from, and whether they include location terms in the search. If your listing is already claimed and fully completed, the main limitation may be distance and search relevance rather than a separate “maps” or “places” listing.

Improve the quality of your links, not just the number of backlinks. The evidence says backlinks quantity is irrelevant; quality matters more. Also, make your URL structure more search-engine friendly, and a keyword in the domain name can help. There are many ranking factors, so a Google Places listing alone doesn’t determine position.

To improve your position in map listings, set up a Places listing yourself. That gives you more control over the location data Google has for your business, which may help Google understand and display your location more effectively. The evidence also points to filling out the listing completely, since that can affect how the information is used and may provide a location-specific search boost.

Submit your site in Bing Webmaster Tools, then check crawl stats and any indexing errors there. Also make sure important pages are discoverable through internal links and that your sitemap is up to date. The advice given also says not to rely on automated sitemap submission tools.

For improving indexing, focus on quality content, good navigation, smaller page size, and faster load time. It also suggests building quality backlinks to important pages so search engines find them more easily.

This does not directly explain how to force a localized view of your data, but it supports making the pages easier for search engines to crawl and index.

Use Google’s alternate language markup. You can mark each page, or your XML sitemap, with the language and country alternatives for that page. Combine that with good linking between the sites and properly optimized content so search engines can find the localized versions and users can navigate to the right one.

Google recommends against automatic redirection based on a user’s perceived language, so it’s better to avoid that if possible.

The supported guidance is that automatic language switching based on Geo-IP or Accept-Language can be problematic, so it’s better not to force it. A safer approach is to create separate language sites or subsites like en.example.com and fr.example.com, let search engines route users naturally, and optionally suggest a language or reorder the language menu based on browser cues.

For hosted website builders, any multilingual CMS could work for behavior-based selection, but using Geo-IP or Accept-Language directly usually requires server-side scripting access, which most hosted CMSs do not provide.

Google’s guidance on “working with multi-regional websites” is the recommended reference for this decision. It covers URL structure options for multilingual sites in detail, including language directories like `/en/` and `/sv/` versus subdomains like `sv.yoursite.com`.

From the evidence here, the closest supported guidance is to follow that Google resource when choosing your SEO-friendly multilingual URL strategy.

The answer in the thread says you should choose the URL structure based on your content, but for language-specific sites it recommends using a subdirectory, like domain.com/language/page, as the standard choice. It also suggests the two formats are not treated the same and points to a technical SEO article comparing subdomains and subdirectories. Based on that, the closest guidance supported is: prefer domain.com/language/page over language.domain.com/page for a multilanguage site.

You’re unlikely to be penalized as long as each language has its own real, unique URL and the content is genuinely translated, not auto-generated.

What matters is not using the same URL for multiple languages via sessions/cookies alone, because search engines would only see one version. Instead, make language switching take users to a language-specific URL, such as separate domains, subdirectories, subdomains, or URL parameters.

So for your setup, don’t just change the session language; also redirect or link users to the correct language URL. That way each version can be found and indexed properly.

The supported approach here is to preprocess the site server-side so each language is delivered as its own apparent copy. The accepted answer says this can be done with PHP conditional includes, which generate a clear version of the site in each language before sending it to the client, so search engines can index each language separately.

It does not compare this with other multilingual SEO setups or say it is definitively the best approach, only that this method can work for SEO indexing.

The thread says there isn’t a clear SEO “winner” from the provided discussion alone. It suggests choosing the structure that best fits your content, and notes that using the main domain with a language path, like domain.com/language/page, was considered the standard and was recommended.

So, based on this, the closest guidance is:
- Both URL styles can work.
- The main-domain subdirectory approach was recommended in that answer.
- The best choice should also be driven by how your content is organized.

A .fr domain is not, by itself, a problem for SEO. The main reason you may get mostly French traffic is that Google.fr is localized to France, while Google.com is a much larger, more competitive pool. Moving to a .com or .org would not, by itself, improve rankings, since the TLD is not a ranking factor in Google.com.

What this supports: your .fr domain can work just as well as .com/.org. If you want more English visitors, focus on making the English version clearly accessible and targeted, rather than changing the domain.

There’s no big SEO advantage to using separate top-level domains, subdomains, or subdirectories for multilingual sites.

The main differences are practical:
- Separate country domains or subdomains can let you host closer to users, which may improve response times and help usability and SEO.
- Subdomains and subdirectories can share cookies, making login and tracking easier across languages.
- Getting separate country-specific domains can be costly and time-consuming.

So from the SEO angle alone, either setup can work. Other factors, like traffic, hosting location, and administration, are likely more important.

GET variables themselves are not said to have bad effects on a page. The answer says Google will recognize and index URLs with GET variables as different pages, such as `page.php?blogId=00001&blogTitle=BlogTitle`.

It also says Google may recognize them better if the URL is written in a cleaner path style like `/00001/BlogTitle/`.

So, based on this, GET variables can be used for separate pages, but the provided guidance suggests cleaner URLs may be preferable for recognition.

GET variables themselves are not described as harmful here. The provided information is about purchased traffic: it says buying visits does not improve rankings, can ruin Analytics data, and is a waste of money because the visits are not real users.

So, based on this, GET variables are not shown to have bad effects on a page. The closest supported guidance is that artificial traffic can distort reporting and may not help SEO, but nothing here says URL parameters themselves are bad.

The main differences are pricing, architecture, and how much management you want to do.

If you want something you don’t have to think about much, traditional hosting is closer to that model. If you want to manage multiple sites without buying a separate hosting account each time, cloud options may fit better.

From the thread:
- Amazon EC2 is more like a VPS: you manage the virtual server, choose the OS, and load your software.
- Google App Engine is a more specialized cloud service, but it only supports Java and Python.
- Azure is Windows-based but can run almost any language through FastCGI.

So the choice depends on your needs:
- Choose web hosting if you want simplicity and minimal server management.
- Choose cloud hosting if you want more flexibility, scalability, and the ability to manage multiple sites or servers yourself.

A shared web host typically keeps your files on one physical machine, and you usually get FTP access to upload them. CloudFront is different: it serves files from many servers around the world, so users get content from the nearest server, which is meant to be faster.

The evidence doesn’t fully compare “web hosting vs cloud hosting” in general, but it does support this: shared hosting is simpler and more like one server with FTP, while CloudFront is a distributed delivery service focused on speed. Amazon’s other cloud services do different things, so the exact choice depends on which cloud service you mean.

Using a CNAME to point `www` to the non-`www` version should not inherently hurt SEO. The guidance here says search engines see a new URL/site either way, so option 1 and option 2 have the same chance for SEO. The main benefit of using your own domain and routing traffic directly is that it’s cleaner for visitors and more professional.

Using a CNAME instead of an A record won’t hurt SEO by itself. Google doesn’t care about the DNS record type; what matters is whether the same content is reachable at both www and non-www URLs.

The SEO issue is duplicate content only if both versions serve the same pages. The usual fix is a 301 redirect from one version to the other. If you can’t do that, use a canonical meta tag to point to your preferred version, and/or set the preferred domain in webmaster tools.

So: CNAME vs A record is not the problem; having both URLs accessible without a clear preferred version is.

You can’t force Google to show your pages exactly the way you want, but you can check the more “real” ranking by using private/incognito browsing so your past visits don’t influence results. You can also check rankings in Google Webmaster Tools, and if you want another option, use an external rank-checking tool like Rankerizer or Serpbook.

You can influence how Google shows your pages by adding proper SEO tags in your page HTML, especially:

<meta name="robots" content="index, follow" />
<meta name="keywords" content="keyword1, keyword2" />
<meta name="description" content="description." />
<title>My Page title</title>

Google also reads the actual page content, so having valid, relevant content and SEO-friendly URLs matters. Just setting tags won’t guarantee how your page appears in search results, but it can help Google understand the title and description you want shown.

If you want Google to find and show your pages differently, the practical step is to have a page that links to the pages you want discovered. Google can follow those links and may crawl them.

That said, this does not guarantee crawl or indexing, even for pages you control. If you don’t control the sites, you can’t use robots.txt or submit a sitemap for them, and there isn’t a simple way here to force Google to scan a list of URLs.

Yes, traffic exchange programs can put you at risk with Google AdSense. The cited AdSense policy says sites displaying Google ads may not use third-party services that generate clicks or impressions, including paid-to-click, paid-to-surf, autosurf, and click-exchange programs.

This evidence only directly covers AdSense, not every pay-per-impression program. The safest guidance supported here is to check each ad network’s policies before using traffic exchange traffic, because at least Google AdSense prohibits it and you could lose your account if you violate that policy.

To preserve SEO, keep enough of the old Crown Heights content on the new /crown-heights page, and don’t change the landing page too much. Use “Crown Heights” as the anchor text for links to that page, and include those links in your menu and/or widget system so they appear on each page. A “Locations” section with “Crown Heights” and “East End” links, plus your sitemap, gives Google stronger cues about which page matches each location search.

Google doesn’t get told directly; it infers the best URL from your content and links. Also, it may still prefer the domain root if it can’t clearly decide.

One recommendation mentioned is SEO PowerSuite from link-assistant.com. The reply says it’s not explicitly endorsed, but suggests it may be cheaper than paying a monthly fee for web-based SEO software. It also notes that the software appears to be updated regularly.

This does not include a comparison of reseller programs, nor does it confirm that this tool provides all the features you listed, such as broken-link reports or title and description recommendations.

Not really. If you don’t want a page to be found for a term like “unicorns,” the supported guidance is to not publish anything about unicorns on that page, or put the unicorn-related content in a private section of your website.

This doesn’t specifically address hiding a whole page from search engines, but it does indicate that simply wanting to exclude a word from indexing on an otherwise public page is not a practical option.

Yes. Search engines can index those as different pages if they are accessible through normal links and the content differs. That applies to URLs like index.php/path/to/page and to query-string URLs like index.php?page=electronics or index.php?page=toys.

If you want a page not to be indexed, this answer does not cover a specific noindex method. The closest supported guidance is to make sure the pages you do want indexed are linked with real links and are crawlable.

If you want a page hidden from users but still crawled by search engines, that pattern is generally discouraged. Showing different content to users and search engines is considered black-hat SEO and may be treated as such.

The guidance here is that if the pages are messy or not useful to users, search engines typically have no need to crawl them, and indexing them could send users there or hurt overall ranking. If your goal is just to keep them out of search results, the safest supported advice is not to rely on cloaking or hiding content differently from users.

For a PDF or other non-HTML file, the supported way is to send an HTTP X-Robots-Tag header with noindex, for example:

X-Robots-Tag: noindex

If you can edit server headers, you can apply it to specific files, such as PDFs, in .htaccess or httpd.conf. For example:

<Files ~ "\.pdf$">
  Header set X-Robots-Tag "noindex, nofollow"
</Files>

robots.txt won’t reliably prevent indexing, because it only blocks crawling. Also, if you block a file in robots.txt, search engines may not be able to see the noindex header.

Use your site’s robots.txt to block the file(s) from being indexed. For example, to block all PDF files:

User-agent: Googlebot
Disallow: /*.pdf$

If you want to block all search engines, use:

Disallow: /*.pdf$

If you only want to block one specific file, block that file path directly:

Disallow: /path/to/pdf/thefilename.pdf

This stops indexing, but it also means any PDF you want indexed later would need a different approach.

The plugin does not automatically submit the sitemap to search engines. It creates a dynamic sitemap at something like /sitemap_index.xml, and you need to submit it yourself to Google, Bing, etc. After submission, you can check the webmaster tools for indexing status. The evidence doesn’t say how often to resubmit; it only supports submitting the sitemap when it’s set up and updated as needed.

You generally only need to submit your sitemap when the site first goes live. After that, the important part is to keep the sitemap up to date so that when Google crawls your site, it can find the latest changes.

A suggested live monitoring option is Chartbeat, which was recommended as a good tool for watching website traffic in real time. Another possibility is using an online chat tool like Olark, since these tools often show who is currently on your website. I can’t confirm more specific features from the provided text, but those are the closest tools it supports.

The thread doesn’t name any SMS APIs or recommend a specific service, so it doesn’t answer which are “best.”

It does indicate the desired features: short code support, opt-in handling, a clean XML/REST API (SOAP acceptable), low cost, easy PHP integration, and US sending.

If you want, I can help narrow options based on those requirements, but I can’t claim any specific APIs from this thread alone.

You can limit scrapers in Apache with modules like mod_security, mod_evasive, or mod_qos. The accepted guidance says these can enforce request-rate limits, concurrent-request limits, and temporary blacklisting of IPs.

mod_evasive is described as blocking an IP if it requests the same page too often, makes too many concurrent requests, or continues while blacklisted. mod_qos can limit requests per second, bandwidth, and connections per source IP.

Fail2ban/IP tables are also mentioned as possible, but the answer says the author personally uses Apache modules. The evidence doesn’t say whether 1000 hits/day is a good threshold or how to exempt Google/Bing specifically.

A practical approach suggested here is to use a spider trap: create a page like /spider-trap/somepage.html, disallow that path in robots.txt, hide a link to it from human visitors, and if a bot reaches it, block that IP for all requests. You can then show a human-readable message and an IP-unlock CAPTCHA page.

This doesn’t fully cover rate-based blacklisting of “too many pages too fast,” but it does support detecting scrapers, blocking them, and requiring a CAPTCHA to regain access.

You can file a DMCA complaint with Google to remove the copied content from search results. You do not need an “official copyright” registration; if you created the content, you already own the copyright. The evidence here supports using Google’s DMCA notice process:

https://www.google.com/webmasters/tools/dmca-notice?rd=1&pli=1

This answer only covers getting content removed from Google search results. It does not say how to force the other site to stop using it or whether Google will take any further action.

The supported way described here is to set up a Promotion. In the Control Panel at google.com/cse, go to Search Features > Promotions, then define “yoga” as the triggering query and yoursite.com/mypage as the promoted URL.

That will ensure /mypage is shown for that query, rather than just loosely boosting it. If you want a “top result” behavior for a specific search term on a single site, this is the closest guidance provided.

Neither page views nor time spent on page affects Google PageRank. If you mean search-result rankings, the closest guidance here is to focus on what makes visitors happiest.

For a single-page site, that usually means helping users find what they want quickly and clearly, rather than chasing more clicks or longer visits. The most important thing mentioned is avoiding “bounce back”: users clicking your result, then returning to the search results because they didn’t find what they wanted.

If users can get the answer on one page, that can be perfectly fine.

The official term is “sitelinks.” A standard listing is just a search result, and a search result with extra links is called a search result with sitelinks.

If you mean improving a single-page site’s appearance in search results, the closest guidance here is to focus on earning sitelinks, since that’s the term Google uses for those expanded results.

If you mean a one-page parallax site with navigation links, the answer depends on what you want for SEO and browser behavior.

Using anchors/hashes is simpler and helps users land on the right section directly, and it avoids needing full browser-history routing code. It also supports your goal of returning to the previous section/page without repeated back clicks.

For SEO, the source suggests that if you use hashes, you need to tell Google how to crawl the hash content so it can index the specific section. If you use full URLs with pushState, you must make those URLs fully accessible to crawlers.

Based on the provided guidance, anchors/hashbangs were considered the cleaner, easier approach.

Based on the provided answer, anchor fragments in URLs do not affect SEO rankings. So `website.com/cotton` and `website.com/cotton#green` are treated the same for ranking purposes.

What it does support is that the anchor part after `#` is not considered to change ranking. If your concern is SEO, the supported guidance here is to use anchors for on-page navigation without expecting ranking differences.

Yes, Google can understand hidden content and take it into account for rankings, so preloading both sub-sections and toggling them with JavaScript is generally fine for SEO.

What this does not fully guarantee is that Google will show multiple separate entries for the same page. Based on the evidence, the closer guidance is that one page with hidden/toggled content is acceptable and may help avoid competing pages. It doesn’t say Google will show multiple separate entries for different sections of the same page. The closest supported guidance is that multiple pages work better for SEO because each page can focus on one topic, and internal links can help a little.

For a one-page website, Google can show multiple results that link to different sections only if it can identify separate section URLs or jump links. The evidence here only covers Google Ads keyword entry and phrase/negative match, not SEO or sitelinks on organic results.

Closest guidance supported: use distinct keywords/phrases for the sections you want to target, but this does not show how Google will display multiple organic entries for one page.

If you mean search results with links to sections on the same page, you’d need section-specific anchors or separate pages; this evidence doesn’t confirm whether Google will show them.

Using heading tags as links is normal and common, and the example given is not considered to have an SEO downside. The evidence says this can be used on pages like WordPress post headers and StackExchange question titles, where the title is both a link and an h1.

It does not specifically say that using h1, h2, h3 links will encourage Google sitelinks. So the closest supported answer is: this linking pattern is acceptable, but there’s no evidence here that it will directly promote sitelinks.

It doesn’t say that using headings as internal links would encourage Google sitelinks. So the closest supported answer is that headings can help signal structure and importance, but there’s no evidence here that internal-linking with headings will trigger or encourage sitelinks.

A single-page website isn’t necessarily “bad” for SEO, but it can be harder to rank well for specific topics. With only one page, you usually have one title, one h1, and one meta description, so the page tends to cover multiple topics instead of being focused on one.

If your services are distinct, multiple pages are generally better because each page can target one topic more clearly. Internal linking between those pages can also help a little.

A single-page website may not be the best for SEO, but that alone doesn’t mean it’s bad. For bad URLs like /anything, the supported guidance here favors a 301 redirect to the front page rather than a 404, mainly for user experience. The answer says this won’t necessarily damage rankings, and that you should use other SEO tactics as well.

I can’t confirm from the available information whether those “unlimited free SSL certificates” are safe or resellable. The only thing the thread shows is that this question was asked and no answer is on record.

The thread doesn’t contain a recorded solution, so it only confirms the issue: AdSense data shows for one site but not the second, and the second site reports that AdSense needs to be connected first.

Short URLs can be better for SEO if they are also descriptive and user-friendly. The guidance here says an SEO-friendly URL should be short, easy to remember, free of strange characters or query strings, and should describe the content and site structure. It also says you do not need a unique number in the URL.

However, shortening just for the sake of shortening is not useful if it hides what the page is about. A short URL does not create extra overhead by itself, but URL shorteners may interfere with PageRank flow unless they use a 301 redirect. In most cases, generate a slug from the page title.

URL length is not likely to affect page load speed in any meaningful way. If the request stays under a typical packet size, a URL of 30 bytes versus 1300 bytes makes no practical difference, and even if it spans two packets the impact is negligible.

For SEO and usability, keep URLs reasonably short, ideally under 100 characters. The main reason is readability and user experience, not speed.

The answer here is that there is no particular hard limit for URI length, and you should keep URLs manageable for usability rather than trying to pack in keywords. For your example, the Unicode form is an IRI, and the %-encoded form is the valid URI version of the same address. Browsers and search engines with IRI support should treat both the same. The evidence does not give a specific SEO length limit or say which exact “length” search engines use, only that both forms are equivalent and that URL length should not be an area of concern beyond keeping it reasonable.

The evidence suggests that some users do care and like to see descriptive URLs before clicking, especially on forums, but many users don’t know or don’t care about URL format. It also says Google gives some weight to SEO-friendly URLs, so descriptive URLs are generally a wise choice. In short, the average user usually isn’t strongly affected, but SEO-friendly URLs can still help both user trust in some cases and search visibility.

Having many single-depth pages should not hurt SEO by itself. The accepted guidance says sites with thousands of pages at the root can still rank well, and the lack of folder depth doesn’t appear to be a ranking factor.

The proposed structure is considered good: category pages like /galleries/rabbits and image landing pages like /photos/bunny1. A useful alternative is to have a main category plus other categories/tags, which can add a keyword to the URL and make the site structure clearer for users.

If an image belongs to multiple galleries, the closest supported suggestion is to choose one main category for the image page and let it also appear in other category pages.

Using an underscore for “private” folders is generally fine for tidiness and separation, and the provided guidance says there are no known negatives to doing that.

For SEO/page rank, this evidence doesn’t show any direct benefit from underscore-based naming. It only supports keeping system folders separate and using regular names for user-facing paths. It also suggests keeping such special folders to a small number at the root, and putting server-side scripts above the document root if you want them truly separated.

So, the closest supported guidance is: use clear, user-friendly folder names in URLs, and reserve underscore-prefixed folders for internal/system files.

If the search term is “John Smith,” the full-name URL `/johnsmith` is the closer match and is likely to be more SEO friendly than `/john`. The guidance here is that a URL matching the full target query can help target a more refined search term. So for that specific name search, `/johnsmith` is the better choice.

The first format is more SEO friendly and more user friendly. If you want the convenience of the second format, you can still make URLs look like the first while behaving like the second using mod_rewrite. A basic mod_rewrite tutorial would show how to do that.

For a blog with posts and categories, the evidence only supports these SEO-friendly steps:

- Use an SEO plugin like WordPress SEO by Yoast, which gives on-page optimization tips.
- Use clean permalink-style URLs for posts and category pages, since the goal is user-friendly and search-friendly structure.
- Generate and submit XML sitemaps through the SEO plugin to Google Webmaster Tools and Bing.
- If you use images or videos, create separate image and video sitemaps too.

It does not list the full “best ways” for URL structure specifically, but the closest supported guidance is to keep URLs simple, descriptive, and backed by sitemaps and on-page SEO tools.

For a blog with posts and categories, the most user-friendly and SEO-friendly URL style supported here is a clean, semantic one like:

mysite.com/category-name/page-name

File extensions like .html or .php are not the important SEO factor. The text in the URL matters more, but content, titles, meta descriptions, and clean markup matter much more than the extension. A trailing slash is also not the key issue.

Best guidance: keep URLs short, readable, and focused on users. If you can, avoid IDs and extra clutter like pageid-123 unless needed for routing. Use the category and post name only when possible.

For user-friendly and SEO-friendly blog URLs, the closest guidance here is to keep URLs targeted to the specific topic rather than forcing everything into one generic category.

A good approach is:
- Use clear, descriptive slugs for each post
- Include the most relevant category only if it helps make the URL more specific
- Prefer targeted URLs that match the page’s main intent
- If you need broader topic variants, use canonical URLs so duplicates point to one main page
- Avoid creating many competing versions of the same post

In practice, more specific URLs tend to rank faster and attract more targeted traffic, while broader URLs may take longer to compete.

The supported options here are to ask for link removal or use Google’s disavow tool. The guidance also suggests disavow is usually unnecessary because Google often ignores spam links on its own, unless the bad backlink profile is especially strong.

So the closest best-practice advice supported by this is:
- Try to remove the offending links if possible.
- If not, disavow the specific bad links/pages.
- Don’t rely on waiting for a warning first; the evidence doesn’t support that as a required step.
- Removing the internal page and leaving a 404 is not presented here as a link-cleanup solution.

The evidence says backlinks are still a major ranking factor in Google, especially high-quality, freely given links. It also says links created by dropping them in forums, comments, or directories are not the kind that help. 

For internal links specifically, this evidence doesn’t directly address them. The closest guidance it supports is to focus on useful, original content and a link strategy that naturally earns or supports relevant citations, rather than artificial link dropping.

Using nofollow on internal links is a bad idea based on this guidance. It says nofollow should generally be used only for links you don’t trust, usually third-party or spammy links, not for your own site’s internal links.

It also says there is no such thing as “too many” internal links confusing search engines in the way described. You don’t need to minimize internal links just to help bots. Internal links are useful for SEO, pass value around your site, and their anchor text helps rankings.

So the closest supported advice is: use clear, relevant internal anchor text for users and SEO, and don’t add nofollow to internal links just to reduce them.

The best-supported method here is to block that URL pattern in robots.txt, for example:

Disallow: /module/get/

If you also want to reduce crawling signals from the link itself, you can add rel="nofollow" to the download link, but that does not guarantee it won’t be indexed. Based on the provided answer, robots.txt disallow is the strongest option for preventing bots from accessing anything under /module/get/.

The most effective use of URL slugs is to make them short, human-readable, and keyword-focused. Use the 2–3 most important words for the page, or up to 4–5 if needed, and keep them conversational rather than long or numeric. Slugs help users understand the page and give search engines a clue about the content, but they are not a major direct ranking factor. If you already have readable slugs, shorter ones are generally better and more memorable.

Google can show a page with a “rich result” style snippet, but from the information here I can only say this: make sure your archive/home page has a strong, concise title tag, a proper meta description, and only one H1 for the page. Blog post titles in the listing should be links, not H1s; H2 is safer if you use headings.

If Google is showing the archive page instead of the post, it may be because it sees that page as the best match. To reduce that, make the post page’s title tag clearly unique and relevant, and keep the archive page’s title/description focused on the archive, not the individual post.

Sign up for Google Webmaster Tools and monitor your site there. The answer also suggests that Google’s results may just be out of sync across different servers and datacenters, so your site can appear on one and not another for a while. Since the site only ranked yesterday, give it some time and watch for changes.

This does not specifically explain how to get a last post date or secondary links in Google results.

The provided information only says that republishing articles from other sites is “content scraping,” and that Google does not like non-original content. It does not explain how to get a site to show on Google with a last post date or secondary links.

Closest guidance supported here: use original content rather than scraped/republished content, because non-original content is discouraged by Google and may violate copyright.

The best choice here is the category/subcategory URL, since it clearly shows relevant search terms and helps search engines relate the page to queries.

So among the options, `/category/:name/subcategory/:name/offer/:title-:number` is the strongest SEO-wise.

As for word order, the evidence doesn’t show a meaningful SEO difference between formats like `/users/:id/offer/:title` and `/offer/:title-:number`; the important part is that the URL is descriptive and includes the relevant terms.

If the URLs are static, there are only minor SEO differences between permalink styles. The main practical advantages mentioned are:

- shorter URLs are more readable and may display better in search results
- avoiding special characters and using hyphens is preferred
- including the date is not necessary for SEO, but can help if you need uniqueness

So a shorter, clean URL like /articolo-d-esempio.htm is supported as a good choice. If uniqueness is a concern, adding the date after the title, like /articolo-d-esempio-22042013.htm, is a reasonable alternative.

If you’re targeting the search term “John Smith,” the `http://example.com/johnsmith` URL is the better fit, since it matches the full query more closely. The evidence supports that this exact-match URL would likely be more SEO friendly for that specific search term.

If you’re targeting the exact search term “John Smith,” the evidence says `http://example.com/johnsmith` would be better, because it matches the full query more closely. It suggests the fuller, more refined term is likely the better SEO choice.

Based on this, the better SEO choice is the shorter URL. There’s no evidence that matching the URL to the breadcrumb helps SEO. A shorter, cleaner URL is clearer for users and easier to remember or type.

There’s no real SEO advantage among those URL variations. The closest guidance supported here is that shorter, clearer directory names are easier for users to read and may be more clickable in search results.

So, for both SEO and usability, the clearest option is:

Without quotes or other modifiers, the default search is broad. So for “back office in mumbai,” the closest match is broad, like:

Keep the URL simple and easy to read.

If you mean the best URL/approach for a cars-related site, the guidance here is to focus on quality, descriptive page titles and content rather than trying to force exact-match anchor text through link trades.

It also suggests starting with easier, more specific car-related keywords first, because they rank faster, bring targeted traffic, and can help you grow into more competitive terms like “used cars.”

There’s no real SEO advantage among those URL variations. The clearest, most readable option is:

Shorter, understandable directory names are easier for users to read and may get more clicks in search results.

You don’t need to use robots.txt to handle those URLs. If they return 404, that’s normal and won’t hurt crawling, indexing, or ranking. In fact, disallowing them can be worse, because if Google can’t crawl a URL, it may still get indexed. If Google can crawl it and see the 404, it won’t index it.

Use Fiddler. It’s an HTTP sniffer that shows all requests made by the page; on a secure page, requests should appear with a padlock and use HTTPS. Anything not shown that way is being served insecurely.

The provided material doesn’t give a direct answer for finding unsecured content on a webpage. It only shows an example where Google Ads served over HTTP caused browsers to warn about unsecured content after SSL was enabled.

Closest guidance supported by this is: unsecured content can come from elements like ads loaded over HTTP on an HTTPS page. To find it, inspect the page for non-HTTPS resources such as ads, images, scripts, or iframes. If you want, I can suggest common browser tools or a checklist for locating mixed content.

Use a traffic inspector like Fiddler to see what the browser is requesting over regular HTTP. In Fiddler’s default setup, HTTPS requests show a lock and CONNECT as the host, while HTTP requests show a non-lock icon. That will help you identify the unsecured content on the page.

Firefox’s warning means the HTTPS page is loading at least one resource over plain HTTP. Typical causes are images, stylesheets, scripts, Flash objects, or content injected by JavaScript. A good way to find the source is to inspect the page’s network requests with a tool like Fiddler; on a secure page, requests should show HTTPS and a padlock. Anything not using HTTPS is the insecure element.

This is most likely because not all page elements are being loaded over HTTPS.

Check the page source for any `http://` references, including scripts, images, CSS, and other resources. Local scripts should use `/path/script.js` or `https://...`, not `http://...`.

If any element is loaded insecurely, Firefox may report the page as partially encrypted or containing non-secure elements.

Firefox is warning because part of the page is not secure, even if the form submits to HTTPS. The setup described is not recommended: the login page, verification page, and return page should all use a secure connection. Collecting credentials on a non-secure page can communicate with the server over a non-secure connection, which is a security issue. If Firefox says an HTTPS page contains non-secure elements, the closest guidance here is to move all login-related pages and resources to HTTPS.

If your robots.txt is empty or removed, Google may treat that as an error for a while. Use an explicit allow-all robots.txt instead:

Google usually takes at least a week, and sometimes up to a month, to index a site after this change. It can index pages it has already crawled before finishing the whole site.

To speed crawling, the main lever mentioned is improving the site’s reputation with more high-quality inbound links, since crawl rate is governed mainly by PageRank.

site:yourdomain.com inurl:pattern text
