The evidence doesn’t provide a self-service way to determine which Google account owns a tracking code.

I can’t confirm a direct fix from the material provided, because the thread has no recorded answer.

What it does show is that someone else’s site is using your Google Analytics tracking code and that this can skew your data. The closest guidance supported here is to treat it as a site compromise / misuse issue and remove or replace the tracking code on any site you control, then verify your Analytics data for unwanted referrals or traffic.

If the other site is not under your control, the evidence does not say whether you can block or disassociate it from Analytics.

The only thing shown here is that the tracking status is “Tracking Not Installed,” but there’s no recorded fix.

Closest guidance: make sure the Google Analytics code is actually installed on the site header you’re testing, and that the tracking ID matches your property. In the example, the code uses `UA-0000000-0`, which is just a placeholder-looking ID. If someone else is using your tracking ID, you’d typically need to change to your own valid tracking code and verify it’s added to the correct page before the redirect happens.

The evidence only addresses product descriptions and meta descriptions, not menu-link descriptions. It says unique product content can help SEO by avoiding duplicate content, but meta descriptions do not affect Google rankings. So for menu links, this evidence does not show a direct SEO benefit. The closest supported guidance is that adding unique descriptive content can be useful where it improves page uniqueness, but description text itself is not shown here to be a ranking factor.

The evidence doesn’t mention descriptions on menu links specifically, so it doesn’t show any direct SEO value from adding them.

What it does support is that well-built menu links in the page source are generally fine for SEO, and navigation helps bots crawl a site. It also suggests keeping link counts reasonable, though not to worry too much beyond that when needed.

So the closest supported answer is: adding descriptions may help users, but there’s no evidence here that it has SEO value by itself.

Based on this, adding a description to menu links isn’t described as having a special SEO benefit. The guidance here says search engines focus more on the page’s content section than on exact placement of the menu, and that internal links can help because they signal importance and improve linking. So the supported takeaway is: descriptions may be useful for users, but this evidence only supports that internal links themselves matter, not that adding descriptions to menu links adds SEO value.

Adding the company or domain name in the title is mainly for branding, not SEO. The guidance here says it has little to no value for search engines by itself. It can make sense on a homepage or if you want users to recognize the brand, especially if the brand already has strong reputation. Otherwise, it may waste title space that could be used for keywords.

Adding the company name to a title attribute is not supported as an SEO benefit here. Search engines don’t use title attributes for keyword relevance, and repeating keywords or adding extra branding there won’t help rankings. If the title attribute is used, it should give users useful supplementary information, not just duplicate or stuff keywords. Overdoing it could be seen as over-optimization.

Not necessarily. The guidance says that if you use a CDN with your hosting, you don’t have to pay attention to where the main server is located, because visitors get content from the nearest CDN server. That can improve loading speed and reduce load on the main server for users in different countries.

If you are not using a CDN, the evidence does not clearly say whether the server must be in the same country. It only supports that a CDN makes location less important.

Not necessarily. The guidance here says content for different regions/languages can be on different URLs without being a duplicate-content problem, as long as it is meant for different users in different countries. It also says there is generally no need to hide duplicates with robots.txt or noindex.

If the same content is shown to the same users on multiple URLs, then choose a preferred version and use redirects or rel=canonical. This does not say you must physically host the site in the target country. It supports using the proper regional URL structure and handling duplicates correctly.

Google gets those links by indexing pages it has crawled and finding pages that link to the queried site. The link: operator then shows pages in Google’s index that point to that site, such as link:stackexchange.com. The provided material does not say how Google initially discovers all those links beyond crawling/indexing. It also notes that Bing does not appear to have an equivalent operator, and Yahoo searches are likely powered by Bing.

The only method supported here is to search Google for your site using the site: operator, for example:

site:www.example.com

That can show you URLs Google has indexed for your site. This doesn’t provide a complete crawl list, but it’s the closest way mentioned to see what Google has indexed.

Google treats links to a URL with a named anchor like /mypage.html#section1 as links to the page itself for ranking purposes. The fragment part mainly helps the browser jump to a section on the page; it does not change the ranking effect of the link.

So if you’re asking where Google “gets” these links from, it can see links pointing either to the full page or to a section anchor, but the anchor part is not counted as a separate ranking signal.

Based on this evidence, URL shorteners like bit.ly mainly affect referrer tracking, not SEO directly. A 301 redirect passes the browser’s referrer again, so analytics can still show the original source, such as Twitter, instead of “direct.” If someone types the short URL directly, it would count as direct. The evidence does not say whether URL shorteners impact search rankings, only that they usually preserve the referrer through redirects.

URL shorteners like bit.ly generally do not hurt SEO. According to the cited answer, they resolve to the full long URL and are treated like a 301 permanent redirect, so they should not hinder crawling, reduce PageRank, or negatively affect organic search results.

What this covers: normal use of short URLs that redirect to your full page. It does not address any separate branding, tracking, or user-experience effects.

It depends on the redirect the shortener uses. If the service uses a 301 permanent redirect, the link equity should pass through to your site. Some shorteners use 302 temporary redirects, but search engines may treat them similarly to 301s in practice because of the service’s reputation/profile. So URL shorteners like bit.ly do not necessarily hurt SEO; the key factor is how they redirect.

Shortened URLs can affect SEO indirectly if they create duplicate content across URLs, but the main risk in the evidence is from the same content appearing on both a Tumblr blog and your website. That can negatively impact rankings unless the content is embedded via an iframe or you use canonical URLs to indicate the preferred page.

The safest supported approach is to show snippets or a feed that links back to the original, or consolidate the content onto one site.

Yes, according to the evidence, keywords in the URL can affect search engine rankings and are described as one of the more important SEO ranking factors, alongside page titles and domain name.

That said, the impact is presented as part of many ranking factors, not the only one. The evidence also suggests pretty URLs are useful for users, since people still type URLs by hand and well-structured URLs can still work even if part is missing.

So the closest supported answer is: URL structure can matter for rankings, but it’s only one factor among many.

Based on the provided answer, URL anchors do not affect SEO rankings. It doesn’t address URL shorteners specifically, but the closest supported guidance is that adding an anchor fragment to a URL does not change ranking.

Short URLs like goo.gl or bitly generally do not hurt ranking. They usually resolve to the full long URL with a 301 permanent redirect, so they don’t block crawling or reduce PageRank. Based on this, they should not negatively affect organic search results.

Short URLs can indirectly affect ranking, but the main issue is usually that they pass less link value than the original URL and add a redirect. They may also be slower, less descriptive, and less trustworthy, which can hurt user experience. Search engines try to surface links users will want, so those factors can matter for SEO.

Best practice: use the original URL whenever possible rather than a shortened one.

Short URLs can affect ranking only through the redirect they use. If the shortener uses a 301 permanent redirect, the link value should pass to your site. Some services use 302 temporary redirects, but search engines often treat them like 301s for well-known shorteners. So short URLs like goo.gl or bitly are generally not a problem for SEO if they redirect properly.

The effective/necessary method is to return HTTP 301 permanent redirects from the bad URLs to the correct URLs. That tells search engines to drop the old URLs and index the target instead. If the URLs are already fixed and now return 404s, Google will eventually remove them, but that can take time.

To help Google recrawl the right pages faster, keep an XML sitemap of the actual pages updated. You can also temporarily increase the crawl rate in Webmaster Tools if your server can handle it.

The evidence does not support a separate batch-removal tool as the best solution; it suggests redirects as the main fix.

The quickest effective methods are to let Google crawl the URL and return a removal signal like 410 Gone or 403 Forbidden, or use a proper noindex directive. Robots.txt disallow alone only stops crawling and won’t remove already indexed pages.

For fast removal, make sure:
- the page is actually returning 410 or 403 to Googlebot site-wide,
- or the page contains a valid noindex, without conflicting robots meta tags,
- and your Google removal request is in place.

In the case described, the suspected issues were that the .htaccess rule may not have been working site-wide, and the meta robots setup was conflicting.

I don’t see any evidence about removing URLs from Google’s index. The provided material only covers reducing page bandwidth: gzip/deflate, minifying JS/CSS, caching, merging files, moving static assets to a separate domain, and using sprites.

For quick index removal, the closest supported guidance I can give is that this evidence does not address it. You’d need a source specifically about Google indexing, such as robots directives, noindex, removals in Search Console, or removing the page itself.

Google does not care about having identical internal markup or templates across pages. Based on the answer provided, Google focuses on the page content, not the graphical design or structure. It may do some basic stylesheet checks for things like cloaking, but duplicate layouts or themes themselves are not treated as duplicate content.

So if your internal subdomains have the same design, that alone is not the issue. The closest guidance supported here is to make the content itself unique and relevant; Google’s concern is the content, not the template.

Use robots.txt or a meta robots tag to stop Google from crawling/indexing the unwanted subdomain pages. Since the pages were never placed on the subdomains, adding canonical tags there may also help signal the main URL as the preferred version. If the subdomains have unique content you want indexed, block only the duplicate pages, not the whole subdomains.

Google is likely not treating those URLs as duplicate content if it’s showing them separately in results. If you want only one version indexed, the supported options are to add a rel="canonical" tag from the parameterized pages to the main URL, use Google’s parameter handling to choose “No URLs,” or 301 redirect the extra URLs to the preferred one. After Google recrawls, the extra URLs should drop from the index, but it can take weeks. If they aren’t hurting traffic or SERPs, you may also leave them as-is.

You can remove a page or site from Google’s search results, but it won’t happen immediately. If you’ve already deleted the old pages and used a URL removal request, Google still may show them for a while before the change takes effect.

To replace old URLs with new ones, make sure the new pages are live and the old ones are removed. Then wait for Google to recrawl and update its index. If the old URLs are still appearing in Webmaster Tools, that may also take time to clear.

Google usually won’t swap old URLs for new ones immediately. The closest guidance here is to make sure Google can crawl the new pages: check that robots.txt isn’t blocking them, make sure there’s no noindex tag, and optionally submit a sitemap. If you already removed the old URLs, the main next step is to wait for reindexing; it can take about 2–4 weeks, depending on the site and crawl frequency. Once Google has indexed the new URLs, the old ones should fade out and the new ones may appear in search and sitelinks.

Google’s cache does not include the CSS, JavaScript, or images from a page—only the HTML is shown. So there isn’t a way to view the currently used CSS from Google’s cached copy. The closest option supported by this is to access the original site source or archive it elsewhere if you need to recreate the styles.

A close match is Paletton (formerly colorschemedesigner.com). It lets you choose colors and shows example pages so you can see how a scheme looks applied to a typical page. It’s more for color schemes than for inspecting the currently used CSS definitions on a live page.

A Firefox add-on called CSS Usage can show which styles are used and unused on a page. It is reported to support multiple pages, though its results may be somewhat unreliable. If you need to check CSS during local development, this is the closest tool mentioned that fits those constraints.

Use `data-href="http://example.com"` on the +1 button for your site. That makes people +1 the specific web page URL you want, instead of your Google+ page. The earlier +1s were being collected for the Google+ page, so they won’t carry over automatically, but you can collect new +1s for the correct URL.

The thread doesn’t provide a solution, and it says there’s no answer on record.

So based on the evidence, there’s no confirmed way shown to make a Google +1 button count for a different specific URL or to transfer +1s from a path like `http://example.com/tag1-tag2/2525` to the domain `http://example.com`.

The closest guidance supported is that the question was about whether +1s could be aggregated at the domain level instead of the path level, but no answer is given.

Yes. Based on the provided answer, if the parent page has `meta name="robots" content="nofollow"`, Google will not index that page or follow links inside it, and the iframe page also will not be indexed unless it’s reachable from another page without `nofollow`. A sitemap is suggested as an alternative way to get the iframe pages indexed.

If you want the widget content to help the SEO of the sites that embed it, using a div is better than an iframe. The provided guidance says Google doesn’t index iframes, so widget content inside an iframe is unlikely to benefit the host page’s SEO. A div, on the other hand, can be indexed on the page where it appears, so that’s the closer match to what you want.

What it does not cover is how much SEO benefit you’ll actually get in practice, only that divs are preferable to iframes for indexing.

A widget like that is generally not a duplicate-content SEO problem if it’s just sidebar or supporting text shown across pages. Search engines can usually tell it isn’t the main content of each page.

The closest guidance here is that duplicate content issues are mainly caused by repeating the main content of a page, not common elements like headers, footers, or sidebars.

This doesn’t directly say how much SEO benefit you get from a widget living on other sites, only that having the same widget text on multiple pages is not, by itself, considered risky for SEO.

A widget on other sites is mainly about easy syndication and reach, not a guaranteed SEO boost.

The example suggests using an iframe/widget with customizable styling, and possibly RSS for content delivery. That helps people place your content on their sites, but the answer does not say it improves search rankings directly.

Closest guidance: if the widget gets your content and links displayed on other sites, it may help exposure and traffic, but SEO value depends on how search engines can crawl and attribute it. If it’s inside an iframe, that often limits SEO benefit compared with crawlable HTML content.

For non-marketing SEO guidance, the best-supported sources here are Google’s guide for webmasters and Yahoo!/Bing’s SEO style guide. A reputable resource also mentioned is seomoz.org. That covers general SEO information, but this thread doesn’t specifically address navigation, company info, or video SEO.

Create crawlable static pages in addition to the search field: pages by company type, alphabetic order, or industry category, each listing the companies in that group. Link those category pages from the home page, since that’s often crawled first. You can also add a “top 10 companies” section on the home page based on search trends. Submitting sitemaps can help too. The evidence doesn’t say how to handle video specifically, but for indexing the company info pages, the strongest guidance is to provide static, linked pages rather than relying only on search queries and tags.

Google is likely to see this more as a bad multilingual user experience than a classic duplicate-content problem.

If the German page only translates menus/navigation but the main video/title/meta content stays in English, German users may land there and not be able to consume the page well. That can hurt the site if it happens broadly.

Closest guidance supported here: don’t let untranslated pages be indexed. Use robots.txt or a meta robots noindex tag for content that isn’t properly translated.

If you want the widget content to help the customer’s page rank, use a div rather than an iframe. The guidance here says Google does not index iframes, so the embedded content is unlikely to benefit SEO on the host page. Using a div is the better option for getting the widget content indexed on other people’s sites.

A shorter, more exact anchor text is generally more targeted for that exact query, but it can still help broader related queries too. So “widget” would tend to help “widget” most, “blue widget” would help both “blue widget” and “widget,” and “best blue widget” would be the most specific and least directly targeted of the three for the shorter terms.

But it’s not a simple 3x3 rule. The value of a link also depends a lot on the linking page’s relevance and strength. A relevant site linking with “best blue widget” may help more than an unrelated site using just “widget.”

An iframe’s content is not considered part of the parent page, so it can be bad for SEO if you’re relying on that embedded content to help the page rank.

The example provided doesn’t prove that frames are good for SEO, since a site can rank for many reasons besides using frames. The closest supported guidance here is: avoid relying on frame/iframe content for SEO, because search engines may not treat it as part of the main page.

The answer provided doesn’t really address SEO directly. It mainly says iFrames are discouraged because ad-blockers may hide iframe content, so some users may not see your images. It also suggests you can float the iframe to wrap text next to it.

So, based on this, the closest guidance is: iFrames aren’t described as a direct SEO problem here, but they are discouraged for usability/visibility reasons. If you want text to wrap beside it, use CSS float, e.g. `iframe { float:left; }`.

Having embed code on other sites is not shown here to increase SEO rank. The only supported guidance is that SEO is more about semantically correct HTML, good content, and good links. Poor or confusing source code is not said to be penalized as long as the HTML uses elements correctly. If the embed makes pages slower, that could affect SEO indirectly, but no direct ranking boost from embeds is supported by this information.

Yes, but only indirectly if the embed creates links pointing to your page. The evidence says Google PageRank itself is based solely on the number and quality of links to a specific page.

For overall search rankings, many factors matter, including PageRank, relevance, titles/headings, and page speed. Good HTML generally does not improve rank by itself unless the code is so bad that search engines can’t read the page.

The provided material does not answer whether embed code on other sites can increase SEO rank. It only says that embedded content from another website may be protected by copyright and recommends getting permission from the rightful owner before using it.

So, based on this evidence, I can’t confirm any SEO benefit. The closest supported guidance is that if you plan to embed someone else’s content, you should first obtain written permission from the site owner.

The evidence suggests improving the widget’s presentation and discoverability rather than changing the widget itself. A good approach is to create a cleaner page for generating the widget and include screenshots so bloggers can see what it looks like. You could also add a small credit in the map itself, such as “This map was generated using Come Hike,” with the site name linked back to your site. That gives bloggers a visible, easy way to recognize and use it.

Use a widget that provides HTML and JavaScript, then copy and paste that code into your post. For example, if you want recent posts displayed inside a Blogger post, you can use FeedBurner’s BuzzBoost widget: set it up in FeedBurner under Publicize > BuzzBoost, generate the HTML, and paste it into the post. This is the closest supported method for adding a widget within a blog post itself.

The closest guidance here is that shorter, more focused anchor text is generally better for ranking that exact term, so a link that says “widget” helps “widget” more than “best blue widget” does. But the value of a link also depends heavily on the linking site’s relevance and authority, so a relevant widget site with “best blue widget” can be more useful than an unrelated site linking with just “widget.”

If your goal is to rank for “widget,” a practical approach is to start with longer-tail phrases like “best blue widget” and work toward more generic terms over time.

If the link is placed in a noscript tag just to show it to search engines, that’s essentially cloaking and violates search engines’ terms. The safer/acceptable use is to put alternate content in noscript for users who don’t support JavaScript.

So, if the backlink is only there for SEO, don’t do it. If it’s genuinely an alternative for non-JavaScript users, then that’s the proper use of noscript.

Using JavaScript to replace real links is not a reliable way to hide them from Google. The answer indicates Google can parse JavaScript pretty well, and links created this way may still pass PageRank, so it may undo the intended effect.

It also says `rel="nofollow"` PageRank sculpting has not worked for years. The practical guidance given is: if links are unverified user-generated content, use `nofollow`; if you or your client added them as editorial content, they should be normal links; if they’re bad links, don’t include them.

Google treats a subdomain and a third-party domain as different sites, so backlinks would not be “one and the same” just because the blog is mapped. If your goal is to make the blog add value to the main domain, the guidance here says subdomains or third-party hosted blogs are probably not what you want; a directory like /blog/ is preferred. If you use a third-party blogging service, the supported way described is reverse proxying the /blog/ path to pull content from their servers. I can’t confirm anything specific about JavaScript-generated backlinks from a third-party site from this evidence.

If you want the widget content to help the customer’s page get indexed, use a div rather than an iframe. The guidance here says Google does not index iframes and is unlikely to start anytime soon. So for SEO benefit on the site where the widget is embedded, serving the content in a div is the supported option.

It likely won’t help SEO to add those link tags in the iframe widget. The answer says search engines should identify the relationship without explicitly adding link tags like those.

If your goal is to prevent crawlers from indexing the widget, the guidance given is to use a noindex-related tag instead.

So, for visibility/SEO, the supported advice here is: adding those `<link>` tags probably won’t make a meaningful difference. If you want, I can help suggest a better way to structure the widget for SEO.

An iframe from another page can have some SEO value if a search engine crawls and recognizes it, but it is not guaranteed to work exactly like a normal backlink. The closest guidance here is that Google may treat crawled iframes similarly to backlinks and pass value to the iframe src URL.

Whether it helps or hurts depends on context and attributes used. The best-supported answer is: it can be positive for the page loaded in the iframe, but the exact ranking benefit is uncertain and may differ from a regular link.

The evidence doesn’t directly answer hidden iframe backlinks or their SEO impact. It only says Google’s results can vary based on many factors and that regular results can’t be previewed.

Closest guidance: because Google uses many signals to display results, a hidden-iframe link is not something you can reliably predict or test with a simulator. If you’re trying to understand whether it helps or hurts, the safest assumption is that anything hidden or manipulated may not be a dependable positive signal.

Backlinks from a hidden iframe are unlikely to give you a normal SEO benefit. The links may be seen as coming from your own site content rather than as external backlinks, and Google may not treat them as a useful signal.  

Also, if the iframe is hidden or used to create duplicate content across sites, that can be risky: at best it may not help SEO, and at worst it could create duplicate-content or manipulative-link issues.  

The closest supported guidance is: if you want third-party sites to publish indexable content from your site, it should be generated server-side and shown as inline HTML, not in an iframe.

A hidden iframe is not a useful SEO tactic and is unlikely to help rankings. The supported guidance says iframes are not SEO friendly, so search engines may not even see that content. It could also be viewed as an attempt to manipulate search results.

As for backlinks pointing to one page with a hidden iframe, the evidence doesn’t say that specifically. The closest supported guidance is that hidden iframe content itself gives no SEO benefit, and if rankings are dropping, the likely issue is low-quality content rather than the iframe.

A hidden iframe can be treated similarly to a backlink by search engines that crawl iframes, like Google, so it may have a positive SEO effect. The exact value may not be the same as a normal link, and it depends on how the iframe is used and whether the search engine recognizes it. The main supported guidance is that iframes can pass value, and attributes like title, longdesc, or noframes can add context. It does not indicate a negative impact by itself.

I can only support this much: the presence of dates on articles is not taken into account for SEO; search engines consider the indexing date. Also, older pages that are not updated or getting new backlinks may drop in search results over time, especially with Google favoring fresh content.

For your hidden-iframe backlink question, I don’t have evidence here about positive or negative impact, so I can’t confirm either way. The closest supported guidance is that getting new backlinks can help keep an old page from dropping, but the quality or nature of those backlinks isn’t covered here.

If you want users to embed your page on secure sites, make sure your embed URLs support HTTPS. The closest guidance here is to provide your embed code with https:// instead of http://, since mixed content can trigger security warnings on HTTPS sites.

So, for any iframe/embed code you offer, use secure URLs and ensure the embedded page and all its resources are also served over HTTPS. If parts of the embedded content still load over HTTP, browsers may warn users even if the main page has SSL.

There isn’t a penalty just for allowing embedded videos or for having pages with YouTube embeds. The SEO concern is that pages made up only of an embedded video usually don’t rank well, because they have little additional text or content for Google to understand and value.

So if you want users to embed your page like YouTube, the closest supported guidance is: make sure the page has meaningful surrounding content, not just the embed alone. That improves the chance of ranking and avoids thin-page issues.

Embedding content in an iframe, like YouTube videos, does not directly help SEO because the embedded content itself is not crawlable or indexable in the page. The closest supported guidance here is that embedding may help indirectly if it leads other sites to link to your page, but the embedded item itself does not add crawlable relevance for keywords.

If your goal is to let others embed your page, the evidence does not provide specific SEO guidelines for that. It does suggest that relying on the embed alone for SEO is weak, and pages with little other content may be seen as low quality or duplicate.

Typically, the easiest way is to use a web host that provides uptime/status monitoring or APIs for checking uptime, ping, latency, and DNS. The answer also notes that you could build your own monitoring, but it would need to check continuously and use bandwidth. If you want “always live” visibility, look for a hosting company or service that includes real-time status monitoring for your site.

If you want a site to stay available while you build a new version, the simplest approach is to put the new version on a subdomain of your main site. That lets it be live on the internet without deleting the old site.

If you don’t want it indexed by search engines, block crawlers. The guidance here says the best way to do that is with Basic Authentication.

To test whether your affiliate links are working, use Amazon’s link checker tool on the Associates site.

For buying books through your own affiliate link, the evidence only says to read the Amazon Associates Agreement and decide whether that use would break the terms.

It doesn’t cover how to keep a website live all the time.

Google has guidance specifically for paginated content, including a “do nothing” option that lets Google decide which results to show. If you’re unhappy with how the results appear, it may be worth trying one of the other options in that guidance. The evidence doesn’t confirm whether a canonical tag on /page/4/ will still make Google point to that exact page for a query, but it does support that paginated pages should be handled using Google’s paginated-content recommendations rather than relying on a canonical tag alone.

No, you can’t directly change how many lines of preview text Google shows for a result.

What you can do is improve the information Google may choose to display by adding relevant site/business details, such as:
- location information
- ratings, price, and author metadata
- event information

These won’t guarantee more preview lines, but they can make your result more prominent and informative in Google’s results.

Being first on the second page usually isn’t a problem by itself. Google ranking depends on article quality, relevancy to the search term, and SEO factors, not just one thing. The guidance given is to improve your page with quality backlinks, social sharing, and avoid over-optimizing.

Also, Google Web Search and Google News rank pages differently, so appearing on the first page in News does not mean the same ranking in Web Search. Some pages can stay in the same spot for a while.

Typically, this kind of live status monitoring is something your web host can provide. The answer suggests that a host may offer uptime, ping, latency, DNS, and similar status information, possibly through APIs. It also notes that you could build your own monitoring tool, but it would need to check continuously and could use bandwidth, which is why it’s usually provided by the hosting company.

So the closest guidance supported here is: check with your hosting provider first, especially for a dashboard or API-based status monitoring.

Use schema.org metadata for WebApplication. The example shown uses:

<body itemscope itemtype="http://schema.org/WebApplication">

with properties like name, about, and browserRequirements.

That supports identifying a site as a web application, rather than a desktop application. If you want Google to recognize it that way, this is the closest guidance provided.

It means Google didn’t find any web pages in its index that it considered relevant for that search phrase. It does not imply Google searched every website live at that moment.

Pages may be missing because they haven’t been crawled yet, are blocked from crawling, or have been filtered out of Google’s index for reasons like low quality or policy violations.

If you’re checking why your own pages don’t appear, make sure they aren’t blocked from Google, then check webmaster tools for issues. If they simply aren’t indexed yet, submitting an XML sitemap and an HTML sitemap can help Google find them.

The only supported suggestion here is Google Keyword Tool, which is noted as a nice reference for this kind of information. The evidence does not say whether Google itself lets you see exact search counts for a specific term, so I can’t confirm that from this thread. If you want search-volume information, Google Keyword Tool is the closest source mentioned.
Google does not index its own search result pages. If you mean Google’s search results page as content on the web, the accepted answer says they are not indexed by Google itself.

Websites can get extra information in Google results by adding useful original content around copied material, and by linking to the original source. In the answer here, the key advice is that if your added summaries, statistics, or other value are genuinely useful, Google is more likely to treat the page better than a plain duplicate.

It also says to credit the original source with a link, since that helps show you are using the information rather than just copying it.

So, the closest guidance supported here is: add substantial value, make the page more than a duplicate, and clearly point to the official source.

To get extra location information in Google results, the supported approach here is to set up a Google Places listing for the business. That gives Google more control-ready data about your location, which can help it show location-specific details such as a map. The thread doesn’t say how to add arbitrary extra information to results in general, only that a Places listing is the way to provide location data Google can use.

Google usually gets this extra info from reputable sources across the web, such as Wikipedia and other known sites. For people, it may show different details depending on the person’s profession, like recent movies for actors or awards and team for athletes. It seems to match query keywords with related entities and then displays the most relevant information in the search results.

The evidence only shows that the question was unresolved. It suggests the “np” entry is understood to mean “not provided,” but it does not explain why website URLs appear in the Google Analytics keywords list.

Use separate virtual hosts with different ServerName and DocumentRoot values, and make sure each site serves from its own directory.

Example:

<VirtualHost W.X.Y.Z:80>
  ServerName serverA.com
  DocumentRoot "/var/www/html/serverA"
</VirtualHost>

<VirtualHost W.X.Y.Z:80>
  ServerName serverB.com
  DocumentRoot "/var/www/html/serverB"
</VirtualHost>

This prevents the two sites from colliding, so serverB files won’t be reachable as /serverB/ under serverA. If serverB is currently inside serverA’s document root, move it to its own separate document root.

The provided answer only suggests that caching may already be working and recommends verifying with tools like Google PageSpeed Insights, the Page Speed browser extension, or YSlow.

It does not explain a proper .htaccess caching setup or whether your current rules are correct. Based on the evidence, the closest guidance is to test with those tools and confirm whether the cache headers are being sent as expected.

There isn’t one ideal cache time. It depends on how often your content changes and what you’re comfortable with.

A practical guide from the answer:
- If content rarely changes, cache for a week or two.
- If content changes daily, 24 hours is appropriate.

So for php/html, js, css, and images, set expiration based on update frequency rather than file type alone.

A true 301 redirect from Blogger isn’t possible from within the blog itself, because it has to happen before HTTP headers are sent.

The closest options supported here are:
- a meta refresh redirect
- a JavaScript redirect

If you use a meta refresh, also add a cross-domain rel=canonical to reduce duplicate-content issues with Google.

If you’re moving to WordPress, the blogger-301-redirect plugin or the seo-blogger-to-wordpress-301-redirector may help.

Blogger can redirect from its own blogspot address to your current custom domain, and it will correctly redirect each post/page when you switch from `www.old-domain.com` to `www.new-domain.com` by stopping publishing to the old domain and starting publishing to the new one.

But Blogger no longer has any connection to `www.old-domain.com`, so redirects from the old domain to the new one are not something Blogger can do. Those redirects have to be handled by the domain registrar or hosting tools for the old domain.

The closest Blogger-based workaround is to create a new blog with a post announcing the move and use Missing post redirection, but that does not provide full per-page redirects.

Your new domain has likely not been indexed by Google yet, so it’s too soon for PageRank to transfer or show up. After a move to a custom domain, it can take a few days to a few weeks for Googlebot to crawl and index the new site. Once that happens, ranking signals may update. You can check indexing status in Google’s Webmaster Tools.

The thread suggests checking your server logs to verify whether Google Analytics is misreporting traffic sources. It also notes that, for many sites, a very high share of traffic can legitimately come from search engines, especially for newer domains.

What it does not cover is a specific Analytics setting or a fix for “(Not Provided).” Based on the evidence, the closest guidance is to compare Analytics with server logs to confirm whether referral/email traffic is being tracked correctly.

“(Not Provided)” in Google Analytics means the search keyword was not passed through in the referrer data, usually because Google chose not to send it.

The Organic/Search view shows visits coming from search engines, but some Google searches will appear as “not provided.”

The SEO > Queries view is different: it shows Google search query data from Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console if connected to Analytics. It’s Google-only, not your site’s internal search terms. It can include terms that Analytics shows as “not provided,” and also provides impressions, CTR, and ranking positions.

Place an .htaccess file in the /shop/ directory and redirect requests to the desired subdomain, for example:

RewriteEngine on
RewriteBase /

RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} !^shop\.mydomain\.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^shop/$ http://shop.mydomain.com [L,NC,R=301]

This keeps the files in /shop/ but prevents access via mydomain.com/shop/ by sending users to shop.mydomain.com. If you also want pg.mydomain.com to be used, you’d need a separate choice/redirect for that domain, since one request can only be sent to one place.

Use an .htaccess rewrite rule in the main domain’s root to block requests that try to reach the add-on directory from `example.com`:

RewriteEngine on
RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^example\.com$ [NC]
RewriteRule ^exampleB/ - [R=404,L]

Replace `exampleB/` with the add-on folder you want to hide. This returns a 404 when someone tries to access that subdirectory through the main domain.

Use a meta description tag in the page head. That’s the best method suggested here.

Google won’t always show the first line of a page in search results; it often chooses the snippet based on which text best matches the search. So the “Download hi-res images” line may not be shown anyway, especially if other content on the page is more relevant.

If you need control over the snippet, a meta description is the closest supported approach. The answer specifically advises not to try to hide text.

Google does not guarantee it will use your meta description for a search result. It may show the meta description, or it may pull text from the page that best matches the query.

To improve the chance of getting a good snippet:
- make each meta description unique
- make it accurately describe the page content
- keep it reasonably short, since Google typically displays around 150 characters

If a page has no meta description, Google will usually use relevant page text instead. If you want no snippet at all, you can use:

<meta name="robots" content="nosnippet">

Google can ignore your meta description and generate its own snippet if it thinks another page text is more relevant to the query. In the case described, the custom site search results were showing text from the page’s drop-down menu instead of the meta description, while normal Google search did use the meta description.

The closest guidance supported here is to make the meta description more natural and descriptive, not a keyword-stuffed list. Google may then be more likely to use it, but there’s no guarantee it will always display it.

If two domains have largely the same content, you should expect one or both to need extra handling to avoid duplicate-content issues. The guidance here is:

- Use rel=canonical on each duplicate page to point to the corresponding page on the other domain, rather than doing it site-wide.
- If you want one domain not to appear in the index, use robots meta NOINDEX,FOLLOW on the duplicate pages.
- Better still, make the second domain meaningfully different and focus it on unique, branded content.

It also notes that using an iframe was once a workaround, but canonical/noindex are the relevant options here.

If you want the simplest SEO setup, use one primary domain, put country/language versions in subfolders, and 301-redirect the other domains to those subfolders. Then use country targeting in Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console and hreflang so Google can match the right page by language and location.

If you want to optimize for local country search, the supported guidance here is to have each domain live, accessible, hosted in its own country, with its own translated content. That is more costly and only really fits a true regional/multilingual strategy.

The evidence supports that ccTLDs can help local search, but it doesn’t say you should keep multiple domains all serving the same content.

It’s worth it, but not every error is equally important. Broken links, missing CSS/JavaScript, and DOCTYPE problems can affect search ranking, browser warnings, or rendering. General HTML/CSS errors can also make pages display incorrectly or load more slowly.

If some errors are outside your control, that’s understandable. The goal should be to reduce errors as much as practical. It’s not necessarily mission-critical to fix every single one, but a no-error site is better for user experience.

Yes, it can be worth it as a general quality check, but for CSS3 vendor-prefixed properties the validation result is often not very useful. The evidence says CSS3 wasn’t fully complete, so using browser-specific gradients or similar features can make the stylesheet technically invalid even when the site works fine.

According to the provided answer, invalid CSS does not affect usability by itself, and it has no effect on SEO. The main thing is whether the page renders and remains usable in the browsers you care about. If you need the newer CSS features, you may have to accept that the CSS won’t strictly validate.

Valid HTML is probably not a direct SEO ranking factor. But it is still worth doing, because valid markup helps ensure your content can be properly crawled and indexed. Invalid HTML can cause problems for crawlers just as it can in a browser. So the closest guidance supported here is: don’t treat validation as a ranking boost, but do try to make your HTML valid and easy to read and interpret.

An XML sitemap is generally good, not bad. It can help search engines by including priority and last-modified dates, which may affect crawl frequency, especially on large sites with both frequently and infrequently changing content. It can also include media info, like video sitemap data.

That said, for a smaller site with mostly static content, there’s probably very little functional difference between XML and a simple text sitemap. The main downside is the chance of mistakes if the extra metadata is inaccurate.

An XML sitemap is generally good, not bad. It helps search engines discover pages they might not otherwise find, but it is not required for indexing. If you hit the 50,000-URL limit, splitting into multiple sitemaps or using a sitemap index are both fine and should not harm SEO. Google won’t de-index pages just because they’re not in a sitemap. A well-written site should still be crawlable without one.

An XML sitemap is generally good, not bad. Compared with a plain text URL list, XML lets you include extra information like the last-modification date and can also support other content types such as images and videos. The main advantage of a text list is simplicity, but that matters less once you’re generating sitemaps with a tool or have many URLs. It’s possible to read XML yourself, but making it by hand is more error-prone, so a sitemap generator is usually the better approach.

There’s no exact timing given for content revisions. The only supported guidance here is that Google rankings can change over time and that timing depends on things like site authority and competition. For site downtime, short interruptions may not delete listings but can still cause rank drops, while long downtime can affect rankings more seriously. If your revised content is indexed and gains authority, recovery or ranking changes may take days to weeks, but no one can say exactly when.

There isn’t a known usual time for Google to “re-calculate page rank” after you revise content. The only evidence here says nobody outside Google engineers knows how often PageRank is recalculated, and that this PageRank notion is considered outdated and not useful.

So I can’t give a reliable timeframe. The closest guidance supported is that changes may not show up quickly, and you shouldn’t judge updates by PageRank alone.

If the site is cleaned up and fully indexed, creating great content should get Google re-crawling the website, and it should be possible to improve rankings with the right SEO practices.

The evidence doesn’t give a specific timeframe for when ranking changes happen after revising content. What it does support is that you should first confirm the site is safe, check for Google warnings, review backlinks, and verify indexing. After that, improvements depend on Google re-crawling and reevaluating the site.

There isn’t a fixed number of days. The update can happen very fast for some sites, but for others it may take days or weeks for Google to update existing pages in the search results. It depends on factors like how often Google crawls your site, how established it is, and how popular or linked your content is.

There isn’t a fixed number of days. The update can take several days to a couple of weeks, depending on how important Google sees the site. For larger or more important sites, it may update in a few hours or the same day. Resubmitting the page doesn’t necessarily speed it up.

Google appears to have been showing the title text from an error page, not your site’s normal page title. The page was temporarily returning HTTP Error 400 to Google, so Google likely indexed or cached that error content instead of the title. Once the server started working again, the issue seemed temporary.

Google is primarily getting it from your page’s HTML `<title>` tag, which in your code is:

`Συγκριση τιμών - Τιμές προϊόντων,Αναζήτηση και προσφορές`

However, Google may show an alternative title instead of that exact one. It does this when its algorithms think another title is more relevant for the query or clearer for users. So the shown title may come from your page title, but rewritten by Google.

The guidance supported here is to keep the title concise, useful, and enticing, and to check Webmaster Tools/Diagnostics for title suggestions.

Google can choose a different title for search results than the one in your <title> tag. It uses many signals, and for some pages it generates an alternative title to better match the query or describe the page.

So it may be getting “sitename: blah blah blah” from your page content or other references to the page, not just the title tag. Google’s title/snippet generation is automated, and you generally can’t manually force a specific search-result title for an individual page.

Google can keep showing an old or different title for a while, especially after a 301 redirect or site move. If your site’s current title is correct, the remaining issue is likely Google’s index or cached view not fully updated yet. Since the thread has no answer on record, the closest guidance is to keep checking that the redirect is working correctly, that Google can crawl the new site, and to wait for reindexing. If the old title still appears after more time, resubmitting for indexing in Google Search Console is the next logical step.

Google can keep showing an old title for a while, even after your site has changed and been crawled. The main remedy supported here is to wait.

It also may not be a fixed title: Google sometimes rewrites titles in search results based on the search query, and it may choose an older title if it seems to match the searched keywords better.

Adding an alt tag for the logo isn’t identified here as a reliable trigger for changing the title.

Google can alter how your titles appear in search results if it thinks the page titles aren’t good enough. In this case, it likely picked up “logo” from an image alt attribute and used it in the SERP because your titles didn’t meet its standards.

To fix it:
- Change the image alt text to something more specific, like “Logo [yourName]”
- Improve your page titles
- Wait for Google to recrawl and update the results

Google may not show all special characters from a title tag in SERPs. The provided thread only indicates that some icon/special characters can sometimes still appear, but the examples seem outdated and the exact current set isn’t given. It also suggests that some sites may get special characters shown through rich snippets or similar markup. If your custom title isn’t being used on the SERP, the closest guidance here is that Google may ignore or alter parts of the title, especially special characters.

Google may ignore a keyword-stuffed title and show a more relevant title from the page body. The evidence suggests that keyword stuffing can negatively affect ranking and is something Google may target, so a title like that could be a problem for SEO.

The safest guidance supported here is to rewrite the `<title>` tag so it is natural, relevant, and follows Google’s quality guidelines. A well-crafted title with relevant keywords should not hurt a page that is already ranking well, and it may reduce the chance of Google replacing it.

The stop keywords themselves don’t seem to matter much here. Google can understand that “thank-you” and “thankyou” both mean “thank you,” so changing the spelling is likely pointless.

The main guidance is that stop words are very common, so trying to rank directly for them is usually not effective. It’s better to focus on related synonyms and long-tail search terms that include those terms.

Search engines can still index a new site even without prior visitors, but you may rank behind established competitors. As your site gains quality content and links from other good sites, you can start appearing more prominently.

The main guidance is not to rely on search engines alone. Use other media and channels too when introducing a new brand or site to the world.

One supported way to keep Google from indexing PDF documents directly, while still allowing bots to crawl them, is to add an X-Robots-Tag header for PDF files in Apache:

<Files ~ "\.pdf$">
    Header set X-Robots-Tag "noindex"
</Files>

This can help give more weight to your web pages instead of the documents in search results. The provided text doesn’t directly explain how to increase overall website visitors, but it does support controlling document indexing so your web pages may be more prominent.

If your goal is more visitors, the evidence doesn’t cover traffic growth tactics directly, only ways to make the site more appealing once people find it.

The evidence does not directly address how to increase total website visitors, only how to test changes to improve user conversion and participation.

Use mod_rewrite, not Redirect/RedirectMatch, because those don’t handle query strings in the source URL. For your case, add this to .htaccess:

RewriteEngine On
RewriteCond %{REQUEST_URI} ^/$
RewriteCond %{QUERY_STRING} ^page_id=1103$
RewriteRule .* http://mysite.com/mypage.html [R=301,L]

This redirects requests for `mysite.com/?page_id=1103` to `mysite.com/mypage.html`.

If needed, you can adjust the pattern to match a different path, but the example above is the closest supported solution from the evidence.

If you don’t add redirects, existing links will break, and Google may treat the new URLs as duplicate content of the old pages and rank them less well.

No. A wildcard DNS record only covers unmatched hostnames at that level; it does not make a specific subdomain an alias of another domain.

To point `sub.domain.com` to another domain/server, you still need a DNS record for that hostname, usually an A/AAAA record or a CNAME if your DNS provider allows it. Then your web server can use a virtual host for that hostname.

So creating Apache virtual hosts alone is not sufficient if DNS does not resolve the subdomain to your server.

A DNS wildcard by itself won’t make one subdomain an alias of another domain. DNS can point names to IPs, but it can’t preserve the .com in the browser URL.

To keep sub.domain.com in the address bar while serving content from another server/domain, you need a reverse proxy on the subdomain, for example Apache ProxyPass / ProxyPassReverse. The other option is an iframe, but that is less ideal and has SEO/SSL drawbacks.

If you only want redirection, DNS alone won’t do it. If the wildcard already covers that level, you’d still need to override the specific subdomain with web server/proxy config.

A CNAME only works if the subdomain itself is not already defined by another record. If a wildcard record exists at that level, it may already cover the name, so you can’t also make that same exact subdomain a separate alias in the DNS zone.

The closest workable approach is to create an explicit record for the subdomain you want to alias, which overrides the wildcard for that name, then point it with a CNAME to the target domain.

If your setup depends on checking the originating domain, this can still be used for trusted subdomains, but the thread does not cover DNS server-specific limits or whether your provider allows a CNAME alongside a wildcard.

You don’t have to host email with the same provider as the website.

The easiest approach is to host the clients’ websites with one web host and use a separate email host for their mail. That keeps email independent, so if the web server goes down, email can still work, and mail won’t use up web hosting space.

The main downside is cost and administration: you’ll pay two providers and manage more logins/passwords.

If you don’t control DNS, you can’t fully redirect email. The closest option supported here is to keep the current MX records unchanged and host only the website.

The simplest option supported here is Google Apps for business email. It’s free for up to 10 users, and even if you have to pay, it’s still recommended because it likely has higher availability than most alternatives, works well with smartphones, and many users are already familiar with Gmail.
