Yes. Based on the accepted answer, shortened URLs can carry less SEO value than the original URL, because they pass a bit less link juice and add a redirect. They can also be slower, less descriptive, and less trustworthy, which may indirectly hurt SEO. The advice given is to use the original URL whenever possible.

To replace old URLs in Google results, set up 301 redirects from each old URL to its matching new URL. That helps Google connect the old pages to the new ones and preserves SEO value.

For old pages that no longer have a replacement, return a 404 error so Google can remove them from its index.

It also helps to use a helpful 404 page that points users to the new site structure or a sitemap.

Use 301 redirects from the old URLs to the new URLs. That tells Google the pages have moved and helps Google associate the old pages with the new ones.

If you don’t want to redirect them, leave the old URLs returning 404. Google will eventually stop crawling and indexing those old URLs. Make sure the new URLs are discoverable through internal links on your site and through your XML sitemap.

Use a 301 redirect from each old URL to its new equivalent. Google will then replace the old URLs with the new ones in its index. This won’t happen immediately, but it should happen over time.

Blocking the old URLs with robots.txt is not the supported fix here; the guidance provided is to redirect the old structure to the new one.

Yes—based on this, iframes are not SEO-friendly, so the content inside them is invisible to search engines and won’t help rankings. Adding an iframe from one site to another is not useful for SEO and could even be seen as an attempt to manipulate search results.

If rankings are dropping, the more likely issue is low-quality content on the second site, not the iframe itself. The best next step is to review that content and improve its quality.

Yes. The evidence says there is no SEO risk in having the same widget text on all pages, because search engines can tell it is not the main content. Duplicate content concerns are generally about duplicating the main page content, not header, footer, or sidebar/widget text.

So a sidebar/text widget with a short introduction and link, shown across pages, is generally fine from an SEO point of view.

A widget like this can be built with an iframe embed and a small generator UI. The generator can let users change options, then use jQuery to update the CSS of the widget container and the embed code shown to the user so they can copy it.

RSS could be part of the content source, but the answer here focuses on the widget display and customization, not SEO specifically. It also suggests embedding images in the RSS feed if you want people to syndicate your content more easily.

Adding those link tags in the iframe widget’s head is unlikely to help SEO or visibility. The answer says search engines will identify the association without explicitly adding such tags.

If your goal is to prevent crawling, the only guidance given is to use a rel=noindex tag. Otherwise, it does not support adding RSS or “index” link tags just to create a logical association between the widget and related pages.

Embedded code on other sites does not directly improve SEO rank, based on the evidence provided. The embedded content itself is not crawlable/indexable in a way that makes it count as SEO content. It may help indirectly if it causes other sites to link to your page, which can support ranking. But the embedded item itself does not appear to add direct keyword relevance. If the page has little else on it, it could even be seen as low quality.

iFrames are not a good way to hide content from Google. The thread says Google does crawl iframes, so they are not “SEO-proof.” It also notes they are not recommended by Google, but you could put the iframe content on separate pages and try noindex and/or robots.txt on those pages.

So, if your goal is to keep names from being indexed while keeping the text indexed, iframes may help only as part of that setup, but they do not reliably prevent indexing on their own.

I can’t determine a direct positive or negative effect on SEO from the evidence provided. It only says Google is not concerned about duplication across tags like title/H1/meta description in the example, and that repetition within tags is generally not a problem.

It does not address hidden iframe backlinks specifically. So the closest guidance supported here is that simple duplication across page elements isn’t seen as harmful by itself, but the evidence gives no basis to say hidden iframe backlinks help or hurt SEO.

Backlinks from a hidden iframe are unlikely to help SEO. The supported guidance here says iframes are not SEO friendly and the content inside them is invisible to search engines, so there’s nothing to gain for rankings from that setup. It could even be viewed as an attempt to manipulate search results.

So the likely effect is negative or none, not positive. If rankings are dropping, the more likely cause is low-quality content or another SEO issue on the page/site itself.

The widget described is using an iframe, so it’s mainly about easy embedding, not SEO linkbacks. The answer says widgets are usually for ease of use, especially for people who don’t want to deal with RSS. It also says you could build a generator that lets users customize CSS styles with jQuery and then updates the embed code they copy.

It does not say that iframe widgets create SEO linkbacks. Based on this, the closest guidance is to focus on the embed widget experience and code generation rather than expecting SEO value from the iframe itself.

Backlinks from a hidden iframe are usually a black-hat link tactic and can be treated as manipulative. The evidence supports that unnatural or bad links pointing to your site can be part of negative SEO, and that Google may not assign importance to deleterious links if your site has enough good, natural authority.

So the likely effect is not positive; it’s more likely neutral or potentially negative if it looks like spam/manipulation. The safest guidance supported here is to focus on building positive SEO and authoritative backlinks so harmful links are less likely to matter.

A hidden iframe itself is not said to lower your page’s ranking.

The SEO issue described is that if search engines crawl content inside an iframe, they may treat the iframed page as the target rather than your page. That means an iframe is not ideal for content you want credited to your page.

So if the backlinks/content are inside a hidden iframe, the closest guidance supported here is: it likely won’t directly penalize your site, but it may not help your page SEO the way visible, integrated content would. If possible, avoid using an iframe for important content.

The evidence doesn’t address hidden iframes or backlinks from them directly. It only says that search engines care about the indexing date, and older content that isn’t updated or getting new backlinks can drop in results.

So the closest guidance supported here is: a backlink from a hidden iframe is not described as giving a positive SEO benefit, and if it’s part of an old page that isn’t updated, the page may still lose position over time.

A one-page site can still be indexed, but it’s harder to rank well for multiple specific topics because you only have one page title, one h1, and one meta description. If all your services are on one page, that page will tend to be less focused on any single topic.

If you split the content into multiple pages, each page can target one service or topic more clearly, and internal linking between them can help a little through anchor text and page-to-page authority transfer.

If the backlinks are in a hidden iframe, they are unlikely to help your SEO much, and could be ignored or treated as coming from your own site rather than as external backlinks. The evidence suggests Google may associate iframe content with the page containing it, and it does not guarantee how those links will be handled.

The safer guidance supported here is: if you want third-party sites to have indexable content that counts as external links, it should be generated server-side as normal HTML, not embedded in an iframe.

Also, be careful: duplicated content across sites can have negative SEO effects, such as the other site being treated as canonical or the setup being seen as manipulative.

I can’t tell from this whether the backlink with a hidden iframe will have a positive or negative impact. The only supported point here is that Google’s regular results can’t be reliably simulated or previewed, and many factors affect what it shows.

So the closest guidance is: don’t expect immediate or predictable SERP impact from a single change, and there isn’t a simulator to test it instantly. For rich snippets or AdWords there are preview tools, but not for normal search results.

To get multiple keywords and a phrase, the guidance here is to put quotes around the phrase you want kept together, like "jump rope", and leave the other words unquoted. For the negative term, enter free in the negative keywords section rather than typing -free.

When adding bidding keywords later, you can paste a list such as:
"best jump rope"
"best jump ropes"
"jumping rope"
"jump rope"

Those quoted entries are phrase matches. The guidance suggests using phrase match at first, and broad match is another option. It also says not to rely on + and - symbols, since Google may treat them as part of the search term.

Websites can’t control how many preview lines Google shows, but they can add extra information that Google may choose to display. Examples include location info through Google Places, metadata like ratings, price, and author information, and event details. Google decides whether to show these additions, which can make a result more prominent and informative.

Google can change search result titles and snippets on its own. It may use page content and references to the page, not just your title tag or meta description. In this case, Google may have extracted the video length from the page or video itself, or from other references. If you want to influence it, check the page content and any structured data or linked references, but Google may still rewrite the result.

Google is likely showing the same snippet because your pages share the same meta description. The accepted guidance says that in Joomla, if you don’t set page-specific metadata, the global meta keywords/description are used for all pages.

To change it, set different meta description data for each article/page or menu item in Joomla rather than relying on the global site metadata. That should give Google distinct descriptions for different sub-pages.

If you want, I can also help you check whether Google is pulling the snippet from the page text instead of the meta description.

Search engines will see the rendered HTML output, not the PHP source. So if your PHP variable outputs `Description of this page`, that’s what they can see in the meta description. They will not see `<?php echo $page_description; ?>` as source code. Also, meta tags do not affect rankings.

Google is showing the text from the page’s meta description, not actually displaying CSS. In the example, the description includes:

`.content { font-family:verdana; font-size:14px; font-weight:normal } ...`

Google often uses the meta description as the search result snippet, so if CSS or other code is inside that tag, it can appear in results. Check and clean up the page’s `<meta name="description" ...>` content.

There isn’t a fixed time. Google updates its index constantly, so ranking changes after content edits can happen quickly and may also be temporary. In the example, the site saw a short-term boost, then dropped back after more changes were made, which could mean the rankings were still fluctuating.

The safest guidance is: after revising content, avoid making more major changes right away so you can tell whether the change was permanent. If you see a sudden drop right after your own edit, then rolling back that change may be worth considering.

Use schema.org markup on your site, if applicable, to display rich snippets. That’s the closest guidance here for showing links in a more structured way like Amazon. You should also make sure each page has a relevant, unique title and use HTML correctly. If your goal is to make links appear as structured results in Google, schema markup is the supported direction in this guidance.

If you mean increasing visitor capacity for a site that may get much more traffic, the guidance is to optimize performance rather than just add hardware. Run benchmark tools like Google Page Speed and YSlow to find simple changes that can improve speed, and do preemptive load/performance tests before and after changes to measure gains. If you mean getting more visitors overall, this doesn’t directly cover marketing or traffic generation, only preparing the site to handle more visitors.

Google may not be showing your site yet because its results can take time to synchronize across Google’s different servers and datacenters. A site can appear in one place and seem missing in another for a while.

The best supported step is to sign up for Webmaster Tools, since it gives you a direct way to monitor your site’s status with Google.

Since your site was only ranking yesterday, give it some time and keep checking for changes.

Blocking crawlers with robots.txt will not help you “build up” visitors or PageRank first. The guidance here says:

- PageRank is based on links to your site, not visitor count.
- Visitor totals or visitor growth are not ranking factors.
- If your site is new, Googlebot likely won’t visit very often anyway, so blocking it usually isn’t useful.
- robots.txt can stop crawling, but URLs may still appear in results in some cases.
- Google may crawl URLs that have Google+ buttons even if robots.txt blocks them.

For increasing visitors, the closest supported advice is to let search engines crawl your site and focus on getting links from other sites.

The available guidance is about reducing unwanted traffic, not increasing it. It suggests that “bad” traffic may ignore robots.txt, change IPs and user agents, and be hard to block manually. For filtering and basic CDN protection, it recommends services like CloudFlare and Incapsula, plus authentication and possibly honeypot-style defenses for repeat bad traffic.

If your goal is to increase visitors, this doesn’t cover growth tactics. The closest supported advice is that search engine indexing should not be overly blocked unless you want less traffic.

Google’s `link:` command is not a reliable way to see all backlinks. It only shows a small, non-updated sample, so it’s normal for links reported in Webmaster Tools to not appear there. The best count to rely on is the links shown in Google Webmaster Tools.  

Also, having a PageRank of zero or using a subdomain is not enough information here to explain the difference. The closest guidance is to trust Webmaster Tools for backlink data rather than the `link:` operator.

Some sites show extended results because they add more than just copied text: summaries, statistics, comparisons, and other useful markup. That can make the page more valuable to users, which can help it perform better in search. The answer also says the ratio of your own content to the original matters, and that linking to the original source is important as courtesy and credit.

It doesn’t specifically explain Google’s “extended search results” feature, but it does support the idea that added useful content and proper source links can improve how a page is treated and ranked.

Google usually shows extended results when it can pull structured information from reputable sources and match it to the query. For people, it may use details from places like Wikipedia or image sources, then display extra profile info, related keywords, awards, recent work, or team/role information.

So websites don’t “create” these extended results directly in this explanation; Google decides based on the information it finds across the web and how relevant and well-tagged it is.

Yes, it’s possible to give a subdomain separate DNS settings, including different MX records, if your host supports managing subdomains that way. You’d typically use your web host’s domain manager to assign different DNS records for the subdomain. 

If you want the subdomain fully separated from the main domain’s nameservers, that may also be possible, but it depends on your hosting provider. The safest next step is to ask your web host whether they support custom nameservers or separate DNS management for subdomains, and how to configure it.

You do not have to host your email with the same company that hosts your website. If you use a different email server, the main benefit is that your email won’t depend on your web hosting, so if your website host goes down, email can still keep working. It may also give you extra email features and keep mail from using your web hosting space.

The tradeoff is cost: you’ll pay two providers instead of one, and you’ll have more logins and passwords to manage.

Google value is not tied to the extension itself in the evidence provided. The guidance given is that you should preserve the existing site’s value by using a 301 redirect or a canonical URL tag when moving to a new domain, rather than starting over and losing backlinks/pagerank. If you’re changing domains, the safest supported advice here is to redirect the old domain to the new one so search value carries over.

Yes, but only a little. For Google, a country-code TLD like .co.uk can make a site rank slightly higher for users in that country, rather than “diverting” everyone else away. The effect is usually small compared with the content itself.

A .com is treated as generic by Google, with no built-in geographic bias. You can also use Webmaster Tools to geotarget a generic domain. Hosting IP may sometimes be considered too. Different search engines may behave differently, but likely not by much.

Based on the evidence, SEO is not inherently affected by using a regional or newer TLD like .me. The cited answer says that if .museum was considered a long TLD, then SEO is not affected, and “same for new gTLDs.” That supports the idea that the TLD itself is not a ranking disadvantage.

What it doesn’t cover is whether a regional TLD has any indirect effects from branding, trust, or user behavior. So the closest guidance supported here is: the TLD alone should not hurt SEO.

Yes. One option mentioned is FireFox Throttle, a Firefox extension for simulating a slow connection. Another is Sloppy, a proxy that slows down your connection and should work across browsers.

The note also says the Firefox extension is no longer available, but a GitHub repo was created for it.

The provided information does not answer the SEO impact of using regional TLDs like .me.

It only covers a related question about moving a website to another server and changing only the IP address, not the domain name. Based on that, the closest guidance is that a server change alone is being treated as separate from a domain-name change. There is no evidence here about regional TLDs, SEO ranking effects, or .me specifically.

For Google, a country-code TLD like .co.uk can give a site a modest boost for users in that country, but it does not mean search engines will divert everyone else away. The effect is small compared with the page content and other basic ranking factors.

A generic TLD like .com is treated as worldwide by Google, with no built-in geographic weighting. Google can also use Webmaster Tools geotargeting, and sometimes IP location is considered too.

So for a regional TLD like .me, the closest supported guidance is that it may influence geographic targeting somewhat, but it should still be mixed in with the broader global results rather than being excluded worldwide.

Using a regional TLD like .me does not, by itself, appear to give search engines extra weight for SEO. The domain can still rank in other languages and regions if the content and publishing locale fit. Regional TLDs are more about signaling location/branding and fitting a country or audience, such as using .co.uk for a UK-focused business, than improving ranking directly.

To help one page rank above others on the same site, the guidance here is to make that page more relevant and better supported than the others: give it a unique, relevant title, keep its content unique, use proper HTML, relevant keywords in the URL, and add a clear meta description. Also make sure it’s linked from other relevant, high-quality sites if possible, and that your internal and outgoing links are relevant. Fast load time, HTTPS, mobile friendliness, and a sitemap submitted in Search Console all help the site overall.

It doesn’t give a page-ordering trick for the same website specifically, but it does support improving that page’s uniqueness, relevance, and link support.

Google’s search result title and its cached-page title can update on different schedules. Even after Googlebot crawls your site, the index and cache may refresh at different times, depending on where they are in Google’s update cycle. That means one can show the new title while the other still shows the old one. It can take anywhere from minutes to about a week. Usually the guidance is just to wait and be patient.

Subdomains are essentially treated the same as subdirectories by Google, and probably by other search engines as well. Based on that, using a subdomain should not inherently help or hurt SEO. The main advice is to choose whichever setup is easier for you to maintain and better fits future growth needs.

No. The URL path does not have to match the page title.

The closest guidance here is that titles and URLs can be different, and often should be: titles may be long and descriptive, while URLs are usually shorter. If a title changes, that does not mean the URL must change or that redirects are required just to keep them aligned.

The provided thread does not answer this directly. It only shows that someone asked why subdomains are important, but there’s no recorded answer or ranking guidance.

So, based on this evidence alone, I can’t confirm whether two subdomains under the same root domain affect each other’s rankings.

If you want the closest supported guidance: the evidence is too limited to make a conclusion about SEO ranking impact between subdomains.

Subdomains generally don’t get a separate Alexa ranking, even if they’re popular. Alexa rank also fluctuates over time, so changes in the root domain’s rank can happen without any special subdomain effect. The evidence doesn’t show subdomains harming the root domain; it says Alexa typically ignores subdomains for ranking.

The provided answer doesn’t directly address subdomains, but it does suggest that putting unrelated content under the same domain can dilute the site’s focus and could be risky for search ranking. So, the closest supported guidance is: yes, content structure on the same domain may affect how search engines understand and rank the root domain, and keeping unrelated content separate is likely safer.

Hidden content can be indexed, but hiding it with CSS or JavaScript does not make it safe for SEO. The provided answer says the method is not the issue; if the content is hidden to manipulate rankings, it is considered cloaking and can violate search engine terms. So the closest guidance is: yes, search engines may still see/index it, and using `display: none`, JavaScript hiding, or similar tricks for keyword stuffing is risky and can be penalized.

Yes, source placement can have some effect: the short answer given is that you want your text content as close to the top of the source as possible. But it’s not a huge factor, so it shouldn’t be a major concern compared with other SEO signals that matter more.

This does not directly address visual text size or on-page visual placement in the rendered page. It only supports that the position of human-readable content in the source can have some SEO impact, though a small one.

Yes, hidden content can be indexed if it’s present in the page source; URLs with parameters can also be returned in search results and work normally when clicked. But if the content is just hidden DIVs shown/hidden by parameters, it may create duplicate content issues. If the content is dynamically generated on each page load instead of being hidden on the page, that avoids the issue.

No. The guidance says search engines are aware of hidden content in elements and will at best ignore it; at worst, the site could be blacklisted. So hidden text like display:none is not a good way to get indexed.

If you want to keep PageRank when moving an existing WordPress project from a subdomain to a new domain, the key step is a 301 redirect from the old address to the new one, as shown with `Redirect 301 / http://www.newdomain.com/`.

The guidance provided covers moving a WordPress install from a subdomain to its own domain. It does not compare “new domain vs subdomain vs new folder” for brand-new projects, but it does support this general point: if you later move content, use proper 301 redirects so the old URLs pass users and search engines to the new site.

For a new project, the closest supported advice is to choose the structure you want long term, because changing later requires the migration steps above.

No. The thread says hiding rich-snippet content with display:none just to benefit search engines is a major violation of their terms and can lead to penalties, including banning. It does not say every hidden element is never indexed, only that content hidden for search-engine-only use is not acceptable. The closest supported guidance is to refactor the HTML so the snippet content can be shown normally instead of hidden.

Not reliably. The evidence says you should assume content generated or hidden by JavaScript is invisible to search engines by default. It notes Google may process JavaScript in some cases, and crawlable Ajax is a supported exception only for Google, but other search engines may not find it. So if content is hidden with display:none or otherwise depends on JavaScript, don’t count on it being indexed. Best practice is to make the content reachable without JavaScript.

Yes, hidden content can still be indexed, but Google expects users to be able to find the text on the page without needing to search for it again or rely on hidden keyword stuffing.

The evidence says there is no absolute ban on hiding content with CSS or JavaScript if a user can later reveal it, such as menus, tooltips, or tabs. Those are generally fine.

But text that is keyword-rich and initially hidden can be risky, and may trigger a hidden-text penalty or lead to lower rankings if users bounce back to Google because they can’t find what they expected.

Not reliably. The evidence says you should assume content generated or revealed by JavaScript is invisible to search engines by default, except for Google’s crawlable Ajax support. It doesn’t specifically address CSS-hidden HTML, but the closest guidance is that anything not accessible without JavaScript should not be relied on for search visibility. The safest approach is to make the content reachable in plain HTML so it can be found without relying on CSS or JavaScript.

Yes, according to the evidence, search engines can see content hidden with CSS such as `position:absolute`, negative margins, or similar techniques. The thread says this worked with Google, Yahoo, Bing, and Yandex, including for structured/rich snippet data.

It also says you can use meta tags like:

`<meta itemprop="xxx" content="yyy">`

So the supported guidance is that hidden HTML may still be indexed, but the evidence only confirms this for those CSS-hiding methods and meta tags.

The provided answer says search engines can index data that is in the HTML but not visible, and it suggests two ways to do that: use meta tags like `<meta itemprop="xxx" content="yyy">`, or hide the content with CSS positioning such as `position:absolute`, large negative top values, z-index, or negative margins.

It does not specifically mention `display:none`, so I can’t confirm that exact technique from the text. The closest supported guidance is to place the structured data in the HTML in a way search engines can read, even if it is not visibly shown on the page.

Search engines may still see text that’s hidden only by CSS, so hiding HTML elements with CSS is not a reliable way to keep keywords out of indexing. The guidance here is to minimize the homepage text, use the company name in the title and h1, and block every other page from search engines. If you need content kept out of search results, put it on pages that are not accessible to search engines rather than relying on CSS hiding.

The evidence does not confirm that Google will crawl a dropdown hidden with `display:none`. It only says that, in general, JavaScript-generated content should be assumed invisible to search engines, with crawlable Ajax as the main exception. It also notes Googlebot may process JavaScript, but that is not confirmed.

So the safest guidance is: don’t rely on hidden dropdown content being crawled. If the content matters, make sure it is available in the HTML and reachable without JavaScript.

You can’t reliably make a page rank only for the company name and not for other related keywords. Even if the homepage is minimal, external links or other signals can still associate it with other terms.

The closest approach is to block all pages except the homepage from search engines, and keep the homepage text to a minimum. Use the company name in the title and H1, and avoid keyword-heavy visible text where possible. If you need more content for users, put it deeper in the site and keep that content inaccessible to search engines.

Preloading web fonts with `visibility: hidden` is not directly covered here, but the guidance says hiding content is generally okay if it’s user-exposed later and not used to hide keyword-rich text for ranking. The risky part is “hidden text” that searchers can’t immediately find when they land on the page.

If the hidden state is just temporary for a user experience reason, and the content is then shown, that’s generally described as fine. If you’re hiding important text or keywords from users, that can be problematic for SEO.

So: temporary hidden-loading behavior is closer to acceptable; hiding meaningful text for search purposes is not.

Google expects that text a searcher came for will be visible without requiring interaction. Hidden keyword-rich text can be treated as hidden text/cloaking and may hurt rankings, especially if users land and can’t find what they searched for.

That said, hiding content and letting users reveal it later is generally okay for normal UI patterns like dropdown menus, tooltips, and tabs. The specific technique matters less than the intent and whether the content is user-facing.

So:
- Hidden for SEO/keywords: risky.
- Hidden for UI, later revealed by user action: generally fine.
- Best practice: don’t put important keyword text in content that starts hidden.

The evidence suggests that hidden content can still be indexed or used for rich snippets. It specifically says placing data in meta tags or hiding it with CSS like absolute positioning and negative margins “worked in 100% cases” for search engines, including Google. It does not directly mention `visibility:hidden` or `display:none`, so I can’t confirm those exact styles from this evidence alone. The closest supported guidance is that search engines may process content even if it is not visible, but this should be treated cautiously.

`display:none` and `visibility:hidden` hide content from users, but the main SEO concern is whether the content is being hidden from search engines to manipulate rankings. That can be risky if it’s used for deceptive cloaking or stuffing keywords.

If you’re just hiding normal UI elements or using it for layout/accessibility reasons, it’s generally not the same as creating lots of broken links. The provided material only clearly addresses 404s: a proper 404 page is usually fine, while many internal links to non-existing pages can be a problem.

So, based on this, hidden content itself isn’t shown here as an SEO issue, but hidden/deceptive use could be.

Visibility:hidden and display:none can affect SEO if they hide important content from users and search engines’ rendered view. The evidence says search engines can understand JavaScript, but complex scripts may be harder to interpret. It also says it’s best practice to provide a non-JavaScript fallback, especially for navigation, so pages can still be viewed without JavaScript.

For SEO safety, hidden menus or text should have accessible fallback content. Using a no-JS class or similar approach can keep content available when JavaScript isn’t available. The evidence doesn’t say hidden-on-click content is always bad, only that fallback support is recommended.

No clear SEO penalty is supported by the evidence. It only says that, from a UI/design perspective, a “Home” menu item usually has a single function and that home items with sub-items are uncommon, though exceptions can exist if there’s a good reason. It does not address SEO directly.

So the closest supported guidance is: having a Home navigation item is normal, and the evidence does not indicate it is negative for SEO.

If search engines find the external product pages, users from search will be directed to those product pages, not your home page.

Hiding product names on the front page with CSS just to get them indexed is not a good idea; that can be treated as cloaking and may hurt SEO.

The safest approach is to use a slider/carousel that works at any resolution and serves the same content to users and search engines, rather than loading different content based on device detection. Also, viewport width is a better basis than device detection.

No. The evidence says search engines generally ignore extra whitespace in HTML, and it doesn’t hurt rankings either way.

It also notes that the only related concern is deceptive hidden text techniques that use lots of blank lines to hide content in source, but normal tabs, spaces, and line breaks are not a SEO problem.

For SEO, the important thing is that Googlebot can fetch the image. The guidance here is to always URL-encode your references/links so they’re standards-compliant and don’t break requests. Google can decode URL-encoded references, so encoding image filenames in the URL is fine.

The source doesn’t say anything specific about keyword-rich filenames for SEO, only that the URL should be valid and accessible.

Choose one domain and redirect the other to it with a 301. The example shown redirects non-www to www, but it uses `http://www.yoursite.com/$1`, which does not preserve the original protocol.

To preserve protocol, the redirect needs to use the incoming scheme rather than hard-coding `http://`. The evidence doesn’t provide the exact Apache rule for that, but it does support using a 301 redirect for consistency and choosing one canonical domain.

Adding .html does not improve SEO by itself. There’s no ranking benefit just from changing a URL from /answer/my-question-no-1 to /answer/my-question-no-1.html.

If your site already serves pages dynamically, adding .html may only introduce extra rewriting/processing, which could be unnecessary. The closest guidance supported here is: keep the cleaner URL unless you have another technical reason to use the extension.

From the evidence, Google is not treating .html and .php differently here. The issue is duplicate URLs, not the file extension itself.

The guidance shown says that using a 301 redirect from the old URL to the preferred URL, and also adding a canonical tag, is effective for preventing Google from treating both as separate pages.

So the closest supported answer is: Google cares about which URL is canonical and whether redirects point to it, not whether it ends in .html or .php.

Google does not appear to treat .html pages differently from .php pages anymore. The guidance here says that, while .html used to be considered better than a URL like index.php?module=test&param=1, that is not believed to be true for Google now.

What still matters is avoiding duplicate or very similar pages. If two URLs show nearly the same content, use rel="canonical" so Google knows which version is the main one; otherwise ranking signals may be split.

No evidence here says a .html extension itself helps SEO. What it does show is that changing a live page’s extension changes the URL, which can make search engines treat it like a new page, and can lose links/bookmarks unless you set up 301 redirects. So the supported guidance is: the extension doesn’t appear to give an SEO benefit by itself; keeping URLs stable matters more. If you do change from one extension to another, use 301 redirects so search engines and users are sent to the new URL.

No. The answer says Google does not treat a blog post page differently from other content pages just because it’s a blog or HTML. It suggests the faster indexing may have happened because the post was fresh, got more internal links, was pinged through a blog/search service, or Google happened to crawl and update its index quickly. You can’t make a dynamic residential connection truly static by assigning the router an IP. If the new site is essentially the same and you keep the same domain, the evidence doesn’t show a clear SEO problem. It only says that changing domain, HTML, and internal linking can risk rankings, and that 301 redirects help when URLs change.

For a one-page web app, SEO is limited because search engines need crawlable URLs and content they can access by links. The guidance here says the key is not whether content comes from static pages or a database, but that every important page can be reached by following links on your site.

For a one-page app, that means you’d need to expose content in linkable sections or, better, provide separate URLs for important content if you want them indexed. To help search engines, add an HTML sitemap for key links and/or an XML sitemap at sitemap.xml in the site root. An XML sitemap lists your page URLs in the proper format so crawlers can find them.

If you want to “change the static IP address to a domain name,” the closest guidance is to use DNS: point the domain name to the server’s IP address, and update the DNS record if the IP changes.

A domain name is usually better than relying on a static IP because:
- it’s easier to remember,
- it can be updated without changing links when the server IP changes,
- a site may not even be hosted at the root of its IP address.

If you need direct access by IP, that may work only for the host root, not necessarily the specific website.

Google may be indexing a different version of your site than the one you added in Webmaster Tools. The guidance here is to register all four variations:

http://domain-name.com/
http://www.domain-name.com/
https://domain-name.com/
https://www.domain-name.com/

Then check which version Google is actually indexing. Since you changed from https no-www to https www, Google may still be seeing the old or another variant. If Google and Bing/Yahoo differ, this may be a version/canonicalization issue rather than a general indexing problem.

It may come back, but it can take time. Bing is known to refresh and update old pages slowly, and Yahoo results come from Bing. Being indexed and ranking well in Google does not mean the site will rank or even appear the same way in Bing/Yahoo.

The closest check supported here is to search for your site with site:yoursite.com in Bing to confirm whether the pages are actually indexed there. If they are not indexed, the issue is not just ranking.

Use a meta robots tag like:

This lets Google crawl the page and follow its links, but not show the page itself in search results. If your pages still aren’t indexed as expected, the only supported guidance here is that this tag controls indexing/display, not other indexing issues.

Add some text-heavy pages describing the site, its structure, and the subject matter, since search engines rely heavily on text. Creating articles about the site’s topic can also help, especially if they attract links and interest. Search engines need something textual to understand and latch onto, not just images.

For redirecting users to a new site, the best guidance supported here is to use a custom routing system and a CMS so the URL structure can be decoupled from the internal file structure. Think about:

- common user scenarios

When the new site is ready, set a 301 redirect from old-domain.com to new-domain.com, and optionally create page-specific redirects from old URLs to the matching new pages.

The suggested 301 to new-domain.com followed by a 302 to new-domain.com/old/ is not a good idea, because it can create indexed traffic to /old/ that you’ll need to clean up later.

A likely reason is that the site is new and many pages look low-quality or mostly unoriginal, with only a title and one-line description on most pages. Google may crawl such sites but index only a small portion.

Google may be crawling the site, but new pages can still take time to appear in search results. Search ranking also depends partly on page content and links from other sites.

Changing hosting itself should not affect SEO or page ranking. The main thing is to minimize downtime and make the transition as seamless as possible. Very slow loading can hurt rankings, but only in extreme cases.

- some link equity loss from 301s
- temporary ranking fluctuation while redirects are processed
- possible ranking impact from changed HTML/markup

If you want both URLs to work, the rewrite rule needs to match the trailing slash too, or not require the end-of-string immediately.

Examples that accept both:

RewriteRule ^first-page(/)?$ /subdir/page.php?id_page=1 [QSA,L]
RewriteRule ^second-page(/)?$ /subdir/page.php?id_page=2 [QSA,L]
RewriteRule ^third-page(/)?$ /subdir/page.php?id_page=161 [QSA,L]

Or you can make the slash part of the rule:

RewriteRule ^first-page/$ /subdir/page.php?id_page=1 [QSA,L]

The first form is the closest fit if you do not want `.../first-page` to 404.

A leading slash in a link means the path starts at the site’s top level, not from the current page’s directory. So `/somedir/somepage.html` goes to `www.mysite.com/somedir/somepage.html`.

If you leave off the leading slash, the link is relative to the current directory, so on `/cream-cakes/`, `blah.html` becomes `/cream-cakes/blah.html`.

Using `/` is usually safer if you want the link to keep working when the site structure changes.

To force internal links to use a full URL, the same general approach applies: add a redirect rule that sends the non-preferred form to the preferred one.

For example, if you want all requests to end up as HTTPS with www:

RewriteCond %{HTTP_HOST} ^example\.com$ [OR]
RewriteCond %{HTTPS} !on
RewriteRule ^(.*)$ https://www.example.com/$1 [R,L]

This will redirect http://example.com, http://www.example.com, and https://example.com to https://www.example.com in one step. If your site has other subdomains, keep the host check as shown.

For database-driven sites, Google bots generally crawl the page URLs your site exposes, not the database itself. The important part is that each page you want indexed has its own unique URL and returns crawlable HTML content.

Google’s bot downloads pages from the site from time to time, but it does not understand dynamic content loaded only by Ajax. So content should be generated into the HTML response, not added only after load.

A good pattern is unique URLs like `http://example.com/thread?id=101` rather than one root page with changing widgets.

To keep a site under construction from being indexed, the supported approach here is to use robots meta tags on the pages themselves.

Allow the main page to be indexed:
<meta name="Robots" content="INDEX, FOLLOW" />

Block the other pages:

Only a 301 redirect from an established, already indexed domain with backlinks may pass some SEO value.

So based on this, the bounce rate on the redirected domain is not something we can say helps you. The closer supported takeaway is that the redirect itself is unlikely to improve SEO unless it’s a proper 301 from a strong existing domain.

A lot of bouncing itself isn’t described as harmful here. The closest guidance says that when URLs are moved properly and redirected, the SEO impact should settle back to normal after about a month, though rankings may fluctuate during that period. It also suggests that if the change improves page speed, that’s generally beneficial for search engines. So the main concern covered is temporary fluctuation after the redirect, not the bounce rate itself.

If both HTTP and HTTPS versions of the same pages are accessible, search engines may treat them as duplicate or very similar content and filter some out of results rather than penalizing the site.

The supported fix is to use one canonical version of each page and have the other version point to it, or make the site consistently accessible on only one preferred URL format. That way, the two versions do not compete in search results.

Google may have indexed the page, but still not rank it for any search terms if it doesn’t consider it relevant. Even when pages are in your XML sitemap and you’ve followed recommended steps, Google doesn’t always index or surface every page.

The best next checks are:
- crawl errors
- robots.txt rules
- whether Google can read the page correctly

Use Search Console/Webmaster Tools to see whether anything is blocking the page and to test how Google sees it. You can also manually submit it for indexing, but Google still decides whether to index and show it.

No, not by itself. HTTPS pages are not automatically considered duplicate content just because they share common site-wide elements like the logo, company name, date, slogan, or navigation menu. The supported guidance is to make sure the rest of each page’s content is unique. If your HTTPS pages differ only by these common elements, that would not normally be a duplicate-content issue.

Multiple results from a site search are not, by themselves, considered duplicate content. Repeated site-wide elements like a logo, company name, date, slideshow, slogan, and navigation menu are generally not treated as duplicate content in a way that would trigger a penalty.

The key is that the main content on each page should be unique. The only part called out for extra care was a slideshow if it is heavily text-based or not very complex; a practical suggestion was to put the slideshow in an iframe with a canonical link.

This does not directly address HTTPS pages specifically, but it supports the idea that shared site-wide content alone is not usually the issue.

Mass different log-in pages by themselves are not supported here as causing duplicate-content or low-quality penalties, provided the main content on each page is genuinely unique. Common repeated elements like logos, company names, slogans, and navigation menus are not normally treated as a duplicate-content issue. The closest guidance supported is to keep the unique parts of each page truly distinct, and avoid trying to make pages seem unique by only changing minor items like company name or menu options.

Duplicate content is when multiple URLs show the same or very similar page content. In the evidence, the issue is described as a concern when the URL changes but the content appears the same.

What it affects negatively is not specified. The closest supported guidance is that it can be a search-engine concern if different URLs are treated as separate pages.

Enforcing HTTPS site-wide does not by itself create a duplicate-content issue in the guidance provided. If you are moving from HTTP to HTTPS, focus on making HTTPS the canonical version and keeping page content consistent and unique. The evidence here does not give specific SSL migration steps, but it does not suggest changing shared site-wide elements just to avoid duplicate content.

Enforcing https site-wide should not create a duplicate-content penalty by itself. Common repeated elements across pages, like the logo, company name, date, slogan, and navigation menu, are not normally treated as duplicate-content penalties.

The safest approach is to make sure the main content on each page remains unique. Don’t change the company name or menu just to try to force uniqueness.

If you have a text-heavy slideshow that appears on many pages, that is the one area that might be questionable, especially if it is very simple and loaded via JavaScript.

Use a canonical link to point search engines to the preferred URL. The provided guidance doesn’t cover the full HTTPS migration process, but it does support choosing one preferred URL and using canonical linking to avoid duplication. Common repeated elements like your logo, navigation, and dates normally do not cause a penalty.

The supported guidance is that duplicate access by another domain does not imply a permanent duplicate-content penalty. Search engines may choose one URL to index over another, and duplication can slow crawling or delay updates.

For an HTTPS site-wide move, the closest supported advice is to remove or fix duplicate URLs so search engines can pick the right version. In practice, that means making the HTTPS URL the preferred one and eliminating alternate accessible versions. Forcing HTTPS site wide is not described here as a duplicate-content penalty risk by itself. The guidance only says duplicate content is usually substantial repeated content that makes it hard for search engines to choose which version to index.

If the same content can be reached through more than one URL, the closest supported fix mentioned is to use a canonical link to point search engines to one preferred version. Also keep the main page content unique from page to page.

Common repeated elements like logos, dates, and navigation menus would not normally trigger a penalty.

If the site is accessible at both HTTP and HTTPS, search engines may treat those pages as duplicates. The supported ways to handle it are:

- Put rel=canonical on each duplicate page so it points to the preferred version.
- If you don’t want one version indexed, use robots meta NOINDEX,FOLLOW on the duplicate pages.
- Best practice is to make one version the only meaningful, indexed version.

The guidance does not say there is an automatic penalty; it says duplicate-content issues can arise and should be handled.

If enforcing https creates two URLs that show almost the same content, they can be treated as near-duplicate content and hurt SEO. The safest approach is to choose one preferred URL and use rel="canonical" on the other page(s) pointing to it. That applies whether the duplicate is from http/https or other URL variants.

The provided guidance does not cover every part of a site-wide SSL migration, but it does support using a single preferred HTTPS URL and canonicalizing the non-preferred versions.

To minimize duplicate-content concerns when switching a site to HTTPS site-wide, focus on keeping the main body content on each page unique. Repeated site-wide elements like the logo, company name, slogan, date, and navigation are normally not the issue and don’t need to be changed just to “fix” duplication.

If any pages use simple, text-heavy slideshows or content that’s crawled from JavaScript, that part may deserve closer review.

The supported guidance here is to make the substantive content on each page distinct, while allowing normal template elements to remain repeated.

Site-wide repeated elements like the logo, company name, date, slogan, and navigation menu are not normally treated as duplicate-content problems. The main thing to keep unique is the primary content on each page. 

For enforcing https across an existing site, the supported guidance here is to avoid changing site-wide text just to “make pages unique.” Instead, keep the page content unique and focus on the main content area. 

The only part that may be questionable from the evidence is a text-heavy slideshow, especially if it is simple and crawled from JavaScript.

If forcing https creates both http and https versions of the same pages, search engines can treat that as duplicate content. The supported way to handle it is to keep only one version indexable and point the duplicates to the preferred version.

Use rel=canonical to the https URL on pages that can be reached in both versions, or use noindex,follow on the duplicate version if you want it excluded from the index. Also make sure the site is consistently using one version sitewide.

The provided guidance does not show an automatic SEO penalty or “punishment”; it only supports that duplicate pages can cause indexing and duplicate-content issues unless managed.

You can’t objectively “control” ranking from the information provided, but you can monitor it with Google Webmaster Tools/Search Console. Enforcing HTTPS site-wide is not described here as causing a permanent duplicate-content penalty. The main concern is that search engines may pick one URL over another, and duplicate versions can slow crawling or delay updates.

Google can index a page without showing it for any search terms if it doesn’t consider the page relevant enough. This can happen even when the page is in your XML sitemap.

If HTTPS enforcement creates multiple URLs for the same content, the main risk is duplicate content: the same content available at more than one URL. To reduce the issue, make sure each page has one preferred URL and avoid exposing the same content on multiple login or page variants. If the same content must exist at different URLs, keep the duplicates to a minimum and ensure the site consistently uses the secure version.

If switching an existing site to HTTPS creates multiple URLs with the same or very similar content, that can hurt SEO because they may be treated as near-duplicate pages. The safest supported approach is to choose one preferred URL version and use rel="canonical" on the others pointing to it.

For a site-wide SSL move, the closest guidance this supports is to consolidate to a single preferred HTTPS URL format and canonicalize alternate versions so search engines understand which page should rank. Forcing HTTPS site wide is not, by itself, a duplicate-content problem in the same sense as repeated page content. - Keep each page’s main content unique.

The only potentially questionable item mentioned is a text-heavy slideshow that is very simple and only crawled from JavaScript.

When enforcing HTTPS site wide, the main thing is to make sure the same content is not accessible on multiple URLs. Since search engines index by URL, duplicate content is mainly a concern when both HTTP and HTTPS versions remain available.

The closest guidance here is to use HTTPS consistently and avoid leaving both versions accessible. That means redirecting HTTP to HTTPS so only one URL version is indexed.

This does not indicate a normal SEO penalty for repeated content on the same page, like menus or layout elements.

If you’re worried about HTTPS pages duplicating content, the closest supported advice is to make sure the main content on each page is unique and not to change common repeated elements just to make pages look different. Generally, avoid dashes in a domain name because they can make it harder to say, spell, and remember. If the unhyphenated version could be confusing or misread, a dash can improve readability and may be worth keeping. So the best choice depends on whether the dash helps clarity or makes the domain less user-friendly.

If you mean the domain name itself, it’s best to avoid dashes unless they improve clarity or help prevent confusion. Hyphens are fine in a path or page slug, but they add unnecessary noise in a domain name. If you meant the URL path rather than the domain, hyphens are preferred over slashes for SEO.

The evidence only supports that a hyphen-heavy exact-match domain may not get an exact-match keyword benefit, which could affect rankings. It does not show a blacklist issue or prove the domain is the cause of the drop.

So, if your webpage rankings are down on a single phrase, the closest supported explanation is that the domain may be one possible factor, especially if the phrase matches the domain closely. Changing the domain might help reduce dependence on exact-match effects, but it is not clearly required and may not fix the issue by itself.

A likely reason is that the site may not have been fully indexed yet, or Google’s indexing and ranking just take time even when the keywords are on the page. The supported next steps are to wait a bit longer and try getting the site listed in reputable web directories with good page rank.

This doesn’t cover every possible reason rankings can drop, but those are the closest actions supported here.

A site can be crawled and indexed yet still rank low or drop in rank. The supported explanation is that ranking can lag, especially if the site is new or competing against stronger sites. If indexing is fine, the issue is more likely ranking strength than crawl or index problems.

The best-supported steps are to keep working on SEO, improve the site over time, and build legitimate visibility and backlinks gradually.

First verify whether your pages are still indexed by searching site:yourdomain.com. If they are, the issue may be a ranking fluctuation rather than full removal from search. A likely explanation is that the pages may still be indexed but are ranking poorly right now. First, check whether they’re still in the index by searching site:yourdomain.com.

So the closest guidance is: verify index status first, then wait and monitor if the pages are still indexed.

The evidence only supports that backlinks are not required for Google to index pages, and that lack of backlinks alone does not explain non-indexing. You can’t choose or directly control which Google sitelinks are shown for your website. Google generates sitelinks automatically, so you can’t force them for specific searches. For different search queries, Google decides separately whether to show sitelinks.

So, based on this, crosslinking itself is not shown to be the reason for a decline. If you want to reduce passing link value, using rel="nofollow" would prevent that.

You generally can’t directly choose or force the Google sitelinks that appear for your website. Google decides whether to show them, and they can change over time. The best-supported way to influence them is to keep adding quality content and make your site navigation easy to understand with semantic HTML, such as a nav element or a nav/navigation id for the menu. Avoid using JavaScript for links and menus. If you already have sitelinks, Google Webmaster Tools may let you control which links appear.

There’s no evidence here that a hyphenated exact-match domain should be changed just because of a Panda-related issue or because it’s not .com.

So, based on this, I wouldn’t change it solely on that basis. If your main concern is SEO, the closest supported guidance is that a cleaner, non-hyphenated exact-match domain may have a small advantage.

For database-generated content, make each item available at a unique, crawlable URL rather than hiding it on one page and switching it with parameters if possible. There isn’t support here for marking just one inline section of the same page as “do not index,” so the iframe workaround is the closest guidance available.

To move hosting to GoDaddy while keeping the domain registration unchanged, change the domain’s nameservers in your GoDaddy account. Go to Domains > Manage My Domains, select the domain, then use the Nameservers dropdown, choose “Set name server,” and select “Standard.”

For SEO- and user-friendly URLs, use clean, human-readable paths like `/blog/how-to-train-a-puppy` or `/category/dog-training`. Keep them short, ideally 10 words or fewer, and make them match the page title/content. Avoid keyword stuffing.

Compared with query parameters, these friendly URLs are the better-supported choice because they’re clearer and less spammy-looking. The evidence here doesn’t say query parameters are always bad, only that clean paths are the preferred approach for posts and categories when you want readability and SEO friendliness.

SEO-friendly URLs are helpful, but they are not the most important SEO factor.

The supported guidance says clean, short, readable, semantic URLs like mysite.com/category-name/page-name are preferred over cluttered ones with IDs or extra parameters when possible. They are more user-friendly and described as the most SEO-friendly URL style here.

That said, the URL itself matters less than the page’s content, titles, meta descriptions, and clean markup. So yes, SEO-friendly URLs are important, but mainly as a supporting factor rather than the main driver of SEO.

SEO-friendly URLs appear to matter in the sense that cleaner path-style URLs are generally more SEO-friendly and user-friendly than query-string URLs. The material supports using readable paths like domain.com/x/y/z/t and, if needed, URL rewriting to hide internal query parameters.

It does not quantify how important they are overall, and it does not say whether +, _, or - is best for SEO. The closest supported guidance is to use clean, readable path segments rather than query strings.

SEO-friendly URLs are important for clarity and usability, and they’re also the preferred option for SEO in the supported guidance here. The best approach is to use short, human-readable URLs that match the page content or title, ideally 10 words or fewer, and avoid keyword stuffing.

Examples:
- `/blog/how-to-train-a-puppy`
- `/category/dog-training`

These are better than query-parameter URLs when you want links to look clearer and less spammy. Query parameters can still be useful in some cases, but the supported guidance mainly favors friendly, meaningful URLs.

Friendly URLs are generally preferable because shorter, simpler URLs with fewer path segments are better for users and tend to be easier to read. Pages closer to the root may also get more prominence.

Query parameters like ?page=something are not identified as inherently bad for SEO, and they are not described as a direct SEO problem. The guidance only supports that simpler URLs are generally better.

So, the supported tradeoff is:
- Friendly URLs: better readability and generally preferred structure
- Query parameters: acceptable, but not as clean or simple

This does not provide a full pro/con comparison beyond that.

Friendly URLs are generally better when you want short, readable, semantic links that users can understand easily, like mysite.com/category-name/page-name. They’re helpful for usability and can support SEO a bit, but they are not the main SEO factor.

Query parameters are not directly covered in the evidence, but the closest guidance is to avoid IDs and extra clutter when possible. So, compared with friendly URLs, query-parameter URLs are usually less clean and less readable.

The main tradeoff supported here is: favor clean, semantic URLs for clarity, and don’t expect URL format alone to outweigh content quality, titles, meta descriptions, and clean markup.

To keep search engines from indexing specific content, the supported approach is to put that content in an iframe and block the iframe URL in robots.txt. That lets the rest of the page be indexed while the iframe content is not.

There isn’t support here for hiding just one inline section of the same page with robots.txt. If your goal is to hide a whole site or page, the closest guidance available from this is to separate the content you want excluded and block that URL.

Using URL parameters is not described as inherently “bad” for SEO here, but the supported guidance favors clean, friendly URLs when possible. Short, readable, semantic URLs like mysite.com/category-name/page-name are presented as the most SEO-friendly style. URLs with IDs or extra clutter are less preferable because they are less user-friendly and less readable. The evidence also says the URL text matters, but content, titles, meta descriptions, and clean markup matter much more than URL style alone. So: parameters are not ruled out, but clean paths are preferred for SEO and usability.

Using URL parameters is not necessarily “bad,” but parameter-heavy URLs are generally less SEO-friendly than friendly, path-style URLs.

Friendly URLs are preferred because they’re cleaner, easier to read and remember, and a better fit for SEO. Query parameters are useful when you need flexibility or dynamic values, but they’re less readable and generally less SEO-friendly.

If you want both benefits, URL rewriting can make the URL look clean while still handling parameters internally.

The supported approach here is only to hide a separate content section by putting it in an iframe and blocking the iframe URL in robots.txt. That can prevent that separate content from being indexed while the rest of the page can still be indexed.

This does not cover hiding just one inline section of the same page with robots.txt, and it also doesn’t provide instructions for hiding an entire website from search engines.

A good approach is to combine validation, CAPTCHA, math checks, and server-side checks to stop automated spam. A client-side timer can also help: require the visitor to stay on the page for a set time, like 1 minute, before the submit button becomes active. That can block quick cut-and-paste submissions and some semi-automated spam.

It won’t stop all manual spam, so it’s best used as a filter rather than a complete fix.

The supported approach here is to separate the content into an iframe and block the iframe URL in robots.txt. That can keep search engines from indexing that content while still allowing the rest of the page to be indexed.

There isn’t support here for marking just one inline section of the same page as “do not index.” So if you want to prevent crawling/indexing of specific content, the iframe workaround is the closest guidance available.

For SEO and usability, keep URLs reasonably short, clear, and readable, ideally under 100 characters. URL length itself is not likely to affect SEO or page load speed in any meaningful way. The main gain is user experience, not speed. So if you have short-lived URLs, the closest supported guidance is to make them concise and understandable rather than trying to extend them for SEO value.

A practical approach is to use a spam-filtering plugin such as Akismet, or block/filter comments that contain .ru links. If the spam includes hotlinked .ru images, .htaccess won’t stop those requests because they don’t come from your server.

This should help stop the spam source and comment handling, but it won’t address any ranking drop directly.

A good supported approach is a client-side timer that prevents submission until the visitor has been on the page for a while, such as 1 minute. That can help block quick cut-and-paste and semi-automated comment spam.

More generally, spam is hard to eliminate completely. Basic validation, CAPTCHA, and server-side checks can still be bypassed by a person, so a layered approach is best. No single filter will stop everything.

A good way is to add friction before links can be posted. For example, require a minimum post count before users can post links, and restrict profile permissions so users with fewer than 5 posts can’t add URLs.

You can also use a waiting period plus a minimum number of prior posts before link posting is allowed, or set a daily post limit just below the number needed to start posting links.

These measures tend to discourage spammers because they usually avoid multi-step requirements.

A good remaining option is to use a plugin like Cyb that requires a minimum post count before users can post links. You can also pair that with restricted profile permissions so users with fewer than 5 posts can’t add URLs in their profile.

Other measures that may help are:
- a waiting period plus a minimum number of prior posts before link posting is allowed

To fix it, remove the duplicate pages/content from the other domain or make sure only one version is publicly available. It doesn’t matter whether the pages are static or generated from a database. What matters is that search engines can reach them by following links on your site.

With 1M articles, putting every URL in a menu is not practical, but you can still help crawling by using an HTML sitemap and/or an XML sitemap. Save sitemap.xml in the root of your site and include the page URLs there.

More pages in one site are not automatically better for SEO; the key is that the pages are accessible and useful.

Adding your other site in an iframe won’t help its rankings. The content in the iframe is generally invisible to search engines, so there’s no SEO benefit from that setup. It could also be viewed as an attempt to manipulate search results.

If the second site’s rankings are dropping, the more likely cause is low-quality content or another quality issue on that site, not the iframe. The useful next step is to review the content and improve its quality.

Google can show extra site-specific links if it can crawl and index those URLs. Backlinks from other sites are usually positive, but if they come from spammy or harmful sites they can be part of negative SEO and may hurt rankings. A hidden iframe on your page is also a bad sign, because the evidence mentions “hiding bad content or links in your site” as a negative SEO technique and says to protect against XSS attacks.

So: many backlinks can be good, but backlinks tied to hidden iframe/spam can have a negative impact.

If the spam is manual, it’s hard to eliminate completely. Captcha, validation, and server-side checks may stop automated spam, but someone can still pay a person to fill out forms.

Use community moderation: let and encourage members to flag spam, since human spammers can get through registration defenses. Also limit what new users can do until they’ve built trust, such as requiring multiple posts before they can add links in profiles or posts, and capping how many links new users can post per day. Automated tools help more with bots, but user moderation is the most effective way to catch human spam accounts.

The guidance here doesn’t specifically cover HTTPS duplicate-content cases. It does say that very similar pages across domains or subdomains can be treated as duplicate content, and the likely result is that some pages may be filtered from search results rather than triggering a spam penalty.

Google does not appear to penalize a site just for duplicate content on multiple URLs within the same site. When you enforce https site wide, the main issue is usually that Google may pick one version of a page to show instead of the one you prefer.

The closest guidance supported here is to:
- use redirects so only the https version is reachable
- add rel=canonical to indicate the preferred URL
- update strong internal links to point to the https version

This doesn’t specifically cover SSL migrations, but it does suggest the duplication itself is generally not a penalty issue; the key is clearly signaling the preferred https URL.

Site-wide HTTPS itself is unlikely to create duplicate-content SEO problems in the way copied pages do. Search engines usually filter duplicate pages so the same content doesn’t appear multiple times.

If you do see ranking changes after moving to HTTPS, the evidence only supports that the cause may be something else, since many factors can affect rankings. The best-supported approach is to make sure the HTTPS version is the one you want indexed and that the site migration is implemented consistently.

If the HTTPS version and the HTTP version both remain accessible, search engines may treat them as duplicate content unless you prevent both from being indexed.

The supported approach is to choose one version as the main one and apply rel=canonical on each duplicate page to point to the matching preferred URL. If you want the nonpreferred version kept out of the index, use noindex,follow on those duplicate pages.

The evidence does not cover SSL migrations specifically, but it does support avoiding indexing both copies rather than expecting an automatic penalty.
